title: LIPPS Learn — University-readiness QA
text:
Version audited: v1.7
Scope: Epidemiology Weeks 1–12; Health Communication Weeks 1–12; public Quarto lessons; Moodle GIFT banks; course and assessment pages.


The LIPPS Learn architecture is strong enough for a university pilot, but the two courses are not yet ready to be sold as validated, stand-alone high-stakes courseware.
The strongest elements are the course sequence, applied public-health framing, clear weekly learning cycle, causal/interpretive restraint in Epidemiology, and the unusually strong treatment of risk communication, community engagement, infodemics, ethics and equity in Health Communication.
The main weakness is assessment validity. The existing Moodle banks are large, but item count should not be mistaken for assessment quality. Many Health Communication items are three paraphrased recognition questions built around the same definition; many Epidemiology items are repeated numerical variants of the same calculation template. These are useful practice generators, but a university-facing mastery bank must contain a much larger proportion of genuinely new scenarios, interpretation problems and decision questions.
A second weakness is constructive alignment. Weekly objective quizzes alone cannot adequately assess skills such as audience analysis, counselling, message design, community engagement, campaign planning, outbreak reasoning or critical appraisal. Both courses need authentic assessed products alongside quizzes.

The sequence from epidemiological thinking → frequency → association → description → study design → bias/causal reasoning → diagnostic testing → surveillance/outbreak → critical appraisal is coherent.
Weeks 1–3 are particularly rich and explanatory.
The course distinguishes what the attached CDC source supports from later LIPPS extensions.
Week 9 correctly separates confounding, mediation, collider bias and effect modification.
Week 10 avoids the common error of treating sensitivity, specificity and predictive value as interchangeable.
Week 12 gives the course an appropriate interpretive endpoint rather than ending with formula recall.





Assessment repetition: large blocks of parameterised items test the same operation repeatedly. Keep some as practice, but mastery banks should sample different reasoning steps.
Infectious-disease foundations: natural history, agent–host–environment reasoning and chain-of-infection concepts are underrepresented for a broad introductory epidemiology course. Add them as a concise supplement or embed them in Week 11.
Standardisation: age adjustment is introduced but not practised deeply. A short applied exercise would improve population-comparison competence.
Sampling: Week 5 introduces sampling logic, but probability sampling, cluster effects and weighting should link more explicitly to the Methods library.
Authentic outputs: add a short study-design critique, outbreak-analysis exercise and final critical-appraisal memo.
Assessment timing: current timings must remain pilot values until actual response-time data are available.





The course does not reduce communication to posters and media products; it treats communication as a decision and implementation process.
Behavioural theory is linked to diagnosis rather than added decoratively after campaign design.
Health literacy, culture, interpersonal communication and community engagement appear before channels and media strategy.
Risk/crisis communication and infodemic management are given their own substantial weeks.
Ethics, equity, privacy, AI and manipulation are integrated rather than treated as footnotes.
The LIPPS SIGNAL framework creates a useful capstone planning structure.





Depth: most weeks are around 1,000–1,300 words. For stand-alone digital courseware, add deeper explanations, comparative tables, worked communication products and assigned readings.
Question bank redesign: the largest current weakness. Many items repeat the same definition in three forms (definition → context label → term recognition). These should be reclassified as practice flash questions, not mastery assessment.
Performance assessment: health communication competence cannot be established using MCQs alone. Students should design, pre-test, revise and evaluate actual communication products.
Theory week overload: Week 2 covers HBM, TPB, Social Cognitive Theory, social-ecological thinking, COM-B and diffusion. Retain the overview, but add a comparison matrix and make students justify theory selection in a case.
Clinical communication: Week 4 needs an assessed teach-back or counselling transcript/role-play task.
Community engagement: Week 5 should assess stakeholder mapping, listening and feedback-loop design.
Media strategy: Week 7 should include a channel-mix budget or reach/frequency trade-off exercise.
Digital communication: Week 8 should distinguish platform engagement metrics from meaningful communication and health outcomes using a worked dashboard example.
Referencing: add a stable core-reading page and week-specific readings.




The Health Communication sequence is broadly consistent with current public-health communication practice. WHO’s communication framework emphasizes communications that are accessible, actionable, credible, relevant, timely and understandable. WHO’s 2024 RCCE competency framework emphasizes professional behavioural competencies for community-centred emergency programmes. CDC’s Clear Communication Index provides a research-based tool for assessing public communication materials, while the current CDC CERC manual remains a practical emergency-communication reference. These should be treated as core benchmarks, not as the only evidence base.
The attached CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition remains a strong foundational source for the Epidemiology course, but it is an older introductory text. LIPPS should retain it as a foundation while clearly identifying modern extensions and updating applied examples and methodological guidance.






15% — weekly mastery quizzes: objective, randomised, mostly interpretation/application.
20% — applied measurement exercises: frequency, association, diagnostic testing and descriptive epidemiology.
20% — study-design critique: critique one published or simulated epidemiological study.
20% — field/outbreak analysis: line list, descriptive output, hypothesis and investigation plan.
25% — final critical-appraisal memo: interpret design, effect estimates, bias, precision, applicability and claim strength.





15% — weekly mastery quizzes: objective checks, but no longer dominated by term recognition.
20% — audience and behaviour diagnosis brief: define audience, determinant and theory-informed response.
20% — message design + pre-test assignment: draft, pre-test evidence, revision rationale.
15% — risk-communication simulation: first announcement, uncertainty statement, action message and update.
30% — campaign capstone: strategy, channel mix, community feedback, implementation indicators, outcome evaluation and ethics/equity review using LIPPS SIGNAL.

These weights are a proposed pilot blueprint and should be adapted to institutional regulations.




Do not delete the current banks. Reclassify them:

Foundation/practice pool: definition checks and repeated calculations.
Mastery pool: genuine scenarios, interpretation, comparison and decision-making.
Institutional assessment pool: separately reviewed, exposure-controlled items with documented blueprint coverage.

A sensible target for the next revision is 25–35 high-quality mastery items per week, not 50 superficially different items. Smaller, better banks are preferable to large templated banks.



LIPPS should not describe either course as high-stakes-ready until all of the following are complete:

second subject-matter-expert review;
explicit course assessment blueprint;
authentic assignments and rubrics;
mastery-bank rewrite;
accessibility review;
native Quarto render and browser/mobile testing;
Moodle import test on the actual hosted instance;
student pilot;
item analysis after pilot;
revision based on completion, difficulty, discrimination and response-time data; and
local curriculum/credit-hour mapping by the adopting institution.




Proceed to pilot. Do not market the current version as a finished high-stakes assessment product.
The curriculum is strong enough to justify a real university pilot. The next build priority is not more content categories; it is assessment quality, authentic student work, references/readings and pilot evidence.



Health Communication Week 1 has now been rebuilt against the recommended assessment standard: 30 distinct scenario-based items in Practice, Mastery and protected Institutional pools, plus an authentic Communication Diagnosis Brief and analytic rubric. Weeks 2–12 remain queued for the same overhaul.

title: About
text:
LIPPS takes inspiration from the Signor–Lipps effect in palaeontology: an incomplete observed record can misrepresent the timing or pattern of what actually occurred.
Research faces the same underlying challenge. Samples are partial. Measurements contain error. Records are missing. Models rely on assumptions. Associations can be misread. Context matters.
Evidence is never the whole story.
LIPPS exists to teach people to reason carefully from evidence rather than merely produce outputs.



Teach concepts before software.
Teach methods through real problems.
Make learners interpret rather than merely calculate.
Treat every result as evidence that requires scrutiny.




Add the founder biography, selected professional work, publications, teaching, CV, ORCID and GitHub links here before public launch.

title: Study Design
text:
Choosing a study design means matching a research question, estimand, source population, feasible data-collection process and threat-to-validity profile.



Cross-sectional studies
Case-control studies
Cohort studies
Randomised controlled trials
Quasi-experimental designs
Before-and-after studies
Interrupted time-series studies
Ecological studies
Diagnostic-accuracy studies
Implementation research designs
Operational research
Programme evaluation designs


What could fool us?
A sophisticated analysis cannot rescue a design that cannot answer the stated question. LIPPS therefore treats causal language—effect, impact, outcome, attributable to—as a design decision, not a writing preference.

title: Survey Analysis Strategies
text:
Survey analysis should begin by reconstructing how the observations entered the dataset. The sampling design determines the weights, dependence structure, variance estimation and often the appropriate modelling strategy.


Define the target population and estimand; reconstruct inclusion probabilities; estimate prevalence or means with uncertainty; then analyse associations using methods appropriate to the outcome and design.



Account for within-cluster correlation and the sampling design. Naïve analyses that treat all observations as independent usually understate uncertainty.



Retain the stratification information in estimation and variance calculation. Disproportionate allocation often requires weights.



Track selection probabilities at every stage: primary sampling units, secondary units, households and individuals. Distinguish household-level from person-level estimands.



Clarify whether facilities were sampled or assessed as a census, distinguish facility-level from service- or patient-level denominators, document tracer-indicator construction, and avoid treating composite readiness scores as inherently comparable without validating the scoring model.



Define constructs before scoring them. Avoid arbitrary categorisation of knowledge or attitude scores unless a defensible threshold exists. Assess item behaviour and measurement properties where appropriate.



Document inaccessible areas, population-frame uncertainty, cluster selection, non-response and operational compromises. Avoid reporting precise sub-area rankings when the design was only powered for pooled estimation.

What could fool us?
Ignoring weights, clustering or stratification can produce estimates that look precise while representing the target population poorly—or confidence intervals that are far too narrow.

Move from model output to defensible scientific statements. Separate statistical evidence from causal claims, programme implications and policy recommendations. Connect analyses to relevant reporting standards where appropriate.

The course progresses from foundations → theory → audience → interpersonal/community → message/channel → digital/emergency information environments → campaign evaluation → ethics/capstone.
Every week opens with a realistic problem, teaches concepts, applies them to an integrated scenario, and ends with practice plus a timed mastery specification.
The banks are deliberately larger than the quiz delivered to any student, but the current bank is not yet predominantly scenario-oriented. A substantial proportion consists of repeated concept-recognition templates. These are suitable for practice and retrieval but should not dominate mastery or formal assessment.
Timing is a pilot parameter, not an accessibility restriction. Approved accommodations must remain available.
Copy/paste is not treated as the primary integrity control. Random banks, scenario-based reasoning, shuffled options and short calibrated windows are the main design choices.
Health Communication is not reduced to mass messaging: service barriers, trust, power, community engagement, ethics, accessibility and evaluation are embedded throughout.
Risk communication, RCCE and infodemic management are aligned with current WHO framing.
The final week integrates the course through LIPPS SIGNAL: Situation; Intended audience and insight; Goal; Narrative and needed action; Access; Listen and learn.




The Moodle banks are candidate teaching and pilot-assessment items, not yet psychometrically validated high-stakes exam banks. After student use, analyse item difficulty, discrimination, distractor performance, response times and differential performance before institutional high-stakes deployment.



A deeper audit found that raw item count overstated assessment maturity. Many concepts were represented by three close paraphrases of the same recognition task. Before institutional assessment use, split the bank into foundation/practice, mastery and protected assessment pools and rewrite the latter two toward novel application scenarios. See QA-UNIVERSITY-READINESS.md.



Week 1 is now the benchmark for future bank revision. The previous 48-item recognition-heavy bank was replaced with 30 distinct scenario-based questions mapped to learning outcomes and cognitive demand. It is explicitly separated into Practice, Mastery and protected Institutional pools.
The redesign also adds an 800–1,000 word Communication Diagnosis Brief with a 20-mark analytic rubric. This ensures that Week 1 assesses more than rapid option recognition.
Remaining Weeks 2–12 retain their v1.8 candidate banks and should be rewritten progressively against the Week 1 standard before high-stakes institutional deployment.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: ORIENT · Regression is a language for conditional distributions
text:
ORIENT · Regression is a language for conditional distributions
Regression models summarise how an outcome distribution changes with exposures and covariates. They do not automatically produce causal effects, and the same scientific question may be estimated with several models.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
text:
LEARN 1 · Binary outcomes
Logistic regression models the log odds:
\[\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1A+\beta_2L.\]
It is numerically stable and widely available, but the exponentiated coefficient is an odds ratio. For common outcomes, this may be less intuitive than a risk ratio.
Log-binomial regression models \(\log(p)\) directly but can have convergence problems. Modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors is commonly used to estimate prevalence or risk ratios for binary outcomes, provided interpretation fits the design.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
text:
LEARN 2 · Counts and person-time
Poisson regression is natural for event counts with an exposure-time offset:
\[\log(E[Y])=\beta_0+\beta_1A+\log(person\ time).\]
Exponentiated coefficients are rate ratios. Overdispersion—variance larger than the Poisson mean—can require robust variance or negative-binomial models.
A rate model should not be used simply because person-time appears in the dataset. Confirm that the event process and follow-up structure fit the estimand.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: LEARN 3 · Continuous exposures should not be categorised casually
text:
LEARN 3 · Continuous exposures should not be categorised casually
Splitting age, BMI or blood pressure into arbitrary categories discards information and creates artificial thresholds. Model non-linear relationships using transformations, polynomial terms or restricted cubic splines where appropriate.
Always plot the fitted relationship. A p-value for a linear term can hide meaningful non-linearity.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
text:
LEARN 4 · Interaction and model scale
An interaction term in a logit or log model represents interaction on that model’s scale. Public-health interaction on the additive risk scale may require post-estimation standardisation even when the fitted model is logistic.
Do not equate “product term p<0.05” with evidence of biological interaction.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: LEARN 5 · Prediction is not causal adjustment
text:
LEARN 5 · Prediction is not causal adjustment
A model selected for prediction may include colliders, mediators and proxies that improve predictive accuracy while damaging causal interpretation. Conversely, a causal adjustment model may deliberately include a weak predictor because it blocks confounding.
State whether the goal is prediction, description or causal estimation before selecting variables and performance metrics.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: PHD EXTENSION · Regression as a nuisance model
text:
PHD EXTENSION · Regression as a nuisance model
In modern causal inference, regression may serve as a nuisance model used to estimate components of a causal functional rather than being the scientific estimand itself. This perspective motivates standardisation, doubly robust estimators and targeted learning.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
text:
APPLY
Take a binary outcome from your own research. Write three analysis plans: logistic regression for a conditional odds ratio, modified Poisson for an adjusted risk ratio, and outcome-regression standardisation for a marginal risk difference. Explain which best matches the substantive question.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Build an epidemiological analysis strategy
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Build an epidemiological analysis strategy
A graduate analysis should be planned as a sequence, not as a single final model.

1. Describe the data-generating structure
Identify outcome type, repeated measures, person-time, clusters, sampling weights, censoring and the temporal order of covariates. A binary variable named outcome does not imply logistic regression if it represents repeated events or a fixed-horizon risk derived from time-to-event data.


2. Inspect distributions and coding
Continuous covariates should be plotted before modelling. Check impossible values, heaping, truncation and whether transformations reflect measurement scales. If BMI has a U-shaped relation with outcome, a linear coefficient is inadequate.


3. Decide the estimand and model family
Examples:








Outcome
Common model
Natural effect parameter




Binary risk
logistic
odds ratio


Binary risk
log-binomial / robust Poisson
risk ratio


Count with person-time
Poisson / negative binomial
rate ratio


Continuous
linear / robust alternatives
mean difference


Time to event
Cox
hazard ratio


Repeated binary
GEE / mixed model
population-average / cluster-specific parameter



The model’s natural parameter may still not be the final scientific estimand; post-estimation standardisation can transform it.


4. Functional form
Restricted cubic splines can represent smooth non-linearity without arbitrary categories. Choose knot locations transparently and avoid interpreting each spline coefficient. Plot predicted relationships with uncertainty.
library(splines)
fit <- glm(y ~ a + ns(age, df=4) + sex + severity,
           family=binomial(), data=d)


5. Correlated observations
If patients are nested within facilities, ordinary model standard errors assume independence incorrectly. Options include cluster-robust standard errors, GEE for population-average effects, or mixed models for cluster-specific effects and variance components.
The choice changes interpretation. An odds ratio from a random-intercept logistic model is conditional on the random effect and need not equal a population-average GEE odds ratio.


6. Separation and sparse data
When some exposure-covariate combinations perfectly predict the outcome, logistic maximum likelihood can diverge. Penalised methods such as Firth regression can reduce small-sample bias, but they do not solve lack of causal positivity.


7. Overdispersion
For count models, compare observed variance with the Poisson assumption and inspect residuals. Negative-binomial models introduce an overdispersion parameter. Robust standard errors can correct variance misspecification while retaining the Poisson mean structure.


8. Model selection
Avoid stepwise p-value selection for causal models. For prediction, use cross-validation and penalisation. For causal adjustment, include variables based on the causal structure and use flexible forms where needed. Different goals require different selection principles.


9. Multiple testing
If dozens of exposures or subgroups are explored, false-positive risk rises. Distinguish prespecified analyses from exploratory analyses and consider multiplicity control or hierarchical shrinkage when appropriate.


10. Reporting
Provide enough information for reproducibility: software/version, model family/link, covariate coding, interaction terms, variance estimator, missing-data strategy, diagnostics and post-estimation method.


Doctoral extension · Estimating equations
Many regression estimators can be understood as solutions to estimating equations. This perspective unifies robust variance, GEE and semiparametric estimation and helps distinguish model assumptions about the mean from assumptions about the full data distribution.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Interpretation discipline across model families
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Interpretation discipline across model families
A model should be judged by whether its parameter and predictions answer the scientific question.

Logistic regression
For a common outcome, an odds ratio can appear numerically farther from 1 than the corresponding risk ratio. Never write “twice the risk” when the model estimated an odds ratio of 2 unless a risk estimate was actually derived.


Robust Poisson for binary data
Using a Poisson mean model with robust standard errors can estimate adjusted risk ratios despite binary variance misspecification. The robust variance addresses standard errors, not impossible predicted probabilities. Inspect predicted values and model fit.


Negative binomial models
When event-count variance greatly exceeds the mean, negative binomial regression can model heterogeneity. But if overdispersion is caused by excess zeros, recurrent-event dependence or unmodelled clustering, a negative binomial fit may hide rather than explain structure.


GEE versus mixed models
GEE estimates population-average associations and uses a working correlation structure. Mixed models include random effects and estimate cluster-specific associations. For nonlinear links, population-average and subject-specific effects differ numerically.
Choose based on the scientific question: policy effects across facilities may favour population-average estimands; heterogeneity across facilities may motivate random-effects models.


Robust standard errors are not universal protection
Sandwich estimators can protect standard errors against some model misspecification, but require enough independent clusters or observations. With few clusters, small-sample corrections or randomisation-based methods may be required.


Missing interactions
If treatment effect varies by baseline severity and the outcome model omits treatment-by-severity interaction, standardised treatment effects may be biased even if the main-effects model seems well calibrated overall.


Reporting continuous effects
For nonlinear exposures, report predicted risks or rates at meaningful values rather than a single coefficient. A spline model can be scientifically transparent if accompanied by a plot and clearly defined contrasts.


Avoiding table-one testing
Do not use p-values in baseline tables to decide whether groups are “balanced.” In observational studies, baseline differences are expected; confounding depends on causal relations and effect sizes, not whether a sample difference reaches p<0.05.

title: Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Regression is an estimation tool, not the research question
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Regression is an estimation tool, not the research question
Graduate epidemiology requires fluency with regression models, but methodological maturity begins when the analyst stops treating the model coefficient as automatically equivalent to the epidemiological estimand.

Linear regression
For continuous outcomes, a model such as
\[E(Y\mid A,L)=\beta_0+\beta_1A+\beta_2L\]
may estimate an adjusted mean difference under strong modelling and causal assumptions. Check linearity, residual structure, influential observations and whether an interaction between \(A\) and \(L\) is scientifically expected. Heteroskedasticity affects standard errors even when the mean model is adequate.


Logistic regression
For binary outcomes:
\[\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=\beta_0+\beta_1A+\beta^TL.\]
Exponentiating \(\beta_1\) gives a conditional odds ratio. When outcomes are common, this can differ substantially from a risk ratio. Even without confounding, the adjusted conditional OR may differ from the marginal OR because odds ratios are non-collapsible. For public-health communication, use model predictions to obtain adjusted risks, risk differences or risk ratios when those are the target quantities.


Log-binomial and modified Poisson models
A log link can target risk ratios directly. Log-binomial models can face convergence problems because fitted probabilities are constrained to \([0,1]\). Modified Poisson regression with robust standard errors is widely used to estimate adjusted prevalence or risk ratios for binary outcomes. The mean-variance relationship is deliberately misspecified, so robust variance is essential.


Poisson regression and rates
For event counts observed over different person-times:
\[\log E(Y_i)=\beta_0+\beta_1A_i+\beta^TL_i+\log(T_i),\]
where \(\log(T_i)\) is an offset. Exponentiated coefficients are incidence-rate ratios. Investigate overdispersion, recurrent events and whether the assumption of a constant rate within intervals is reasonable.


Cox proportional hazards model
The Cox model specifies:
\[h(t\mid A,L)=h_0(t)\exp(\beta_1A+\beta^TL).\]
\(\exp(\beta_1)\) is a conditional hazard ratio if proportional hazards holds. Hazard ratios are not risk ratios and can be difficult to interpret causally. Report survival probabilities or restricted mean survival time when they better answer the substantive question.


Correlated data
Clustered facility data, repeated measures and matched designs violate independence assumptions. Options include cluster-robust standard errors, generalised estimating equations (population-average interpretation) and mixed-effects models (cluster-specific interpretation). Choosing between them should reflect the target estimand and data-generating structure, not software familiarity.


Functional form
A continuous covariate need not have a linear association with the link-scale outcome. Restricted cubic splines, fractional polynomials or principled transformation can reduce residual confounding and model misspecification. Arbitrary categorisation wastes information and creates artificial thresholds.


Interactions
If effect modification is plausible, include interaction terms that correspond to the scale of interest. An interaction in a logistic model concerns multiplicativity of odds, not necessarily additivity of risks. Use predicted risks to examine interaction on clinically meaningful scales.


Missing data inside regression
Complete-case analysis changes the analysed population and relies on assumptions about the missingness process. Multiple imputation can preserve information under missing-at-random assumptions if the imputation model includes appropriate predictors and reflects the analysis model. Imputation is not a generic repair for selection bias or MNAR processes.


Model diagnostics as epidemiological diagnostics
Do not stop at residual plots. Ask whether estimates depend on unsupported extrapolation, a few influential clusters, separation, extreme covariate patterns, or inappropriate adjustment variables. Diagnostics should interrogate both statistical fit and causal support.


Reporting model results
A graduate report should include the model family/link, covariates and rationale, handling of continuous variables, clustering/repeated measures, missing data, effect measure, uncertainty, relevant diagnostics and—where appropriate—standardised predictions. “Multivariable regression was performed” is not enough.


MSc standard
Fit and interpret linear, logistic, modified Poisson and Poisson-rate models; choose the model based on outcome and estimand; produce adjusted absolute risks from regression predictions.


PhD standard
Defend the estimand implied by the model, distinguish marginal from conditional effects, address nonlinearity/correlation/missingness, and show whether conclusions persist under plausible alternative modelling specifications.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
section: ORIENT · Internal validity is not the end of epidemiology
text:
ORIENT · Internal validity is not the end of epidemiology
A well-estimated effect in one population may not answer the decision problem in another. Effects can differ because baseline risk, effect modifiers, competing events, intervention delivery and healthcare context differ.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
text:
LEARN 1 · Generalisability and transportability
Generalisability usually refers to extending results from a study sample to its source/target population. Transportability often refers to extending to a different population.
A formal approach models selection into the study and reweights or standardises the study to the covariate distribution of the target population. This requires measured effect modifiers and positivity across populations.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
section: LEARN 2 · Selection diagrams and target populations
text:
LEARN 2 · Selection diagrams and target populations
Selection into a study can be represented as a node affected by variables that also modify treatment effects. If effect modifiers are distributed differently between study and target populations, transport requires adjustment for those differences.
Always name the target population before claiming external validity.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
text:
LEARN 3 · Triangulation
Triangulation strengthens inference when studies with different biases converge on a similar conclusion. A cohort, case-control study, natural experiment and negative-control analysis may each have weaknesses, but those weaknesses need not point in the same direction.
Triangulation is strongest when the expected bias structures are explicitly different rather than when many studies repeat the same design and data source.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
section: LEARN 4 · Robustness values are not truth meters
text:
LEARN 4 · Robustness values are not truth meters
Sensitivity analyses, E-values, specification curves and negative controls can test aspects of robustness. None converts an observational result into proof. Interpret them as evidence about how conclusions respond to plausible violations.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
text:
CAPSTONE · The LIPPS EVIDENCE defence
Use the LIPPS EVIDENCE framework on one real study:
E — Exact question: What estimand and target population?
V — Valid design: Does the design emulate a credible comparison?
I — Information quality: How were exposure, outcome and covariates measured?
D — Denominators/data structure: Is time, sampling, clustering and censoring handled correctly?
E — Explanations competing: Which confounding, selection and measurement explanations remain?
N — Numerical meaning: What are the absolute and relative effects and uncertainty?
C — Context: Does the effect transport to the decision population?
E — Expression: Does the conclusion match the estimand and assumptions?
The final submission should include a reproducible analysis or re-analysis plan and a 10-minute oral methods defence.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
text:
PHD EXTENSION · Methodological contribution
Doctoral work should eventually move beyond competent application. A PhD epidemiologist should be able to identify where existing methods are inadequate, compare alternative identification or estimation strategies, conduct simulation studies when appropriate, and justify a methodological contribution or sophisticated application that advances knowledge rather than merely repeats a standard analysis.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Build an evidence argument, not a significance claim
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Build an evidence argument, not a significance claim
At the end of an advanced analysis, assemble an evidence map around the causal conclusion.

Layer 1 · Design credibility

Was time zero aligned?
Was the comparison group generated from the same target population?
Was treatment assignment approximated credibly?
Were key design decisions prespecified?



Layer 2 · Measurement credibility

Were exposure and outcome measured consistently across groups?
Were assessors blinded where possible?
Were validation data available?
Did definitions change across sites or time?



Layer 3 · Adjustment and support

What DAG justified adjustment?
Was overlap adequate?
Were weights stable?
Were model forms plausible?
Did alternative valid estimators agree?



Layer 4 · Missingness and selection

Who was excluded from the analytic sample?
Why were data missing?
Was censoring informative?
Did complete-case restriction alter the target population?



Layer 5 · Sensitivity
A mature analysis should include at least one sensitivity analysis directed at the main threat, not merely alternative covariate lists. Examples: - unmeasured confounding scenarios; - quantitative misclassification correction; - alternate time-zero definitions; - weight truncation; - missing-not-at-random shifts; - negative controls; - alternative outcome definitions.


Layer 6 · Transportability
Describe differences between study and target populations in baseline risk and effect modifiers. If external covariate data are available, reweight or standardise to the target and compare transported with study-population effects.


Triangulation matrix
Construct a matrix of evidence sources:









Evidence source
Main bias likely
Direction expected
Result




Cohort
residual confounding
away/toward null?



Natural experiment
instrument/parallel trend assumptions
uncertain



Negative control

should be null



Trial/substudy

Convergence is more persuasive when biases differ.


From estimate to recommendation
A causal effect does not automatically imply policy. Decisions also depend on baseline risk, harms, costs, feasibility, equity and implementation fidelity. Epidemiology informs the effect component of the decision.


Writing the conclusion
A strong conclusion might say:

In the study population, the standardised 12-month risk under strategy A was estimated to be 4.1 percentage points lower than under strategy B. The causal interpretation depends primarily on exchangeability with respect to disease severity and care-seeking, adequate overlap, and non-informative outcome ascertainment. Results were similar across outcome-regression and weighting estimators and remained materially protective under prespecified unmeasured-confounding scenarios. Transport to rural facilities is uncertain because those facilities were poorly represented.

That is more informative than either “A caused better outcomes” or “causality cannot be inferred from observational data.”


Doctoral extension · Contribution beyond application
For dissertation-level work, ask whether your research contributes one or more of: - a novel causal question or target population; - improved measurement; - a stronger design; - a methodological comparison; - an extension of an estimator; - simulation evidence about performance; - improved transportability or bias analysis; - substantive evidence strong enough to change scientific understanding.
A doctoral epidemiologist should be able to explain not only which method was used, but why that method is justified, what would invalidate it, and what new knowledge the analysis contributes.

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
section: SEMINAR NOTES · A publication-ready causal results section

title: Transportability, Triangulation and Defensible Causal Claims
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · The final epidemiological task is deciding how far the evidence can travel
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · The final epidemiological task is deciding how far the evidence can travel
A technically valid effect estimate for one study population is not automatically an answer for another population, setting, policy period or implementation system. Advanced interpretation separates internal validity, transportability, generalisability, triangulation and decision relevance.

Generalisability and transportability
Generalisability typically refers to extending results from a study sample to its target/source population, whereas transportability extends findings to a different population. Both require assumptions about effect modifiers and the selection mechanism.
Let \(S=1\) indicate inclusion in the study and \(S=0\) the target population. If all variables that jointly affect selection and treatment effect are measured, selection weights can reweight the study to resemble the target population.


Selection weighting
Estimate the probability of study participation \(P(S=1\mid X)\) and weight study participants toward the target distribution. Extreme selection weights again indicate poor overlap. Do not transport into covariate regions absent from the study merely because a model returns predictions.


Standardisation to an external population
If outcome models are transportable conditional on effect modifiers \(X\), predict counterfactual outcomes for the target population’s covariate distribution. This is conceptually the same standardisation logic used for confounding adjustment, now applied to population selection.


Effect modification drives transportability
Variables associated with participation but not with treatment effect need not threaten transported effects. Conversely, a modestly imbalanced true effect modifier can matter substantially. Therefore transport models should be guided by a causal model of selection and effect heterogeneity, not by indiscriminate prediction of study membership.


Triangulation
Triangulation asks whether evidence from methods with different bias structures converges. A randomised trial, target-trial emulation, natural experiment and negative-control analysis may each have different limitations. Agreement is informative when biases are unlikely to align in the same direction; disagreement can reveal hidden assumptions.


Bradford Hill considerations are not a causal algorithm
Temporality, strength, dose-response, plausibility and consistency can organise reasoning, but they do not mechanically establish causation. Modern causal inference focuses more explicitly on counterfactual contrasts, identification assumptions and study design.


Statistical uncertainty versus total uncertainty
A narrow 95% confidence interval quantifies sampling uncertainty under the fitted model. It does not include unmeasured confounding, exposure misclassification, outcome misclassification, selection bias, model uncertainty or transportability uncertainty. A defensible conclusion discusses these qualitatively and, where possible, quantitatively.


Robustness and specification curves
When multiple reasonable analytic decisions exist, multiverse or specification-curve analyses can reveal whether conclusions depend on one defensible choice. However, including implausible specifications simply to create a large multiverse can obscure rather than clarify uncertainty.


Bayesian evidence synthesis
Bayesian models can formally combine external evidence and current data, but prior distributions encode assumptions that require transparency. Bayesian estimation does not repair a biased design. Hierarchical models can support partial pooling across sites or subgroups while preserving heterogeneity.


Decision thresholds
Public-health decisions may require action before causal certainty is complete. Separate the evidence statement from the decision rule. Expected benefit, harm, cost, reversibility and urgency can justify action even when uncertainty remains; they should not be disguised as stronger causal evidence.


Reproducibility and provenance
A doctoral-quality analysis should make the route from raw data to claim auditable: data provenance, versioned code, prespecified or time-stamped decisions, analytic dataset construction, model diagnostics, sensitivity analyses and deviations from protocol.


The LIPPS final claim ladder
Before writing the abstract conclusion, move through these levels:

Observed: what pattern exists in the analysed data?
Adjusted: what association remains after the stated modelling choices?
Causal: under which explicit assumptions can it be interpreted as an intervention contrast?
Transported: to which population/settings can the contrast reasonably be extended?
Decision: what action, if any, is justified given effect magnitude, uncertainty, feasibility and harms?

Do not skip levels.


MSc standard
Produce a final causal interpretation that distinguishes association, adjusted effect, causal assumptions, target population and sensitivity results.


PhD standard
Construct a transportability argument, triangulate across designs or analyses with different bias structures, quantify at least one systematic uncertainty, and defend the final claim orally against plausible alternative explanations.


Final oral examination prompts

What is the strongest claim your design supports without modelling assumptions?
Which assumption, if false, would change your conclusion most?
Which population is unsupported by your data?
What independent design could challenge your causal interpretation?
What evidence would make you reverse your recommendation?

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
section: ORIENT · Separate the causal estimand from the estimator
text:
ORIENT · Separate the causal estimand from the estimator
Suppose the target is the 1-year risk difference under treatment versus no treatment. Outcome regression, standardisation, propensity-score matching and inverse-probability weighting can all target that contrast under related identification assumptions, but their modelling choices and diagnostics differ.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
text:
LEARN 1 · Parametric g-formula
For a point treatment, fit an outcome model conditional on treatment and confounders, predict each person’s outcome under each strategy, then average predictions over the target population.
Strengths: direct estimation of marginal risks and flexible contrasts. Weakness: dependence on correct outcome modelling, especially in sparse regions.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
text:
LEARN 2 · Propensity score
The propensity score is \(e(L)=P(A=1\mid L)\). Conditioning on a correctly specified propensity score can balance measured confounders between treatment groups.
Uses include matching, stratification, covariate adjustment and weighting. A high c-statistic is not the objective; covariate balance and overlap are.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
text:
LEARN 3 · Inverse-probability weighting
For an ATE, simple treatment weights are:
\[w_i=\frac{A_i}{e(L_i)}+\frac{1-A_i}{1-e(L_i)}.\]
These create a pseudo-population in which measured baseline confounders are independent of treatment when the propensity model is correct and positivity holds.
Stabilised weights reduce variance. Truncation can control extreme weights but changes the effective estimand and should be treated as a sensitivity choice rather than an invisible cleaning step.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
text:
LEARN 4 · Balance diagnostics
After weighting or matching, assess standardised mean differences, distributional overlap and effective sample size. Do not declare success because the propensity model coefficients are statistically significant or because treatment prediction is accurate.
Inspect the tails of the propensity distribution. If treated and untreated populations barely overlap, the causal question may be unsupported for part of the target population.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
text:
LEARN 5 · Doubly robust estimators
Augmented inverse-probability weighting combines an outcome model and a treatment model. Under appropriate regularity conditions it can remain consistent if one of the two nuisance models is correctly specified.
“Doubly robust” does not mean robust to unmeasured confounding, positivity violations or measurement error.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
section: PHD EXTENSION · TMLE and machine learning
text:
PHD EXTENSION · TMLE and machine learning
Targeted maximum likelihood estimation and related semiparametric approaches can combine flexible nuisance estimation with targeted causal parameters. Cross-fitting and ensemble learners can reduce overfitting bias. These tools increase estimation flexibility but do not weaken causal identification assumptions.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
text:
R LAB

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Compare estimators on the same causal question
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Compare estimators on the same causal question
Use one dataset and estimate the same ATE four ways: outcome standardisation, propensity-score weighting, matching and augmented IPW. Differences reveal estimator sensitivity rather than different scientific questions.

Propensity model construction
Include baseline causes of treatment and outcome, guided by the DAG. Variables strongly predicting outcome can improve precision. Do not include post-treatment variables.
ps <- glm(a ~ age + severity + comorbidity + facility,
          family=binomial(), data=d)
d$e <- predict(ps, type="response")


Overlap
Plot propensity distributions by treatment. If treated participants have scores near 1 while controls have scores near 0, weights explode. Consider redefining the target population to an overlap population rather than pretending unsupported counterfactuals exist.


Stabilised weights
For ATE weighting:
pA <- mean(d$a)
d$sw <- ifelse(d$a==1, pA/d$e, (1-pA)/(1-d$e))
summary(d$sw)
Inspect mean, percentiles, maxima and effective sample size. A weighted pseudo-population with a handful of observations carrying enormous weights is fragile.


Covariate balance
Use standardised mean differences before and after weighting. Balance should be assessed on the covariates themselves, not by p-values that depend on sample size.


Weighted outcome model
A marginal structural model for a point treatment can estimate the weighted outcome contrast. Use robust standard errors appropriate to weighting.


Matching
Nearest-neighbour propensity matching estimates an effect in the matched population and may discard non-overlapping participants. Caliper choices and matching with/without replacement affect precision and target population.


Doubly robust analysis
AIPW combines outcome predictions with inverse-probability residual corrections. If either nuisance model is correctly specified—under the relevant conditions—the estimator can remain consistent. But both models can fail in the same unsupported region.


Machine learning nuisance models
Random forests, boosting or super learner can flexibly estimate propensity or outcome functions. Cross-fitting separates nuisance-model training from causal-effect evaluation, reducing overfitting bias. However, black-box nuisance models do not make the causal assumptions less important.


Estimator comparison table
Your report should contain a table like:



Estimator
Risk under A=1
Risk under A=0
RD
Key diagnostic




G-computation



outcome-model checks


IPTW



balance + weight tails


Matching



balance + matched target


AIPW



both nuisance models



If estimates differ materially, investigate support, modelling and target-population differences rather than averaging them.


Doctoral extension · Efficiency bound
Semiparametric theory characterises the lowest achievable asymptotic variance among regular estimators under a model. Efficient influence functions underpin AIPW and TMLE. This is the bridge from applied causal inference to methodological research.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Positivity and the geometry of causal estimation
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Positivity and the geometry of causal estimation

Structural positivity
If national guidelines prohibit treatment B for pregnant patients, there is no data-supported causal contrast of A versus B among pregnant patients. No amount of modelling can create that counterfactual.


Practical positivity
Treatment B may technically occur but in only 1% of very severe patients. Estimates then depend on a few observations and become unstable.


Redefining the target population
Instead of truncating extreme weights without discussion, consider restricting the estimand to people with clinical equipoise or using overlap weights that emphasise patients with substantial probability of either treatment.


Matching estimands
1:1 propensity matching without replacement often targets the effect in the matched treated population rather than the original ATE. Report who was discarded and how the matched population differs from the source population.


Weight diagnostics beyond mean
Report min/max, percentiles, coefficient of variation and effective sample size. Plot weights against key covariates to identify which clinical profiles drive instability.


Balance beyond means
Standardised mean differences assess first moments. For continuous variables, compare distributions, variance ratios and density plots. Interactions and nonlinear terms that confound treatment effects should also be balanced.


Outcome-model extrapolation
G-computation can hide positivity problems because predictions are produced even where no untreated patients exist. Therefore inspect propensity overlap even when the final estimator does not use propensity weights.


Doubly robust misconception
If both treatment and outcome models use the same mismeasured confounders, double robustness does not help. It protects against some nuisance-model misspecification, not wrong causal variables.


Bootstrap with matching/weighting
Variance estimation must reflect the estimator. Some matching estimators have non-standard bootstrap behaviour; use established package procedures or analytic variance methods rather than blindly resampling.

title: G-formula, Propensity Scores and IP Weighting
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Estimator choice should expose, not hide, the identifying assumptions
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Estimator choice should expose, not hide, the identifying assumptions
G-computation, propensity-score weighting, matching and augmented estimators are often presented as competing “methods.” A more useful view is that they are different numerical strategies for recovering the same counterfactual contrast under common causal assumptions.

G-computation in more detail
For the ATE with baseline confounders \(L\):
\[E(Y^a)=\sum_l E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)P(L=l).\]
In practice, estimate \(m(a,l)=E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)\), predict \(m(1,L_i)\) and \(m(0,L_i)\) for every member of the target population, and average. This makes the target population explicit. Flexible modelling is particularly important when outcome risk is nonlinear or treatment effects vary with \(L\).


Inverse-probability weighting as population reconstruction
Weights create a pseudo-population in which measured baseline confounders are balanced across treatment strategies. For binary treatment, unstabilised ATE weights are \(1/e(L)\) for treated and \(1/[1-e(L)]\) for untreated. Stabilised weights retain the same target under ideal conditions while often reducing variance.


Positivity diagnostics
Report treatment-specific propensity distributions, extreme weight percentiles, effective sample size and covariate balance. An average weight near one does not rule out dangerous tails. Practical positivity problems often occur in clinically recognisable strata; inspect which patients generate extreme weights.


Trimming and truncation
Capping weights can improve precision but may introduce bias and alter the implicit target. Report thresholds and re-estimate under alternative thresholds. Restricting to a pre-specified overlap population can be scientifically cleaner than arbitrary post hoc trimming.


Matching estimands
Nearest-neighbour matching often estimates an effect among matched treated persons, not the population ATE. Calipers, replacement and ratio matching change who contributes. Report both balance and the population retained after matching.


Augmented IPW and double robustness
AIPW combines treatment and outcome models. Its consistency if either nuisance model is correct is valuable, but “double robust” does not protect against an omitted confounder, measurement error, violations of consistency or absent overlap.


Targeted maximum likelihood estimation
TMLE starts with initial outcome and treatment models and then updates the outcome prediction along a fluctuation submodel targeted to the parameter of interest. The efficient influence curve supports valid inference under suitable conditions. Super Learner can combine candidate algorithms for nuisance estimation.


Cross-fitting
When machine-learning methods are used for nuisance functions, using the same observations to fit complex models and estimate the target can overfit. Cross-fitting separates nuisance learning from target evaluation across folds and is central to modern double/debiased machine-learning approaches.


Choosing between methods
Use g-computation when outcome modelling and direct marginal risks are natural; weighting when balance diagnostics and pseudo-population interpretation are attractive; matching when a region of common support and treated-population effect are substantively useful; doubly robust methods when nuisance modelling flexibility is needed. The causal assumptions remain largely shared.


Sensitivity to unmeasured confounding
No measured-confounding estimator solves unmeasured confounding. Add quantitative sensitivity analyses, negative controls, instrumental-variable arguments or triangulation where appropriate. E-values can summarise one type of sensitivity but should not substitute for a realistic bias model.


MSc standard
Estimate the same ATE by at least two approaches, compare diagnostics and effect estimates, and explain why differences arise.


PhD standard
Use flexible nuisance models with cross-fitting, justify the target parameter, report influence-function-based uncertainty where appropriate, and distinguish estimator robustness from causal-identification robustness.

LAB PROTOCOL · Graduate submission standard

Epidemiological question
How robust is the substantive conclusion to missing data, misclassification and plausible unmeasured confounding?


Before opening R
Write down the target population, exposure/treatment contrast, outcome, time horizon and effect measure. State the design and the assumptions that would make the proposed estimate meaningful. This paragraph is part of the submission: code without an estimand is incomplete.


Required analysis products
Compare complete-case and multiply-imputed estimates, perform at least one deterministic misclassification correction, and present a bias/sensitivity plot or table for unmeasured confounding.
Every numerical result should be accompanied by a plain-language interpretation. Avoid reporting software output as though coefficients interpret themselves. If a model is used, state the link function, covariates, rationale for adjustment and how uncertainty was calculated.


Diagnostics that must appear in the report
Check the imputation model, fraction of missing information, convergence, plausibility of sensitivity/specificity values and whether bias parameters are evidence-based.
A diagnostic is not a ceremonial plot. State what failure it is intended to reveal and what you would change if that failure were present.


Reproducibility requirements
Your submission should run from a clean R session. Use relative paths, set no user-specific working directory, keep data cleaning separate from analysis, label derived variables, and generate the final tables/figures from code. Include sessionInfo() or an equivalent dependency record. Do not manually copy numbers from the console into the final table.


Interpretation discipline
End with four statements: 1. Estimate: what was estimated, on what scale and with what uncertainty? 2. Assumptions: which design/identification assumptions matter most? 3. Diagnostics: what evidence supports or challenges those assumptions? 4. Claim: what can be concluded, and what stronger claim would not be justified?


PhD extension
Run a probabilistic QBA with distributions for at least two bias parameters and distinguish sampling uncertainty from systematic-error uncertainty.

Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
section: ORIENT · Bias does not disappear because it is acknowledged
text:
ORIENT · Bias does not disappear because it is acknowledged
“Recall bias may have occurred” tells the reader little about the likely direction or magnitude of error. Advanced epidemiology turns missingness, misclassification and unmeasured confounding into explicit sensitivity analyses.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
LEARN 1 · Missing-data mechanisms
MCAR: missingness is unrelated to observed or unobserved data relevant to the analysis.
MAR: after conditioning on observed variables, missingness is independent of the missing value.
MNAR: missingness still depends on unobserved information after conditioning on observed data.
These are modelling assumptions, not labels that software can verify conclusively.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
LEARN 2 · Complete-case analysis
Complete-case analysis is unbiased only under particular missingness structures and can lose substantial precision. It can also change the target population to people with complete data.
Always report the extent and pattern of missingness by key variables and exposure/outcome groups.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
LEARN 3 · Multiple imputation
Multiple imputation draws plausible values from an imputation model, analyses each completed dataset and combines estimates using Rubin’s rules. The imputation model should include variables that predict missingness and the missing values, the outcome, exposure and analysis-model structure.
Imputation cannot recover information absent from the data without assumptions. Sensitivity analyses for departures from MAR may be needed.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
LEARN 4 · Misclassification
For binary variables, define sensitivity and specificity of classification. Non-differential misclassification does not universally bias associations toward the null, especially with multiple categories, correlated errors or adjusted analyses.
Probabilistic bias analysis samples plausible misclassification parameters and propagates them into corrected effect estimates.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
LEARN 5 · Unmeasured confounding
Sensitivity analysis can specify plausible associations of an unmeasured confounder with exposure and outcome, then estimate how much the observed effect could shift. E-values are one summary of the minimum confounding strength needed to explain a risk-ratio estimate under specific assumptions, but they do not replace a full bias model.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
LEARN 6 · Negative controls
A negative-control outcome should not plausibly be affected by the exposure but should share similar confounding or measurement structures. A negative-control exposure should not causally affect the outcome. Unexpected associations can reveal residual bias, though null results do not prove absence of confounding.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
R LAB

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Turn uncertainty about bias into numbers
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Turn uncertainty about bias into numbers
Suppose an adjusted cohort analysis estimates RR=1.80 for occupational exposure and respiratory disease.

Unmeasured confounding scenario
Postulate an unmeasured confounder \(U\) that is twice as common among exposed participants and triples disease risk. Use algebraic or simulation-based bias formulas to estimate the confounding-adjusted RR under this scenario. Repeat across plausible parameter ranges.
The purpose is not to discover the “true” value but to show what combinations of bias parameters would materially change the conclusion.


Probabilistic bias analysis
Instead of one sensitivity value, assign distributions to bias parameters, such as exposure-classification sensitivity and specificity. Draw thousands of parameter sets, correct the data under each and obtain a distribution of bias-adjusted estimates.
This separates systematic uncertainty from ordinary sampling uncertainty.


Multiple imputation workflow

inspect missingness patterns;
identify variables predicting missingness and missing values;
include exposure, outcome and analysis-model terms;
create multiple imputed datasets;
fit the substantive model within each;
combine estimates using Rubin’s rules;
compare with complete-case and alternative assumptions.



Imputation model compatibility
If the analysis includes non-linear terms or interactions, the imputation model should preserve those structures. Passive imputation or substantive-model-compatible methods may be needed.


MNAR sensitivity
Pattern-mixture models can shift imputed values by a delta representing how missing values might differ from MAR predictions. Tipping-point analyses identify how large departures from MAR must be to change a conclusion.


Measurement error in continuous variables
Classical random error in a continuous exposure often attenuates simple linear associations but can have more complicated effects in nonlinear/multivariable models. Regression calibration and simulation-extrapolation (SIMEX) are possible correction methods when validation information is available.


Validation subsamples
A gold-standard measure on a subset can estimate misclassification or measurement-error parameters. Two-phase methods can then correct the full analysis. Validation design should be planned, not treated as a post-hoc convenience sample.


E-values carefully
For ratio measures, an E-value summarises the minimum joint strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would need with exposure and outcome to explain away an effect, under assumptions. It says nothing about whether such confounding is plausible. Pair it with subject-matter bias scenarios.


Negative controls
If an exposure is associated with an outcome it cannot plausibly cause, residual bias is suggested. Choose controls that share the same data-generation mechanisms; an arbitrary unrelated variable is not a useful negative control.


Doctoral extension · Joint bias analysis
Real studies may have confounding, selection, missingness and measurement error simultaneously. Monte Carlo bias analysis can propagate multiple bias processes, but parameter elicitation becomes the central scientific task.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Bias parameter elicitation
Quantitative bias analysis is only as credible as its sensitivity parameters. Do not choose values solely to show robustness.

Sources for parameters
Use validation studies, repeatability studies, expert elicitation, previous literature and internal subsamples. Document why the chosen ranges are plausible in your setting.


Correlated sensitivity parameters
Sensitivity and specificity may vary together by site, disease severity or instrument version. Independent draws can be unrealistic. Probabilistic bias analysis can model correlation when information permits.


Differential misclassification
Allow classification parameters to differ by outcome or exposure status. Differential error can produce bias in any direction and can even create an association from a null truth.


Selection bias weights
If selection probabilities can be modelled from observed data, inverse-probability-of-selection weights can target the source population. If important selection determinants are unmeasured, conduct sensitivity analysis over selection odds.


Missing outcomes versus missing confounders
Missing outcomes can reduce event ascertainment and create censoring problems; missing confounders affect adjustment. The same imputation strategy is not automatically appropriate for both.


Auxiliary variables
Variables not in the substantive model can improve imputation if they predict missingness or the missing value. Include them without confusing them with causal confounders.


Delta adjustment
After MAR imputation, shift imputed continuous values by plausible deltas or alter binary-event odds among missing records to evaluate MNAR sensitivity. Plot the causal estimate against delta to identify a tipping point.


Bias-analysis reporting
Report both conventional and bias-adjusted estimates, parameter ranges/distributions, data sources for parameters and which biases were not modelled. Quantitative sensitivity analysis should increase transparency, not create false certainty.

title: Missing Data, Measurement Error and Quantitative Bias Analysis
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Bias analysis turns “limitations” into quantitative questions
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Bias analysis turns “limitations” into quantitative questions
A mature epidemiological analysis asks not only whether bias is possible, but how large and in what direction the bias would need to be to change the conclusion.

Missing-data mechanisms
Let \(R\) indicate whether a value is observed. Under MCAR, missingness is independent of observed and unobserved data. Under MAR, missingness may depend on observed variables but not the missing value after conditioning. Under MNAR, missingness still depends on the unobserved value or related unmeasured information.
These labels are assumptions about the data-generating process, not testable categories assigned by software.


Complete-case analysis
Complete-case estimates can be unbiased under conditions weaker than MCAR for some regression parameters, but the target population changes and precision is lost. Draw the missingness mechanism and ask whether conditioning on complete observation creates selection bias.


Multiple imputation
Multiple imputation creates repeated plausible values from an imputation model, analyses each completed dataset and pools estimates using Rubin’s rules. The imputation model should include outcome, exposure, confounders, auxiliary predictors of missingness and nonlinear/interacting terms needed by the analysis.


Sensitivity to MNAR
Pattern-mixture models, selection models or delta adjustments can evaluate departures from MAR. Report conclusions across clinically plausible departures rather than presenting MAR as certain.


Measurement error
For binary exposure/outcome, describe sensitivity and specificity of classification and whether errors differ by true outcome/exposure status. Nondifferential misclassification does not universally bias toward the null, particularly with multi-category variables or correlated errors.
For continuous variables, classical random measurement error in an exposure often attenuates linear-regression slopes, but more complex settings behave differently. Regression calibration, validation subsamples and SIMEX are possible correction approaches.


Probabilistic quantitative bias analysis
Assign probability distributions to bias parameters rather than single values, repeatedly correct the observed data, and obtain a distribution of bias-adjusted effects. This separates systematic-error uncertainty from ordinary sampling uncertainty.


Unmeasured confounding
A simple bias factor for a binary unmeasured confounder depends on its prevalence imbalance across exposure groups and its association with outcome. More realistic QBA uses external data or elicited distributions. The point is to quantify what confounding structure would be required to explain the association.


E-values
E-values summarise the minimum strength of association that an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome, conditional on measured covariates, to explain away a risk-ratio association. They are one sensitivity metric, not proof of robustness, and do not address selection or measurement bias.


Negative controls
A negative-control outcome should not plausibly be affected by exposure but may share confounding pathways; a negative-control exposure should not causally affect the outcome but may share bias structures. Unexpected associations can reveal residual bias, although null controls cannot prove absence of bias.


Bias direction is often uncertain
Selection, confounding and misclassification can interact. Avoid ritual statements such as “bias was toward the null” unless justified. Construct a causal/bias diagram and specify plausible parameter ranges.


MSc standard
Perform multiple imputation under MAR and at least one deterministic sensitivity analysis for misclassification or unmeasured confounding.


PhD standard
Develop a probabilistic QBA, justify bias-parameter distributions from external evidence, examine joint biases, and show whether inferential conclusions are robust to credible systematic-error scenarios.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
ORIENT · Treatment-confounder feedback
Consider ART adherence measured monthly. Prior adherence improves viral load; viral load predicts future adherence and mortality. Viral load is therefore both a predictor of subsequent treatment and a consequence of prior treatment.
A conventional model that adjusts for current viral load can block part of the prior treatment effect while trying to control confounding of later treatment.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
LEARN 1 · Longitudinal treatment strategies
The estimand may compare sustained strategies such as “remain ≥95% adherent each month” versus “remain <95% adherent.” A strategy must define what happens over time, not just baseline exposure.
Time-varying regimes can also be dynamic: initiate treatment when a biomarker crosses a threshold rather than at a fixed calendar time.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
LEARN 2 · Sequential exchangeability
Longitudinal causal inference requires exchangeability at each treatment decision conditional on prior measured history. This is stronger than baseline adjustment because all important time-varying determinants of subsequent treatment and outcome must be measured appropriately.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
LEARN 3 · Marginal structural models
Inverse-probability weights can reweight each observed treatment history by the inverse probability of receiving that history given past covariates. The weighted pseudo-population aims to break the association between time-varying confounders and subsequent treatment while preserving pathways from earlier treatment through those confounders.
A simple stabilised treatment weight is a product over time:
\[SW_i=\prod_t \frac{P(A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1})}{P(A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1},\bar L_t)}.\]
Censoring weights can be multiplied in when loss to follow-up is informative conditional on measured history.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
LEARN 4 · Diagnostics
Longitudinal weights can become extremely variable. Examine weight distributions, means, tails, positivity by time, effective sample size and sensitivity to truncation.
A model that converges is not evidence that the weighted population is credible.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
LEARN 5 · Cloning, censoring and weighting
When sustained strategies are indistinguishable at baseline, one target-trial emulation approach clones eligible individuals into each strategy, censors a clone when it deviates from that strategy, and weights to adjust for informative artificial censoring.
This approach makes treatment strategies explicit but depends heavily on data granularity and measured time-varying confounding.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
PHD EXTENSION
The parametric longitudinal g-formula and structural nested models are alternative g-methods. Understanding why ordinary conditioning fails in treatment-confounder feedback is more important than memorising one estimator.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
text:
R LAB
