title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Construct longitudinal weights without hiding instability
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Construct longitudinal weights without hiding instability
Suppose patients are observed monthly for six months with adherence \(A_t\), viral load \(L_t\) and death \(Y\). Prior adherence affects future viral load, and viral load affects subsequent adherence.

Long format
Each participant contributes one row per decision time with baseline covariates, prior treatment history, current time-varying covariates, current treatment and censoring status.


Denominator treatment model
Estimate the probability of observed treatment given full measured history:
\[P(A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1}, \bar L_t, V).\]


Numerator treatment model
For stabilised weights, estimate a reduced probability often conditional on baseline variables and prior treatment:
\[P(A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1}, V).\]
Multiply numerator/denominator ratios over time.


Censoring weights
Similarly estimate the probability of remaining uncensored. Multiply treatment and censoring weights to create a pseudo-population where treatment/censoring are independent of measured time-varying prognostic factors conditional on the model.


Positivity diagnostics over time
A treatment strategy may be feasible at baseline but impossible later for certain histories. For example, severely ill patients may always intensify treatment. Inspect predicted treatment probabilities at each time and by clinically important histories.


Weight truncation
Truncating weights at the 1st/99th percentiles can reduce variance but introduces bias and changes the effective target. Report untruncated and several truncation thresholds as sensitivity analyses.


Marginal structural model
A weighted pooled logistic model can approximate a discrete-time hazard model and estimate survival under treatment histories. The MSM should represent the causal contrast of interest; it is not simply the model used to calculate weights.


Artificial censoring
For sustained strategy comparisons, participants can be censored when their observed history deviates from the strategy. This censoring is informative by construction, so censoring weights are essential.


Grace-period example
Compare “initiate therapy within 30 days” versus “do not initiate within 30 days.” At baseline, both strategies can be compatible with the same observed patient. Cloning assigns a copy to each strategy, then copies are censored when their data become incompatible. Weighted follow-up approximates randomised assignment to dynamic strategies under assumptions.


Doctoral extension · Parametric g-formula
Instead of weighting, model the full longitudinal data process, simulate covariate and outcome trajectories under each intervention, and average outcomes. This requires models for time-varying covariates and outcomes and can be sensitive to cumulative model misspecification.


Research discipline
Longitudinal causal analyses should include a timeline diagram. If readers cannot see when covariates, treatment, censoring and outcomes occur, they cannot assess the identification strategy.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Data requirements for longitudinal causal inference
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Data requirements for longitudinal causal inference
Longitudinal g-methods fail when the data are too coarse to represent treatment decisions. Monthly treatment data paired with annual confounder measurements may not capture the temporal ordering needed for sequential exchangeability.

Measurement interval
Choose intervals short enough that treatment, confounders and outcomes can be ordered. If adherence changes weekly but viral load is measured every six months, the analysis must acknowledge substantial latent history.


Time-varying confounder measurement
Variables used in treatment models should be measured before the treatment decision they predict. Using a lab value recorded after dispensing can accidentally adjust for a treatment consequence.


Weight-model specification
Include flexible time functions, prior treatment and relevant interactions. Fit separate models by time when treatment mechanisms change sharply, or include treatment-time interactions.


Censoring due to death
Death may be an outcome, competing event or censoring event depending on the estimand. Do not mechanically create inverse-probability censoring weights for death without defining the hypothetical intervention that makes death censorable.


Artificial censoring and adherence
In per-protocol analyses, censor participants when they deviate from the assigned strategy. This creates informative censoring because deviation is related to prognosis; censoring weights attempt to restore comparability.


Weight explosion
Products of many probabilities can generate extreme longitudinal weights. Stabilisation, truncation and strategy simplification can help. If positivity is fundamentally absent, redefine the question.


Simulation as a design tool
Before analysing real data, simulate a simplified longitudinal process with known treatment effects and confounding. Verify that your code recovers the known effect under correct models and fails in expected ways under misspecification. This is excellent doctoral practice.

title: Time-varying Treatment and Confounding
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Longitudinal causal inference is about treatment-confounder feedback
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Longitudinal causal inference is about treatment-confounder feedback
The hardest longitudinal problem occurs when a time-varying variable both predicts future treatment and predicts outcome and has itself been affected by earlier treatment. Standard regression adjustment can then block part of the treatment effect or induce selection bias.

Longitudinal notation
Let \(A_t\) denote treatment at time \(t\), \(L_t\) time-varying covariates and \(Y\) the final outcome. A treatment history is \(\bar A_t=(A_0,\ldots,A_t)\) and covariate history is \(\bar L_t\). A sustained strategy might be “treat at every visit while eligible” or a dynamic rule such as “initiate treatment when CD4 < 350.”


Sequential exchangeability
Longitudinal identification requires that, at each time, treatment assignment is conditionally exchangeable given measured history:
\[Y^{\bar a}\perp A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1},\bar L_t.\]
This is stronger than baseline exchangeability because confounders must be adequately measured over time.


Why standard time-updated regression can fail
Suppose earlier ART improves CD4 count, CD4 predicts later ART continuation, and CD4 also predicts mortality. Adjusting for current CD4 in an ordinary outcome model conditions on a mediator of earlier ART while trying to control confounding of later ART. This mixes two roles and can bias sustained-treatment effects.


Marginal structural models
Inverse-probability treatment weights create a pseudo-population in which treatment history is independent of measured time-varying confounder history. A stabilised weight is the product of treatment probabilities across visits, with simpler history in the numerator and full confounder history in the denominator.
\[SW_i=\prod_t \frac{P(A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1},L_0)}{P(A_t\mid \bar A_{t-1},\bar L_t)}.\]
Censoring weights can be multiplied in when loss to follow-up is informative under measured history.


Weight instability over time
Products of probabilities generate more extreme weights as follow-up grows. Diagnose weights at each interval and cumulatively. Consider model flexibility, pooling sparse treatment categories, redefining strategies or restricting the target population before resorting to arbitrary truncation.


Parametric g-formula
The longitudinal g-formula models the joint evolution of time-varying covariates and outcome, then simulates outcomes under specified treatment strategies. It is powerful for dynamic regimes but depends on correct models for multiple components of the data-generating process.


Structural nested models and g-estimation
Structural nested models parameterise causal effects of treatment “blips” over time and use g-estimation to exploit treatment-assignment models. They are less commonly taught operationally but are important in the theory of time-varying treatment.


Cloning, censoring and weighting
For strategies defined by future adherence (for example “initiate within 30 days” versus “do not initiate”), each person may initially be compatible with multiple strategies. Clone records into each compatible strategy, censor a clone when observed behaviour deviates, and weight for that artificial censoring. This is widely used in target-trial emulations of sustained strategies.


Grace periods
A treatment strategy may permit initiation within a window. Naïvely classifying people based on whether they initiate during the window creates immortal-time bias. Proper emulation treats strategy assignment and follow-up carefully, often using cloning/censoring/weighting or sequential trials.


Time-varying effect modification
Treatment effects may differ by evolving disease state. Dynamic treatment regimes make such state-dependence explicit. The scientific question becomes: which treatment rule performs best for which evolving history?


MSc standard
Recognise treatment-confounder feedback, build a person-period dataset, estimate stabilised weights and fit a simple marginal structural model.


PhD standard
Formally state sequential exchangeability and positivity, evaluate dynamic interventions, use longitudinal g-formula or MSMs appropriately, and justify handling of grace periods, artificial censoring and competing events.

Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: DAGs and Identification
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: DAGs and Identification
DAGs and Identification
section: ORIENT · A covariate table does not reveal causal structure
text:
ORIENT · A covariate table does not reveal causal structure
The same variable can be a confounder, mediator or collider depending on the causal question. DAGs make those assumptions explicit and allow adjustment strategies to be discussed before models are fit.

title: DAGs and Identification
text:
LEARN 1 · Paths and d-separation
A path between exposure and outcome can transmit association even when it is not causal. Backdoor paths enter the exposure through an arrow pointing into it. A sufficient adjustment set blocks all open non-causal backdoor paths without blocking the causal path of interest.
D-separation is the graphical rule used to determine whether paths are open or blocked after conditioning.

title: DAGs and Identification
text:
LEARN 2 · Colliders
If \(A \rightarrow C \leftarrow U\), conditioning on collider \(C\) can create association between \(A\) and \(U\). If \(U\) also affects outcome \(Y\), conditioning on \(C\) can create a spurious path from \(A\) to \(Y\).
Common colliders include hospital admission, study participation, test receipt and survival to recruitment when each is affected by multiple causes.

title: DAGs and Identification
section: LEARN 3 · Mediators and total versus direct effects
text:
LEARN 3 · Mediators and total versus direct effects
If \(A \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y\), adjusting for \(M\) changes the question. A total effect allows the mediated pathway to operate; a controlled direct effect compares exposure strategies while fixing the mediator to a specified value. Natural direct and indirect effects require additional cross-world assumptions and are treated later.

title: DAGs and Identification
text:
LEARN 4 · Descendants and selection
Conditioning on descendants of colliders can also open biasing paths. Restricting analysis to people who attend clinic, survive long enough, have complete laboratory data or consent to a sub-study may create selection bias if those processes are common effects of exposure-related and outcome-related causes.

title: DAGs and Identification
text:
LEARN 5 · DAGs cannot encode everything
DAGs encode qualitative causal structure, not effect sizes, measurement error, functional form or random error. They are only as credible as the subject-matter assumptions used to draw them.
Cycles are also excluded from simple DAGs; feedback over time is represented by time-indexed variables rather than a literal directed cycle.

title: DAGs and Identification
text:
LEARN 6 · From graph to estimand
The graph supports identification; it does not choose the estimator. Once an adjustment set is identified, effects can be estimated by standardisation, regression, matching, weighting or other approaches.
A useful workflow is: question → target trial/estimand → DAG → identification set → estimator → diagnostics → sensitivity analysis.

title: DAGs and Identification
text:
ASSESSMENT · DAG defence
Draw a DAG for one of your own research questions, identify a minimally sufficient adjustment set and defend why at least three measured covariates should or should not be adjusted for. Include one plausible unmeasured variable and describe how it threatens identification.

title: DAGs and Identification
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · DAGs as a protocol language
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · DAGs as a protocol language
Take the question: does facility-level staffing improve viral suppression? Let staffing \(A\) affect counselling quality \(M\), which affects suppression \(Y\). Facility resources \(L\) affect both staffing and suppression. Patient severity \(S\) influences facility choice and suppression.
A DAG forces you to decide whether facility choice is a confounder pathway, a selection mechanism or both.

Backdoor criterion in practice
A set \(Z\) is sufficient if it blocks every backdoor path from \(A\) to \(Y\) without including descendants that induce bias. In the staffing example, facility resources and patient mix may be required. Counselling quality should not be adjusted for when estimating the total staffing effect because it is a mediator.


M-bias and collider intuition
Suppose staffing is influenced by district funding and patient complexity; suppression is influenced by patient complexity and NGO support; selection of “well-documented facilities” depends on both staffing and NGO support. Restricting to well-documented facilities may open a path between staffing and NGO support through the collider selection variable.


Selection diagrams
Add a selection node \(S\) indicating inclusion in the analytic sample. Arrows into \(S\) encode variables influencing participation or data completeness. This makes complete-case analysis a causal selection problem rather than a purely statistical missing-data issue.


Measurement nodes
A DAG can distinguish true exposure \(A\) from measured exposure \(A^*\) and true outcome \(Y\) from recorded outcome \(Y^*\). Differential measurement can arise when \(A\) influences how \(Y\) is measured or vice versa.


DAGs and instrumental variables
A proposed instrument \(Z\) should affect treatment \(A\), have no direct path to outcome \(Y\) except through \(A\), and share no unblocked common causes with \(Y\). DAGs make the exclusion restriction and independence assumptions visible, though they cannot prove them.


Minimal versus maximal adjustment
A minimally sufficient set may improve precision by avoiding unnecessary variables. A larger valid set may sometimes improve precision if variables strongly predict outcome without inducing bias. The graph identifies valid sets; efficiency remains an estimation question.


Temporal DAGs
Longitudinal settings require time-indexed variables: \(A_0 \rightarrow L_1 \rightarrow A_1 \rightarrow Y\). Feedback is represented across time rather than through cycles. This structure reveals why \(L_1\) can simultaneously mediate \(A_0\) and confound \(A_1\).


Practical exercise
For your dissertation: 1. draw a pre-data DAG; 2. label measured and unmeasured nodes; 3. identify a minimal sufficient adjustment set; 4. identify variables you must not adjust for in the total-effect analysis; 5. identify the selection mechanism; 6. identify at least one measurement process; 7. write one sentence describing the untestable assumptions encoded by the graph.


Doctoral extension · SWIGs
Single-world intervention graphs (SWIGs) merge graphical and potential-outcome notation to represent interventions and counterfactual independencies. They are useful when advanced doctoral work requires a more formal link between graphs and causal identification.

title: DAGs and Identification
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Graphical mistakes that matter in real analyses
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Graphical mistakes that matter in real analyses

Conditioning on healthcare use
Suppose obesity increases clinic attendance and diabetes symptoms also increase attendance. A study restricted to clinic attendees conditions on a collider influenced by obesity and latent diabetes risk, potentially distorting their association.


Survivor bias
If exposure and unmeasured frailty both influence survival to study enrolment, conditioning on being alive at enrolment opens a path between exposure and frailty. This is common in studies of long-term survivors.


Mediator-outcome confounders affected by exposure
Suppose treatment affects depression, depression influences adherence, and adherence mediates the treatment effect on viral suppression. Depression is then a treatment-induced confounder of the adherence-outcome relation. Standard mediation regression is biased; longitudinal g-methods or interventional effects may be required.


Precision variables and instruments
DAGs identify variables required for bias control but do not always dictate variables useful for precision. Distinguish a valid adjustment set from the statistically efficient set within valid options.


Unmeasured nodes
Do not omit a node because it was not measured. DAGs represent the causal world, not the columns available in the dataset. Mark unmeasured variables explicitly; that makes residual confounding visible rather than silently assumed away.


DAG falsification limits
A DAG can imply conditional independencies testable in data, but failure to reject an implication does not prove the graph is correct. Multiple graphs can be compatible with the same observed distribution.


Selection into measurement
Laboratory testing may depend on symptoms and clinician suspicion. Analysing only tested patients conditions on a post-exposure selection process. This is particularly important in diagnostic and electronic health-record studies.


Documentation standard
Include the DAG, node definitions, temporal ordering, minimally sufficient set and rationale in the analysis plan. If the final adjustment differs from the prespecified graph, explain why.

title: DAGs and Identification
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · DAGs are tools for identification, not decorative figures
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · DAGs are tools for identification, not decorative figures
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) represents assumptions about causal relations. Its value is not visual sophistication; it forces the analyst to state which variables are causes of exposure, causes of outcome, consequences of exposure, shared causes and selection variables.

Nodes, arrows and acyclicity
An arrow \(X\rightarrow Y\) means that \(X\) is assumed to be a direct cause of \(Y\) relative to the graph’s level of detail. Absence of an arrow is also an assumption. A DAG cannot contain directed cycles, so feedback processes must be represented across time (for example \(L_0\rightarrow A_0\rightarrow L_1\rightarrow A_1\)).


Backdoor paths
A backdoor path from exposure \(A\) to outcome \(Y\) begins with an arrow into \(A\). Such paths create non-causal association. A sufficient adjustment set blocks all open backdoor paths without blocking the causal pathway of interest or opening collider paths.


Colliders
If \(A\rightarrow C\leftarrow U\), \(C\) is a collider. The path through \(C\) is naturally blocked; conditioning on \(C\) or its descendants can open an association between its causes. Hospital-based samples frequently create collider structures when both exposure and disease influence admission.


Mediators
If \(A\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y\), adjusting for \(M\) removes part of the total effect and can introduce additional bias if mediator-outcome confounding is affected by exposure. Whether to adjust depends on whether the target is a total effect, controlled direct effect, natural/interventional direct effect or something else.


Minimal sufficient adjustment sets
There may be several sufficient sets. A minimal set blocks confounding without unnecessary variables. More adjustment is not always safer. Variables that only predict exposure can worsen positivity and precision; colliders can create bias; mediators change the estimand.


M-bias and practical judgement
Theoretical structures exist where adjustment for a pre-exposure variable introduces bias. In practice, concern should be proportional to plausible causal structure and effect size. DAGs do not replace substantive knowledge; they organise it.


Selection bias on a DAG
Introduce a selection node \(S\) representing entry or remaining in the analysed sample. Conditioning on \(S=1\) can create associations if selection is caused by exposure/outcome or their causes. Loss to follow-up, complete-case analysis and conditioning on testing can all be framed this way.


Measurement nodes
The recorded variable \(A^*\) is not always the causal exposure \(A\). Explicitly representing measurement error can reveal pathways that ordinary adjustment diagrams omit. The same is true for outcome misclassification and mismeasured confounders.


From DAG to estimand
A DAG can identify a covariate set for total-effect estimation, but it does not choose the effect measure, time horizon or target population. Start with the estimand; use the DAG to ask whether the effect is identifiable from measured variables.


SWIGs and counterfactual graphs
Single-world intervention graphs (SWIGs) split treatment nodes into observed and intervened components and connect graphical assumptions directly to counterfactual independencies. They are useful for advanced identification arguments but require comfort with potential outcomes.


Worked example
Consider socioeconomic position \(L\), vaccination \(A\), infection \(Y\) and health-service use \(H\). If \(L\rightarrow A\), \(L\rightarrow H\), and \(H\rightarrow Y\) through exposure opportunities or care, then \(L\) and/or \(H\) may be needed depending on the exact structure. If vaccination itself changes later healthcare use, post-vaccination \(H\) is no longer a simple baseline confounder. Time ordering changes the adjustment strategy.


MSc standard
Draw a DAG from substantive knowledge, identify at least one sufficient adjustment set, explain why mediators/colliders are excluded, and translate the set into an analysis plan.


PhD standard
Defend missing arrows, selection mechanisms and measurement structures; consider time-indexed DAGs or SWIGs; and distinguish graphical identification from empirical estimator performance.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
section: ORIENT · One dataset can answer several different questions

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
section: LEARN 1 · Potential outcomes and causal effects
text:
LEARN 1 · Potential outcomes and causal effects
Let \(Y^1\) denote the outcome that would occur under treatment strategy 1 and \(Y^0\) under strategy 0. For a binary outcome, a population average treatment effect can be expressed as:
\[ATE=E(Y^1)-E(Y^0)\]
or on a ratio scale:
\[RR=E(Y^1)/E(Y^0).\]
The individual causal effect \(Y^1-Y^0\) cannot be observed because each person follows only one treatment history. Epidemiology therefore uses groups plus assumptions to estimate population contrasts between unobserved potential outcomes.
This notation is useful because it prevents the word “effect” from floating free of a defined intervention and population.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
LEARN 2 · The estimand has components
A defensible estimand usually requires at least:

Population: who is targeted?
Treatment/exposure strategies: what exactly is compared?
Outcome: what is measured and how?
Time horizon: by when?
Summary measure: risk difference, risk ratio, mean difference, survival difference, etc.
Intercurrent events: how are competing events, treatment switching or death handled?

Modern trial guidance increasingly emphasises these components because ambiguous treatment effects lead to ambiguous analyses.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
LEARN 3 · Consistency and well-defined interventions
Consistency links observed outcomes to potential outcomes under the strategy actually received. It is difficult to defend when “exposure” bundles together many versions with different consequences.
“High-quality care” is not one intervention. “A facility delivers quarterly medication review, automated refill reminders and pharmacist reconciliation” is more specific. For non-manipulable attributes such as sex or genotype, causal questions need additional care because hypothetical interventions are not straightforward.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
LEARN 4 · Exchangeability and positivity
Conditional exchangeability requires that, after conditioning on appropriate covariates \(L\), treatment groups are comparable with respect to potential outcomes:
\[Y^a \perp A \mid L.\]
This is an assumption, not a test result.
Positivity requires that every covariate pattern relevant to the target population has a non-zero probability of receiving each strategy under comparison. If no critically ill patient ever remains untreated, the untreated counterfactual for critically ill patients is unsupported by the data.
Near-violations create unstable weights and model extrapolation even when mathematical positivity is not exactly zero.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
section: LEARN 5 · Time zero and immortal time
text:
LEARN 5 · Time zero and immortal time
Eligibility, treatment assignment/classification and start of follow-up should align. If treatment is defined using information that occurs after follow-up has begun, participants may have to survive event-free to be classified as treated. This creates immortal time.
A target-trial mindset asks: At what moment would a real trial randomise eligible participants? Observational emulation should align exposure assignment and outcome follow-up to that same moment.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · Same-day ART
Target population: treatment-naïve adults newly eligible for ART at participating facilities.
Strategies: initiate ART on the day of eligibility versus initiate 1–7 days later.
Time zero: date eligibility is confirmed.
Outcome: all-cause mortality by 12 months.
Estimand: 12-month risk difference and risk ratio under the two strategies.
Identification concerns: baseline disease severity, pregnancy, TB status, facility readiness and calendar time may influence both treatment timing and mortality; loss to follow-up may be informative; treatment strategy needs a rule for people who die before delayed initiation.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
WHAT COULD FOOL US?

Defining the treatment using future information.
Adjusting for variables measured after treatment begins.
Estimating an odds ratio when the policy question concerns absolute 12-month risk.
Claiming exchangeability because covariate balance “looks good.”
Ignoring patients with covariate patterns for whom one strategy never occurs.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
section: PHD EXTENSION · Identification is not estimation
text:
PHD EXTENSION · Identification is not estimation
Identification asks whether the causal estimand can be expressed as a function of the observed-data distribution under stated assumptions. Estimation asks how to approximate that function with finite data. A better estimator cannot repair a non-identified causal question.
This distinction becomes central when comparing g-computation, weighting, matching and doubly robust estimators later in the course.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
APPLY
Write a one-page estimand specification for a dissertation question. Include a hypothetical target trial even if your final study is observational. Explicitly state one exchangeability, one positivity and one consistency concern.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Write the protocol before the model
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Write the protocol before the model
A useful discipline is to write the observational analysis as though a protocol committee will reject any ambiguity. For the same-day ART example, specify each component in operational language.
Eligibility: adults aged 18 years or older, treatment-naïve, confirmed eligible for ART, with no prior ART in the preceding 12 months, entering one of the participating facilities during the study period.
Strategy 1: initiate ART on the eligibility date.
Strategy 2: initiate ART between day 1 and day 7 after eligibility, provided the patient remains alive and eligible.
Immediately a problem appears: strategy 2 is not defined for patients who die before day 7. A real trial would assign them to a strategy at baseline, not wait to see whether they survive. That forces the analyst to decide whether the intervention is assignment to delayed initiation or actual initiation in a grace period. Those are different strategies.

Grace periods
A grace period allows treatment to start within a window after eligibility. Observational emulation must avoid giving treated patients guaranteed survival time during the grace period. Approaches include cloning individuals into compatible strategies and censoring clones when their observed treatment history becomes incompatible, then weighting for the induced censoring.
At MSc level, the important point is conceptual: a grace period changes the treatment strategy and the analysis. At doctoral level, the implementation should be explicit enough that another analyst could reproduce the person-time classification.


Competing events
Suppose the outcome is TB diagnosis by 12 months and death prevents future TB diagnosis. Two estimands are possible:

the risk of TB in a hypothetical world where death is somehow eliminated;
the real-world cumulative incidence of TB where death is allowed to compete.

These correspond to different decision questions. A study must not treat the handling of death as a technical afterthought.


Descriptive versus causal contrasts
The observed difference
\[E(Y\mid A=1)-E(Y\mid A=0)\]
is an associational contrast. The causal contrast
\[E(Y^1)-E(Y^0)\]
requires identification assumptions. The two coincide under conditions such as exchangeability, positivity and consistency. This distinction is the intellectual centre of advanced epidemiology.


Estimands beyond ATE
The ATE asks about the whole target population. The ATT asks about people who actually received treatment. The ATU asks about untreated people. Policy questions may target one rather than another. If a programme is deciding whether to expand an intervention to those not currently receiving it, the ATU can sometimes be more directly relevant than the ATE.


A practical estimand template
Complete this before any analysis:

Among [target population] eligible at [time zero], what is the [time horizon] risk/mean/rate of [outcome] if everyone followed [strategy A] compared with if everyone followed [strategy B], summarised as [risk difference/risk ratio/etc.]?

Then add:

Identification requires [exchangeability statement], [positivity statement], [consistency statement], and valid measurement/selection assumptions.



R design object before data analysis
Even without a specialised package, encode the protocol in an analysis object or script header:
estimand <- list(
  population = "ART-naive adults newly eligible for ART",
  treatment_a = "same-day initiation",
  treatment_b = "initiation days 1-7",
  time_zero = "eligibility date",
  outcome = "all-cause mortality",
  horizon_days = 365,
  measure = c("risk_difference", "risk_ratio")
)
This may seem trivial, but it prevents analytic drift when code becomes complex.


Common failure modes

Prevalent-user bias: including long-term users selects survivors and mixes treatment history.
Depletion of susceptibles: early adverse events may remove vulnerable users before study entry.
Time-lag bias: treatment groups differ in disease duration or severity because they enter at different treatment stages.
Eligibility drift: inclusion criteria change across calendar periods or facilities.
Outcome-window asymmetry: one group is observed longer or from a different starting point.



Doctoral exercise
Take a published observational causal study and reconstruct its target trial. If you cannot determine one of the seven protocol components from the paper, record that as a reporting or design ambiguity. Then state whether the published analysis estimates the same effect as the reconstructed trial.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Ambiguity audits
Before analysing a causal question, conduct an ambiguity audit. Circle every word that could represent more than one intervention or outcome. “Early treatment,” “high exposure,” “adequate care,” “improved survival” and “routine follow-up” all require operational definitions.
For each ambiguous phrase, specify what data would distinguish alternative versions. If “early ART” means within 7 days, determine whether time is measured from diagnosis, eligibility, enrolment or first prescription. Different anchors create different cohorts and can change the estimate.

Eligibility and treatment assignment are linked
In a well-specified trial, eligibility is determined before assignment. Observational analyses often violate this by using information accumulated after treatment to define eligibility. For example, excluding patients who die within 30 days because they lacked a follow-up viral load conditions on a post-baseline event. This can create survivor selection.


Multiple versions of treatment
Consistency assumes that the observed treatment corresponds sufficiently to the strategy being evaluated. If “community ART” includes home delivery, peer groups, outreach vans and pharmacy pickup, each with different effects, a single binary variable may conceal treatment-version heterogeneity. Either define a composite intervention deliberately or model versions separately.


Interference
Standard causal notation often assumes one person’s treatment does not affect another person’s outcome. This can fail in infectious disease, vaccination, network interventions and facility-level programmes. Vaccinating one person changes exposure risk for others; improving one facility can shift patients from neighbouring facilities.
When interference is plausible, specify whether the estimand is a direct effect, indirect/spillover effect, total effect or policy effect under a coverage strategy. Cluster-level interventions may be a more natural unit.


Dynamic treatment strategies
Some causal questions compare rules rather than fixed treatments. Example: “start antihypertensive therapy when systolic BP exceeds 160 mmHg” versus “start when it exceeds 140 mmHg.” The intervention depends on evolving patient history. This distinction becomes critical in longitudinal g-methods.


Estimands and decision makers
A ministry may care about population-average risk reduction; a clinician may care about individual predicted benefit; an implementation team may care about effect among those reachable by the programme. These are not merely communication preferences—they can correspond to different target populations and estimands.


Reproducibility check
A colleague who sees only your estimand statement should be able to construct the skeleton of the study design. If they cannot determine who enters, when follow-up starts, what strategies are compared and when outcome is measured, the estimand is still too vague.

title: Estimands and Counterfactual Reasoning
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · From a vague question to an estimand that can actually be estimated
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · From a vague question to an estimand that can actually be estimated
At advanced level, the phrase “the effect of exposure A on outcome Y” is incomplete. Before any modelling, specify at least five components: the target population, the treatment or exposure strategies being contrasted, the outcome, the time horizon, and the summary measure. For a vaccine example, “effectiveness” could mean the 6-month risk ratio for laboratory-confirmed infection among vaccine-eligible adults, the 12-month risk difference for hospitalisation in the national adult population, or the per-protocol effect among people who would adhere to either strategy. These are different scientific questions.

Potential outcomes and individual causal effects
Let \(Y^1\) denote the outcome that would be observed under treatment and \(Y^0\) the outcome under no treatment. The individual causal effect \(Y^1-Y^0\) cannot generally be observed because only one treatment is received. Epidemiology therefore targets population summaries such as:
\[ATE = E(Y^1)-E(Y^0).\]
For binary outcomes, the same counterfactual risks can be summarised as a risk difference, risk ratio or odds ratio. The effect measure is not cosmetic: additive effects answer questions about excess burden and prevention; relative effects answer proportional questions; odds ratios can be useful for some designs but are less directly interpretable as risk contrasts.


Consistency
Consistency links the observed outcome to the corresponding potential outcome: if a person actually receives strategy \(A=a\), then under a sufficiently well-defined intervention \(Y=Y^a\). This becomes difficult when “treatment” hides multiple versions. “Received hypertension care” might include different drugs, doses, adherence patterns and co-interventions. A causal estimand is only as coherent as the intervention it describes.


Exchangeability
Conditional exchangeability means that after controlling for a sufficient set of pre-exposure variables \(L\):
\[Y^a \perp A \mid L.\]
This is the formal version of “no uncontrolled confounding” for the specified contrast. It is not a statistical property that can be proved from the observed data. It is an argument based on design, subject-matter knowledge, causal structure and measurement quality.


Positivity
For every covariate pattern included in the target population, each treatment strategy must have a non-zero probability:
\[0 < P(A=a\mid L=l) < 1.\]
If critically ill patients always receive treatment A and never treatment B, the data contain no direct information about the B counterfactual in that stratum. Flexible models may still output predictions, but that is extrapolation, not recovered evidence.


Identification versus estimation
Identification asks whether the causal estimand can be expressed as a function of the observed-data distribution under stated assumptions. Estimation asks how to calculate that function from a finite sample. A beautifully estimated quantity can still lack causal identification. Conversely, an identifiable causal effect may be estimated imprecisely because of small samples or weak overlap.


Target population versus study sample
A study sample is not automatically the target population. If a cohort is drawn from tertiary hospitals, the causal effect among those patients may differ from the effect among all people with the condition. Define whether the target is the source population, trial-eligible population, treated population, overlap population or a larger population to which results will later be transported.


Time zero is part of the estimand
Eligibility, treatment assignment and start of follow-up should align. If treatment is classified using information collected after follow-up begins, immortal-time and selection problems can arise. A doctoral-level protocol should be able to point to one unambiguous time zero for each strategy.


Competing events and intercurrent events
Death, treatment switching, loss to follow-up and rescue therapy may alter what the causal question means. Do you want a total effect regardless of switching, an effect under sustained treatment, an effect in a hypothetical world without the competing event, or an effect on a composite endpoint? Naming the estimand forces these decisions into the protocol rather than burying them in analysis.


MSc standard
Given a substantive question, write a one-paragraph estimand statement and identify consistency, exchangeability and positivity assumptions. Then show how a crude association differs from the intended causal contrast.


PhD standard
Translate the question into potential-outcome notation, state the identification assumptions formally, distinguish the observed-data functional from the estimator, and defend the target population and intercurrent-event strategy. If any assumption is implausible, reformulate the question rather than merely adding a limitation paragraph.


Oral examination prompts

What exactly would have to be randomised in your ideal experiment?
Which part of your causal question is not encoded by the regression model?
Where does positivity fail, and what population remains supportable?
Which versions of treatment threaten consistency?
If death prevents the outcome, what estimand are you actually targeting?

title: Epidemiology I
text:
Graduate pathway
LIPPS now treats epidemiology as a sequence, not a single survey course.


Epidemiology I — this course
Build disciplined population reasoning: frequency, effect measures, descriptive epidemiology, study designs, bias, diagnostic studies, surveillance and causal interpretation. Graduate deepening sections add standardisation, survey design, survival concepts, quasi-experimental reasoning and explicit identification assumptions.


Epidemiology II — Advanced Methods
Move into regression-based epidemiologic analysis, causal diagrams, standardisation, propensity methods, inverse-probability weighting, time-varying confounding, missing data, quantitative bias analysis, quasi-experimental methods and target-trial emulation.

text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 05





Foundation Cross-sectional Prevalence Survey reasoning

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text: Foundation Cross-sectional Prevalence Survey reasoning

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
This week in one sentence
Use cross-sectional designs to estimate prevalence and describe populations while recognising the limits created by simultaneous measurement of exposure and outcome.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
Cross-sectional Studies
section: ORIENT · The survey found an association. What happened first?
text:
ORIENT · The survey found an association. What happened first?
A university surveys 2,000 students during one semester. Current depressive symptoms and current heavy social-media use are measured in the same questionnaire. Heavy users have more depressive symptoms.
What can the study establish?
It can estimate the prevalence of each measured state and quantify their association at the time of measurement. But unless the timing of exposure and outcome is reconstructed with credible additional information, the design does not tell us whether heavy social-media use preceded depressive symptoms, whether symptoms changed social-media use, or whether another factor influenced both.
That is the central discipline of cross-sectional interpretation: a strong snapshot is still a snapshot.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 1 · What makes a study cross-sectional?
text:
LEARN 1 · What makes a study cross-sectional?
The defining feature is not simply “a questionnaire.” It is the measurement structure: a sample is observed at a point or short period, and exposure and outcome status are measured at essentially the same time.
Cross-sectional studies can use interviews, records, examinations, laboratory tests or several sources together. A health-facility readiness assessment can also be cross-sectional even though the unit is a facility rather than a person.
The attached CDC source characterises cross-sectional studies as simultaneous measurement of exposures and health outcomes and notes their value for documenting prevalence.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 2 · The natural frequency measure is prevalence
text:
LEARN 2 · The natural frequency measure is prevalence
If a survey asks who currently has hypertension, the numerator includes people whose hypertension began yesterday and people who have lived with it for years.
That is prevalence:
\[
P = \frac{\text{existing cases at the specified time}}{\text{population observed at that time}}
\]
A cross-sectional study generally cannot estimate the probability of developing hypertension during a prior period unless incidence information was separately and reliably reconstructed.
This distinction matters because prevalence reflects both incidence and duration. A condition can have high prevalence because many new cases occur, because people live with it for a long time, or both.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 3 · Population language must be precise
text:
LEARN 3 · Population language must be precise
A survey can be technically competent and still answer the wrong population question.
Target population — the population about which you ultimately want to make an inference.
Study population — the population from which study participants can actually be drawn under the protocol.
Sampling frame — the operational list or mechanism used to select units.
Sampling unit — the unit selected at a given sampling stage.
Observation unit — the unit on which measurements are ultimately recorded.
Example: a household survey may target adults in a district, select villages first, households second, and one adult within each household. The village and household are sampling units at different stages; the adult is the observation unit.
If the sampling frame excludes remote settlements, the “district estimate” may not represent the whole district even when the sample size is large.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 4 · A sample becomes an estimate only through its design
text:
LEARN 4 · A sample becomes an estimate only through its design
Simple random sampling is conceptually straightforward because each sampled unit has a known selection probability. Many public-health surveys, however, use stratified, cluster or multistage designs.
Those design features can affect:

weights, because some units have different selection probabilities;
standard errors, because people sampled within the same cluster may be correlated;
precision, because stratification and clustering change the information structure; and
population estimates, when weighted and unweighted distributions differ.


LIPPS extension
The attached CDC chapter defines cross-sectional surveys but does not provide a full complex-survey analysis framework. Survey weights, clustering and stratification are included here because they are essential for analysing modern population surveys correctly.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 5 · Non-response is not just a smaller sample
text:
LEARN 5 · Non-response is not just a smaller sample
Suppose 80% of sampled adults participate. The main question is not merely whether 20% were lost; it is whether non-participants differ systematically from participants on variables related to the outcome.
If people with severe illness are less able to participate, prevalence may be underestimated. If people particularly interested in the topic are more likely to respond, prevalence may be overestimated.
A large final sample does not automatically remove non-response bias. Bias is about systematic difference, not simply sample size.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
LEARN 6 · Comparing prevalence
Two groups can be compared using absolute or relative measures.
If hypertension prevalence is 30% in Group A and 20% in Group B:
Prevalence difference
\[
PD = 0.30 - 0.20 = 0.10
\]
There are 10 additional prevalent cases per 100 people in Group A.
Prevalence ratio
\[
PR = 0.30 / 0.20 = 1.50
\]
Prevalence in Group A is 1.5 times that in Group B.

LIPPS extension
Prevalence ratio and prevalence difference are included as modern cross-sectional effect measures. They are not explicitly developed in the attached CDC cross-sectional section.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 7 · Why the odds ratio can be awkward for common outcomes
text:
LEARN 7 · Why the odds ratio can be awkward for common outcomes
An odds ratio can be calculated from cross-sectional binary data, and logistic regression often produces one naturally. But odds are not risks or prevalences.
When an outcome is common, an odds ratio can be numerically much farther from 1 than the corresponding prevalence ratio. That does not make logistic regression invalid; it means the estimand and wording must be correct.
If the scientific question is about relative prevalence, a prevalence ratio may be easier to communicate. If the model estimates odds, report odds honestly.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 8 · Temporality: the fundamental causal limitation
text:
LEARN 8 · Temporality: the fundamental causal limitation
For many causal questions, the exposure must precede the outcome.
Cross-sectional simultaneous measurement often leaves that order uncertain. This produces several possibilities:

exposure → outcome;
outcome → exposure (reverse causation);
a third factor → both; or
measurement artifacts producing the association.

A survey showing that people with chronic back pain exercise less cannot by itself establish whether low exercise increased pain risk or pain reduced exercise.
Additional temporal questions can help, but retrospective recall introduces its own error. The design should still be described honestly.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
LEARN 9 · Prevalence can select survivors
Because prevalence includes existing cases, it tends to over-represent conditions or cases of longer duration.
Imagine two diseases with the same incidence. Disease A resolves in days; Disease B persists for years. A cross-sectional survey is much more likely to capture Disease B.
This is sometimes called length or prevalence-incidence bias in broader epidemiological literature.

LIPPS extension
The attached text explains that prevalence depends on incidence and duration. The explicit survival-selection interpretation is developed here as an instructional extension.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: LEARN 10 · Cross-sectional does not mean weak
text:
LEARN 10 · Cross-sectional does not mean weak
“Cannot establish temporal sequence well” is not the same as “useless.”
Cross-sectional designs are excellent for questions such as:

What proportion of health facilities currently have oxygen?
What is the prevalence of hypertension among adults?
What proportion of adolescents report a behaviour?
How does current coverage vary by district?
Which groups currently have the greatest burden?

The strength of a design is judged against the question it was designed to answer. A cross-sectional survey can be the ideal design for prevalence and service-readiness questions.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district household survey samples 1,800 adults using 30 villages as first-stage clusters. Current hypertension is measured using a standard protocol. Current physical activity, medication use, age, sex and residence are also recorded.
Hypertension prevalence is 28%. Prevalence is 36% among adults reporting low physical activity and 22% among those reporting higher activity.
Before making a causal claim:

Identify the target population, likely sampling units and observation unit.
State the primary frequency measure.
Calculate the crude prevalence ratio and prevalence difference.
Explain why the crude association does not establish that low physical activity caused hypertension.
List at least three plausible confounding or reverse-causation explanations.
Explain why cluster sampling may affect the confidence interval.
State what weighting information you would need to estimate district-level prevalence appropriately.
Rewrite this statement: “Low physical activity increased hypertension by 64% in the district.”

A defensible version might say that low activity was associated with higher hypertension prevalence, while causal direction requires stronger temporal and confounding evidence.

title: Cross-sectional Studies
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Sampling, survey weights and prevalence modelling
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · Sampling, survey weights and prevalence modelling
Cross-sectional studies are often analysed as though every observation were an independent simple random sample. That assumption is frequently false in public-health surveys.

Probability sampling and inclusion probabilities
In a probability sample, each sampled unit has a known or calculable probability of selection. A basic sampling weight is the inverse of that probability:
\[
w_i=1/\pi_i
\]
If one household had a 1-in-50 chance of selection and another had a 1-in-100 chance, treating both as equally representative distorts population estimates unless the design is self-weighting for the estimand of interest.
Weights may also incorporate non-response adjustment, calibration or post-stratification. Each additional adjustment adds assumptions; weights should never be described simply as “applied” without explaining how they were constructed.


Clustering and stratification
Cluster sampling reduces field costs but observations within clusters tend to be correlated. Ignoring clustering usually produces standard errors that are too small. Stratification can improve precision when strata are internally homogeneous and appropriately represented.
A survey analysis should therefore identify at least:

the primary sampling unit;
strata;
final survey weight;
whether finite-population corrections matter;
how variance estimation accounts for the design.



The prevalence ratio is often more interpretable than the odds ratio
For common cross-sectional outcomes, odds ratios can exaggerate the impression created by a prevalence ratio when casually interpreted as a relative prevalence. Common approaches for adjusted prevalence ratios include log-binomial models or Poisson regression with robust standard errors.
The model choice should follow the estimand, not software habit.


Non-response is a selection problem
A 90% response rate is reassuring only if the missing 10% would not materially alter the estimate. Conversely, a lower response rate may still yield useful estimates if non-response is well understood and adjusted using strong auxiliary information.
Ask whether participation depends on both exposure and outcome-related characteristics. If so, weighting by observed variables may not fully repair the selection process.


Temporality and reverse causation
Cross-sectional data can support causal reasoning only under special conditions. For stable historical exposures, temporality may be defensible even if the outcome is measured concurrently. But for behaviours that can change after disease develops, reverse causation is a major concern.
Example: an association between low physical activity and chronic pain may reflect physical inactivity causing pain, pain causing inactivity, or both.


Reporting standard
STROBE asks cross-sectional reports to describe participant selection, variables, measurement, bias, study size, statistical methods, missing data and—where relevant—analysis that accounts for the sampling strategy. Treat the checklist as a reporting aid, not a substitute for good design.


R laboratory
Graduate Lab 3 — Survey prevalence, weighting and adjusted prevalence ratios →

title: Cross-sectional Studies
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why is prevalence the natural frequency measure in a typical cross-sectional survey?
Can a cross-sectional study ever collect historical exposure information? If it does, does that automatically make the design longitudinal?
What is the difference between the target population and the study population?
Why can 5,000 poorly selected respondents produce a worse population estimate than 1,000 probability-sampled respondents?
If prevalence is 40% versus 20%, what are the prevalence ratio and prevalence difference?
Why might a chronic disease be easier to capture in a cross-sectional survey than a rapidly fatal disease?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.
