text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 04





Foundation Person · Place · Time Epi curves Hypothesis generation

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text: Foundation Person · Place · Time Epi curves Hypothesis generation

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
This week in one sentence
Describe health events systematically by person, place and time, use appropriate denominators and displays, and turn observed patterns into testable hypotheses.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
ORIENT · “Cases doubled” — is that enough?
A district reports 80 malaria cases this week compared with 40 during the same week last year. That sounds like a doubling, but an epidemiologist should immediately ask what else changed.

Did the district population change?
Did testing volume change?
Did the case definition change?
Did a new reporting facility open?
Are the cases concentrated in one place, age group or time period?
Is the comparison week an appropriate expected baseline?

Descriptive epidemiology is not “just making tables.” It is the disciplined first attempt to understand what happened, to whom, where and when, and to decide what deserves explanation.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 1 · Start by defining what you are counting
text:
LEARN 1 · Start by defining what you are counting
A descriptive analysis is only as coherent as its event definition. Before counting, specify the disease, condition, injury, behaviour or other health event.
For outbreak work, a practical case definition commonly combines clinical criteria with restrictions on time, place and person. The suspected exposure should generally not be built into the case definition when that exposure will later be evaluated, because doing so can manufacture an association.
A useful first question is therefore:

If two analysts used this definition independently, would they classify the same people in the same way?

Definitions may legitimately evolve as knowledge improves, but changes must be documented because a broader or narrower definition can change the apparent pattern.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 2 · Build the line list before the story
text:
LEARN 2 · Build the line list before the story
A line list is a compact dataset in which each row represents one case or observation and each column represents a variable needed for description or investigation.
A practical outbreak line list might include:







Domain
Example variables




Identifier
unique case ID


Person
age, sex, occupation, population group


Place
village, parish, facility, residence or exposure location


Time
date of onset, date reported, date admitted


Clinical
symptoms, laboratory status, outcome


Investigation
selected exposures, contact status, vaccination status



Before analysis, check duplicates, impossible dates, missing age or location, inconsistent categories and the relationship between onset date and report date.

A graph can make bad data look authoritative.
Inspect the line list before you admire the curve.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 3 · Time: choose the clock that matches the process
text:
LEARN 3 · Time: choose the clock that matches the process
Time can be described at very different scales.
Secular trend examines long-term change over years or decades.
Seasonality examines recurring patterns within the year.
Day-of-week or time-of-day patterns can reveal scheduled occupational, behavioural or environmental exposures.
Epidemic time focuses on the short interval relevant to an outbreak.
The x-axis should therefore match the biology and operational question. Annual bins can hide a short outbreak; hourly bins can add noise to a chronic-disease trend.
Events such as a new intervention, a reporting change or a suspected exposure can be annotated on a time plot, but temporal coincidence by itself does not prove effect.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 4 · Epidemic curves are compressed epidemiological arguments
text:
LEARN 4 · Epidemic curves are compressed epidemiological arguments
An epidemic curve plots the number of cases by time of onset, diagnosis or another clearly stated event. Its shape can suggest—but does not by itself prove—the pattern of spread.
Common patterns include:

a concentrated peak compatible with a point-source exposure;
a prolonged or irregular pattern compatible with continuous or intermittent common-source exposure;
successive waves compatible with propagated person-to-person transmission.

The curve can also reveal the magnitude and stage of an outbreak, possible outliers and a plausible exposure window when the incubation period is known.
Do not classify an outbreak from shape alone. Reporting delays, mixed exposures, secondary transmission and missing onset dates can distort the curve.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 5 · Outliers can be clues rather than rubbish

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 6 · Place is whatever geography matters to transmission or risk
text:
LEARN 6 · Place is whatever geography matters to transmission or risk
“Place” is broader than residence. Depending on the question, the relevant location may be a workplace, school, hospital ward, water point, market, travel destination or place of exposure.
Two main mapping approaches have different purposes:
Spot maps show where individual events occurred and are useful for small clusters or outbreaks.
Area maps compare numbers or rates across geographic units. When populations differ substantially, rates are usually more meaningful than raw counts.
A map shows spatial pattern; it does not automatically identify the mechanism producing that pattern. Population density, access to care, diagnostic capacity and reporting completeness can all create geographic differences.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 7 · Person: categories can reveal or conceal risk
text:
LEARN 7 · Person: categories can reveal or conceal risk
Person variables can include age, sex, occupation, socioeconomic measures, behaviours, immune status and other characteristics relevant to the problem.
Age deserves particular care. A broad 0–4 year category may hide that nearly all excess disease is concentrated among infants. Category boundaries should therefore be chosen for epidemiological meaning, not merely because they are convenient.
Similarly, an apparent difference between social groups should not be interpreted as an inherent biological difference without examining exposure, access, measurement and structural context.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 8 · Counts answer burden; rates answer comparative frequency
text:
LEARN 8 · Counts answer burden; rates answer comparative frequency
A district with 500 cases may have a lower disease frequency than a district with 100 cases if their populations differ greatly.
Counts are useful for operational planning: beds, medicines, staff and laboratory workload.
Rates or proportions put events in relation to a population at risk and are more useful for comparing groups of different sizes.
Example:



District
Cases
Population
Cases per 1,000




A
500
500,000
1.0


B
100
20,000
5.0



The smaller district has fewer cases but five times the rate.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 9 · Description generates hypotheses; it rarely settles them
text:
LEARN 9 · Description generates hypotheses; it rarely settles them
Suppose cases cluster among children under five, peak after heavy rainfall and are concentrated around two water sources. Those observations can generate hypotheses about exposure and transmission.
A hypothesis should connect the pattern to a mechanism that can be evaluated. For example:

Households relying on selected surface-water sources experienced higher risk of acute watery diarrhoea than households using protected sources.

That hypothesis now suggests what comparison data must be collected.
Descriptive epidemiology therefore bridges observation → hypothesis, while analytic epidemiology adds a comparison capable of testing that hypothesis more rigorously.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district receives 46 reports of acute watery diarrhoea over 10 days. Thirty-four reports come from two neighbouring villages. Onset dates show a sharp rise over three days, followed by a slower decline. Most patients are children, but one case occurred a week earlier in an adult trader who regularly visits both villages. A new private clinic also began reporting during the same month.
Work through the problem before looking for an exposure:

Draft a usable working case definition.
Identify the minimum variables for the line list.
Decide whether onset date or report date should drive the epidemic curve and explain why.
Calculate village-specific rates if population denominators are available.
Identify which observations might be useful outliers.
List at least three hypotheses suggested by the person-place-time pattern.
Identify at least three non-disease explanations for the apparent increase that must be checked.
State what comparison you would need next to test your leading hypothesis.

The point is not to guess the cause. The point is to produce a description strong enough to justify the next question.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Describing populations without being fooled by composition

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why can an epidemic curve based on report date tell a different story from one based on symptom-onset date?
A village has twice as many cases as another village but ten times the population. Which comparison is more informative: counts or rates, and why?
What is wrong with including “drank from Water Point X” in the case definition when Water Point X is the exposure you plan to test?
Give two plausible explanations for a late outlier on an epidemic curve other than data-entry error.
Why might five-year age bands hide an important disease pattern among infants?
Does a spatial cluster around a health facility prove that the facility is the source of infection? Explain.

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 09





Intermediate Bias Confounding Effect modification

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text: Intermediate Bias Confounding Effect modification

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
This week in one sentence
Recognise systematic error, distinguish confounding from effect modification, and choose adjustment strategies that answer the intended epidemiological question.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: ORIENT · “We adjusted for everything” is not reassuring
text:
ORIENT · “We adjusted for everything” is not reassuring
A paper reports an association between an exposure and hypertension. The authors say the model is reliable because they adjusted for age, sex, BMI, medication use, clinic attendance, kidney disease, physical activity, income, diet and several laboratory markers.
More adjustment is not automatically better.
Some variables may be confounders. Some may be consequences of the exposure. Some may be consequences of the outcome. Some may be colliders. Some may be measured poorly.
The first question is not “How many variables are in the model?” It is “What causal question is the model trying to answer?”

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 1 · Bias is systematic error
The attached CDC glossary defines bias as a systematic deviation of results or inferences from the truth. It explicitly notes that epidemiological bias does not imply intentional misconduct.
Random error makes estimates vary unpredictably around a target. Bias moves the expected estimate systematically away from the target.
Increasing sample size reduces random error but does not automatically remove bias. A very large biased study can estimate the wrong quantity with extraordinary precision.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 4 · Confounding is a mixing of effects
text:
LEARN 4 · Confounding is a mixing of effects
The attached CDC glossary defines confounding as distortion of the exposure-outcome association by a third variable related to both.
Suppose coffee drinking appears associated with lung cancer, but smokers drink more coffee and smoking strongly causes lung cancer. Smoking can mix into the coffee-cancer comparison.
A plausible confounder generally:

is associated with the exposure in the source population;
is a cause, marker or proxy of a cause of the outcome; and
is not simply a consequence of the exposure along the causal pathway being estimated.

These are conceptual conditions, not a mechanical checklist based only on statistical significance.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 5 · Crude and adjusted estimates answer different comparisons
text:
LEARN 5 · Crude and adjusted estimates answer different comparisons
Imagine a crude risk ratio of 2.4 between an exposure and outcome. After appropriate age adjustment, the estimate becomes 1.2.
That change may indicate important confounding by age—but the magnitude of change alone does not prove the adjustment set is correct.
Adjustment aims to compare exposure groups as if they were similar with respect to selected confounding variables.
Methods include:

restriction;
matching;
stratification;
standardisation; and
multivariable modelling.

The method matters less than whether the selected variables are appropriate for the causal question.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 6 · A mediator is not a confounder
text:
LEARN 6 · A mediator is not a confounder

LIPPS extension Mediators and collider bias are not developed in the attached CDC text. They are included because modern epidemiological analysis requires students to understand why adjustment can be harmful.

A mediator lies on a causal pathway from exposure to outcome.
Example:
High salt intake → higher blood pressure → stroke
If the question is the total effect of salt intake on stroke, adjusting for blood pressure removes part of the pathway we intend to estimate.
If the question is a direct effect not operating through blood pressure, the estimand is different and stronger assumptions are needed.
Adjustment therefore changes the question.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 7 · Collider bias: adjustment can create association
text:
LEARN 7 · Collider bias: adjustment can create association
A collider is a variable caused by two other variables.
Suppose both severe disease and high socioeconomic status increase the probability of receiving specialist care. If analysis is restricted to specialist-clinic patients, conditioning on clinic attendance can create an artificial association between disease and socioeconomic status even if none existed in the source population.
This is why “adjust for every variable associated with the outcome” is not a safe epidemiological rule.

Adjustment is not a cleansing ritual. Every variable you control for changes the comparison your model is making.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: LEARN 8 · Effect modification is not bias
text:
LEARN 8 · Effect modification is not bias
Effect modification occurs when the size—or sometimes direction—of an exposure-outcome association genuinely differs across levels of another variable.
Example:
A prevention programme may reduce disease strongly in younger adults but have little effect in older adults.
If the stratum-specific estimates truly differ, averaging them into one number may hide important heterogeneity.
Unlike confounding, effect modification is generally something to describe and understand, not “adjust away.”

LIPPS extension The attached source does not develop effect modification. This treatment is an added modern epidemiology component.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 9 · Stratified reasoning
Suppose a crude RR is 1.8. After stratifying by sex:

women: RR = 1.1
men: RR = 1.0

The similar stratum-specific estimates, both much closer to 1 than the crude estimate, are compatible with confounding.
Now suppose:

women: RR = 3.0
men: RR = 0.9

Those estimates are not naturally summarised by a single common effect. They suggest effect heterogeneity that deserves interpretation.
This logic should be understood before relying on regression interaction terms.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 10 · Interaction depends on scale

LIPPS extension Interaction can look different on additive and multiplicative scales.

An exposure may show no multiplicative interaction on the risk-ratio scale while showing an important difference in absolute risk.
Public-health decisions often care deeply about the additive scale because it reflects additional cases that might be prevented.
Do not ask only:

Is the interaction-term p-value below 0.05?

Ask:

On which scale is effect heterogeneity scientifically meaningful for this question?

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
LEARN 11 · A practical adjustment workflow
Before fitting a multivariable model:

State the exposure, outcome and causal estimand.
Draw or verbally specify the presumed causal structure.
Identify causes of the outcome that also influence exposure.
Exclude clear descendants of the exposure when estimating total effects.
Avoid conditioning on plausible colliders.
Check measurement quality.
Examine whether meaningful effect modification is expected.
Report crude and appropriately adjusted estimates.
Perform sensitivity analyses when assumptions are uncertain.

This workflow is more defensible than automatic variable selection based on bivariable p-values.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional cross-sectional survey finds that current pesticide exposure is associated with chronic respiratory symptoms: crude prevalence ratio 2.0.
Age is associated with both pesticide work and respiratory symptoms. Smoking is more common among pesticide workers and causes respiratory symptoms. Current clinic attendance is influenced by respiratory symptoms and by employer-provided insurance, which is more common among pesticide workers. Reduced physical activity may be a consequence of respiratory symptoms.

Identify plausible confounders.
Explain why current clinic attendance could behave as a collider.
Explain why reduced physical activity could be a consequence of outcome rather than a confounder.
Propose a defensible minimal adjustment set for the total exposure-outcome association.
Suppose the adjusted PR is 1.35. Interpret the change from 2.0 without claiming that all bias has disappeared.
Suppose adjusted PRs are 2.2 among workers without respirators and 1.0 among workers consistently using respirators. Is respirator use behaving more like confounding or effect modification in this result?
State what further design and measurement information you would need before causal interpretation.

title: Bias, Confounding and Effect Modification
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Causal diagrams, adjustment strategies and interaction
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · Causal diagrams, adjustment strategies and interaction
Confounding control should begin with a causal model, not a p-value table. Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are useful because they force assumptions about causal structure to be drawn before variables are selected for adjustment.

Three roles that look similar in a dataset but behave differently
A confounder is a common cause of exposure and outcome (or a variable that helps block a confounding path). Adjustment may be needed.
A mediator lies on a causal pathway from exposure to outcome. Adjusting for it changes the estimand from a total effect toward some form of direct effect and can introduce additional bias.
A collider is caused by two variables on a path. Conditioning on it can open a non-causal association between its causes.
The same measured variable can play different roles in different causal questions. There is no universal list of “confounders.”


Minimally sufficient adjustment sets
A good adjustment set blocks open backdoor paths between exposure and outcome without conditioning on descendants that create bias. More variables are not automatically better. Automated selection based only on statistical significance can omit weak but important confounders or include colliders and mediators.


Regression is one adjustment method, not the definition of adjustment
Confounding can be addressed through design (randomisation, restriction, matching) or analysis (stratification, standardisation, regression, weighting, matching on propensity scores, g-methods). These approaches can estimate different marginal or conditional quantities.


Effect modification and interaction
Effect-measure modification asks whether the effect differs across levels of another variable. Always name the scale:

additive interaction concerns differences in risk differences;
multiplicative interaction concerns ratios of risk ratios or other multiplicative measures.

A single product-term p-value does not fully describe heterogeneity. Report stratum-specific effects with uncertainty and discuss whether subgroup analyses were prespecified, sufficiently powered and plausible.


Quantitative bias analysis preview
Instead of writing “residual confounding may remain,” advanced epidemiology asks how strong an unmeasured confounder or misclassification would have to be to explain the result. Quantitative bias analysis converts vague limitations into explicit sensitivity parameters.


PhD bridge
Epidemiology II develops DAG-based identification, standardisation, inverse-probability weighting, marginal structural models and quantitative bias analysis. The key shift is from “Which covariates are statistically associated?” to “Which assumptions identify the causal contrast?”

text:

What three conceptual conditions make a variable a plausible confounder?
Why can controlling for a mediator be inappropriate when estimating a total effect?
What is the danger of conditioning on a collider?
Why should genuine effect modification usually be reported rather than averaged away?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: ORIENT · Time-to-event data are not ordinary binary outcomes
text:
ORIENT · Time-to-event data are not ordinary binary outcomes
Two participants can both be event-free at study end but contribute very different information if one is followed for six years and another for six weeks. Survival methods use partial follow-up rather than discarding it.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: LEARN 1 · Survival, hazards and cumulative incidence
text:
LEARN 1 · Survival, hazards and cumulative incidence
The survival function \(S(t)\) is the probability of remaining event-free beyond \(t\). The hazard is an instantaneous rate among those currently event-free. Cumulative incidence describes the probability of experiencing an event by time \(t\).
These are linked but not interchangeable. Scientific communication is often clearer when a hazard ratio is accompanied by absolute survival or cumulative-incidence estimates at clinically meaningful times.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 2 · Censoring assumptions
Right censoring is not automatically harmless. Standard survival estimators require censoring to be independent of future outcome under appropriate conditioning. Administrative end of follow-up is often easier to defend than dropout due to worsening illness.
Inverse-probability-of-censoring weights can address informative loss under measured predictors, but extreme weights reveal weak support.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: LEARN 3 · Cox model and proportional hazards
text:
LEARN 3 · Cox model and proportional hazards
The Cox model estimates hazard ratios without specifying the baseline hazard. Check proportional hazards using graphical and residual-based diagnostics. If the effect varies over time, report time-specific effects or use a model that represents non-proportionality.
A statistically significant proportional-hazards test in a very large sample does not automatically make the model useless; judge the magnitude and substantive importance of non-proportionality.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 4 · Competing risks
When competing events prevent the event of interest, choose between cause-specific hazard questions and real-world cumulative-incidence questions. The Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard is one modelling approach, but its coefficient should not be casually interpreted as a causal risk ratio.
Often the most interpretable outputs are standardised cumulative incidences under clearly defined strategies.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: LEARN 5 · Recurrent events and multi-state processes
text:
LEARN 5 · Recurrent events and multi-state processes
Hospital admissions, malaria episodes and exacerbations can recur. First-event analyses discard later events. Depending on the question, consider event-rate models, Andersen-Gill approaches, gap-time models, frailty models or multi-state models.
Multi-state thinking is useful even without complex software: patients may transition from diagnosis → treatment → suppression → loss → re-engagement → death. The process itself may be the epidemiological object.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 6 · Time-dependent covariates
CD4 count, viral load, medication adherence and employment can change during follow-up. A time-updated Cox model can incorporate changing predictors, but if a time-varying confounder is itself affected by prior treatment, conventional adjustment can block part of the treatment effect and induce bias. That problem motivates Week 8.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Move from a survival curve to a defensible estimand
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Move from a survival curve to a defensible estimand
Suppose an oncology cohort compares treatment A with treatment B for 3-year mortality.

Kaplan-Meier first
Plot unadjusted survival and numbers at risk. This reveals follow-up support and whether one group has little information late in time.
library(survival)
km <- survfit(Surv(time, death) ~ treatment, data=d)
plot(km)
Do not report survival curves without numbers at risk; tails based on very few participants are unstable.


Cox model second
Fit the model only after defining covariates and time scale.
cox <- coxph(Surv(time, death) ~ treatment + age + stage, data=d)
cox.zph(cox)
The time scale itself matters. Age-as-time-scale can control age finely in some chronic-disease cohorts, while time-since-entry may better match the clinical process in others.


Absolute survival contrasts
Use the fitted model to estimate standardised survival curves under each treatment and report survival probabilities at 1 and 3 years. This often communicates treatment impact more clearly than a hazard ratio alone.


Left truncation
Participants who enter a cohort after becoming at risk contribute only after entry. If the analysis ignores delayed entry, survivors who live long enough to enrol can create length or survivor bias. Survival objects can represent start-stop intervals.


Time-dependent exposure
For medication initiation during follow-up, split person-time at treatment changes. Never assign the eventual treatment status backward to baseline.
# conceptual start-stop structure
Surv(tstart, tstop, event)


Competing risk worked example
If recurrence is the event and death precludes recurrence, report cumulative incidence of recurrence in the presence of death. A cause-specific Cox model addresses etiologic rate questions; a cumulative-incidence function addresses real-world probability. Choose based on the scientific objective.


Recurrent event strategies
For hospital readmission: - time-to-first-event ignores later admissions; - Andersen-Gill treats recurrent events on a common time scale; - Prentice-Williams-Peterson models ordered events; - frailty models introduce latent heterogeneity.
No method is universally best. Ask whether the policy question concerns any admission, total burden, gap time or transition process.


Multi-state models
Represent states such as “in care,” “lost,” “re-engaged,” and “dead.” Estimate transition hazards or probabilities. This is useful when programme pathways matter more than a single endpoint.


Doctoral extension · Causal survival
Causal survival analysis requires careful handling of competing events, censoring and treatment changes. Marginal structural survival models and g-formula approaches can estimate standardised survival under interventions, but interpretation depends on whether competing events are treated as part of the outcome process or hypothetical censoring events.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Time scales, hazards and clinically meaningful contrasts
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Time scales, hazards and clinically meaningful contrasts

Choosing the time scale
Time since treatment initiation, age and calendar time each answer different questions. Age can be used as the underlying time scale when age is the dominant risk process, with delayed entry at age of cohort enrolment. Calendar time may matter during epidemics or policy changes.


Non-proportional hazards
If survival curves cross, one hazard ratio can obscure early harm and later benefit. Options include time-varying coefficients, restricted mean survival time (RMST) differences and time-specific survival contrasts.
RMST up to time \(\tau\) is the area under the survival curve:
\[RMST(\tau)=\int_0^\tau S(t)dt.\]
The difference in RMST has a direct interpretation as average event-free time gained within the horizon.


Informative entry
Left truncation assumes individuals are observed only after an entry time and survived event-free until entry. Failing to account for delayed entry can produce survivor bias in occupational and chronic-disease cohorts.


Competing-event estimands
If death competes with kidney failure, an intervention that reduces death may paradoxically increase observed kidney failure because more people survive long enough to experience it. This is not necessarily harm. Separate etiologic effects on cause-specific hazards from policy effects on cumulative incidence.


Administrative versus informative censoring
Study end is often plausibly independent of prognosis conditional on calendar time. Loss because a patient becomes too sick to attend clinic is not. Distinguish reasons for censoring and model them when possible.


Recurrent events and terminal events
For repeated hospitalisations followed by death, treating death as ordinary censoring can distort recurrent-event estimates. Joint frailty or multi-state models can account for dependence between recurrent events and terminal death.


Dynamic prediction versus causal effect
Survival models are also used for prognosis. A strong prognostic Cox model may include post-treatment biomarkers and be inappropriate for estimating a treatment effect. Again, prediction and causal inference have different variable-selection rules.

title: Survival and Longitudinal Epidemiology
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Time-to-event data require a risk-set way of thinking
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Time-to-event data require a risk-set way of thinking
Survival analysis is not simply “regression with time.” The fundamental object is the evolving risk set: at each event time, who was still under observation and capable of experiencing the event?

Survival, hazard and cumulative hazard
The survival function is
\[S(t)=P(T>t).\]
The hazard \(h(t)\) is the instantaneous event rate among those event-free immediately before \(t\). The cumulative hazard \(H(t)\) integrates hazard over time, and under standard conditions:
\[S(t)=\exp[-H(t)].\]
Hazards and risks answer different questions. A hazard ratio is a ratio of instantaneous rates conditional on survival to that time; it is not generally a ratio of cumulative risks.


Kaplan-Meier estimator
The Kaplan-Meier estimator updates survival at each event time:
\[\hat S(t)=\prod_{t_j\le t}\left(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\right),\]
where \(d_j\) events occur among \(n_j\) people at risk. Censoring removes people from later risk sets. The estimator relies on censoring being conditionally independent of the future event process, given what has been accounted for.


Informative censoring
Loss to follow-up is not harmless merely because the proportion is small. If people with worsening disease preferentially leave care, censoring may be informative. Compare baseline and time-updated characteristics of censored versus retained participants; use inverse-probability-of-censoring weights when justified.


Cox proportional hazards
Cox regression leaves baseline hazard unspecified while assuming covariate effects multiply the hazard proportionally. Assess proportional hazards using time interactions, Schoenfeld residuals and substantive knowledge. If proportional hazards fails, consider time-varying coefficients, stratified Cox models or alternative estimands.


Absolute survival contrasts
Even when Cox regression is used, present standardised survival curves or risks at clinically meaningful times. A hazard ratio alone can conceal how much absolute event probability differs.


Restricted mean survival time
The restricted mean survival time (RMST) up to \(\tau\) is the expected event-free time through \(\tau\):
\[RMST(\tau)=\int_0^\tau S(t)dt.\]
The difference in RMST provides an absolute time-scale contrast and does not require proportional hazards.


Competing risks
If death prevents subsequent occurrence of the non-fatal outcome, censoring death as though it were ordinary loss to follow-up changes interpretation. The cause-specific hazard addresses the instantaneous event process among those currently event-free; the cumulative incidence function estimates the probability of the event in the presence of competing events. Fine-Gray subdistribution hazards answer yet another question. Match method to estimand.


Recurrent events
Repeated malaria episodes, hospitalisations or exacerbations violate a single-failure framework. Options include event-rate models, Andersen-Gill models, gap-time models and frailty approaches. Define whether the scientific target is total event burden, first event, recurrent intensity or subject-specific heterogeneity.


Time-varying covariates
Biomarkers, adherence and treatment can change during follow-up. Update covariate histories using start-stop data structures. Beware adjusting conventionally for time-varying variables that are both confounders and consequences of earlier treatment; that problem motivates marginal structural models.


Immortal-time bias
If exposure is defined by surviving long enough to receive treatment, the pre-treatment period can be incorrectly credited to the exposed group. Align eligibility, exposure assignment and follow-up; use time-varying exposure or target-trial designs when necessary.


MSc standard
Produce a Kaplan-Meier curve, estimate survival at prespecified times, fit/diagnose a Cox model, and report at least one absolute measure. Explain censoring assumptions.


PhD standard
Defend the causal meaning of the survival estimand, handle competing events and informative censoring explicitly, consider RMST and time-varying effects, and distinguish statistical proportionality from substantive causal assumptions.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: ORIENT · Adjustment is a transformation of the comparison
text:
ORIENT · Adjustment is a transformation of the comparison
Suppose treated patients are older and sicker than untreated patients. A crude risk difference mixes treatment effects with baseline prognosis. Adjustment aims to reconstruct a comparison in which prognosis is balanced according to a defined target population.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: LEARN 1 · Stratification as the conceptual foundation
text:
LEARN 1 · Stratification as the conceptual foundation
Within levels of confounders \(L\), compare treated and untreated outcomes, then standardise stratum-specific estimates to a target covariate distribution.
For a binary outcome, the standardised risk under treatment \(a\) can be written:
\[P(Y^a=1)=\sum_l P(Y=1\mid A=a,L=l)P(L=l).\]
This is the g-formula for a simple point treatment. Regression is often used because direct stratification becomes sparse with many covariates.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 2 · Outcome regression and g-computation
Fit a model for the outcome conditional on exposure and confounders. Then create two copies of the study population: set everyone to treatment and predict outcomes; set everyone to no treatment and predict again. Average predictions within each scenario.
This separates modelling from estimand construction. The regression coefficients are intermediate quantities; the final marginal risks can be more interpretable for public-health decisions.
fit <- glm(outcome ~ treatment + age + severity + facility,
           family = binomial(), data = d)
d1 <- transform(d, treatment = 1)
d0 <- transform(d, treatment = 0)
r1 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata=d1, type="response"))
r0 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata=d0, type="response"))
c(RD=r1-r0, RR=r1/r0)

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 3 · Model dependence
Outcome-regression standardisation is valid only if the outcome model is sufficiently correct in the parts of covariate space used for prediction. Flexible modelling can reduce rigid functional-form assumptions, but all methods still require data support.
Check continuous covariate form, interactions that matter for outcome prediction, influential observations and extrapolation into unsupported regions.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 4 · Conditional versus marginal targets
A logistic-regression coefficient estimates a conditional log odds ratio under the model. Standardised risks create a marginal, population-average contrast. These quantities need not agree numerically even without confounding because odds ratios are non-collapsible.
Decide whether the scientific question is about an individual covariate-defined stratum or a population-average intervention effect.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 5 · Standard population choice
You can standardise to the study population, exposed population, unexposed population or an external target population. Each choice defines a different estimand.
The average treatment effect (ATE) standardises to the whole target population. The average treatment effect among the treated (ATT) standardises to the treated population. Do not use these labels without defining the population.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · Hypertension outreach
A programme compares community outreach with usual facility-based screening. Outreach communities are younger and more urban. Crude detection is higher with outreach. The analysis models 6-month diagnosis as a function of strategy, age, sex, urbanicity and baseline care access, then standardises to the entire eligible population.
Report: standardised risk under outreach, standardised risk under usual care, risk difference and risk ratio. Then state that causal interpretation requires no important unmeasured confounding and adequate overlap.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
WHAT COULD FOOL US?

Treating every baseline predictor as a confounder.
Using data-driven covariate selection without a causal model.
Interpreting conditional odds ratios as population-average risk ratios.
Standardising to an undefined population.
Ignoring unsupported combinations of confounders and treatment.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Standardisation step by step
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Standardisation step by step
Consider a cohort with treatment \(A\), binary outcome \(Y\), age, baseline severity and facility type. The target is the 1-year ATE.

Step 1 · Specify the adjustment set before looking at coefficients
Use subject-matter knowledge and a DAG to choose baseline confounders. Do not select variables because their univariable p-value is below 0.20. A variable can be an important confounder even if weakly associated with outcome in this sample.


Step 2 · Fit an outcome model
For a binary outcome, a flexible logistic model might include non-linear age terms and interactions that improve outcome prediction:
fit <- glm(
  y ~ a + splines::ns(age, 4) + severity + facility + a:severity,
  family = binomial(), data = d
)
The treatment coefficient is not yet the target estimand.


Step 3 · Create counterfactual copies
Predict each participant’s outcome under \(A=1\) and \(A=0\) while keeping baseline covariates unchanged.
d1 <- transform(d, a = 1)
d0 <- transform(d, a = 0)
p1 <- predict(fit, newdata=d1, type="response")
p0 <- predict(fit, newdata=d0, type="response")


Step 4 · Average over the target population
risk1 <- mean(p1)
risk0 <- mean(p0)
rd <- risk1 - risk0
rr <- risk1 / risk0
Now the estimand is marginal because predictions are averaged over the covariate distribution of the target sample.


Step 5 · Quantify uncertainty
Naïvely treating predicted risks as fixed understates uncertainty. Use the nonparametric bootstrap, influence-function methods or package-specific standardisation tools to obtain valid confidence intervals.


Standardising to another target population
If the study sample differs from a target population, replace the covariate distribution used in averaging. For example, if a national survey provides age/sex/severity distributions, standardise model predictions to those weights. This becomes a transportability problem and requires adequate overlap.


Sparse-data bias
When treatment is rare in some confounder strata, outcome regression extrapolates into regions with little or no data. Inspect treatment prevalence across clinically meaningful covariate strata and use propensity-score overlap plots even if propensity scores are not the final estimator.


Regression versus standardisation
Regression coefficients answer model-conditional questions. Standardisation uses the regression model as a tool to reconstruct population outcomes under intervention strategies. This is why “adjusted odds ratio = 0.63” is often less decision-relevant than “standardised 1-year risks were 8.2% versus 11.7%, risk difference −3.5 percentage points.”


Parametric g-formula assumptions
For point treatments, g-computation requires:

consistency;
exchangeability conditional on measured covariates;
positivity;
correct estimation of the conditional outcome mean.

Model flexibility can address the last assumption but not the first three.


Sensitivity to model form
Repeat standardisation using plausible alternative specifications: linear versus spline age effects, treatment-by-severity interaction, alternate outcome definitions. If the causal estimate changes materially, explain why.


Doctoral extension · Nonparametric identification
The g-formula is an identification result before it is a regression algorithm. The equality
\[E(Y^a)=\sum_l E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)P(L=l)\]
follows from causal assumptions. Parametric regression is only one way to estimate the terms on the right-hand side. Flexible learners, super learner and targeted estimators can be substituted without changing the underlying identification logic.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Confounding control as population reconstruction
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Confounding control as population reconstruction
Think of adjustment as reconstructing the counterfactual outcome distribution that would have been observed had treatment groups shared a common covariate distribution.

Stratified standardisation example
Suppose severe disease is present in 60% of treated and 20% of untreated patients. Within severity strata, treatment has the same protective risk ratio, but crude treated risk is higher because treated patients are much sicker.
Calculate stratum-specific risks, then standardise both treatment strategies to the total population’s severity distribution. The standardised comparison reverses the crude association. This is not statistical manipulation; it reflects a different comparison population.


Confounding versus non-collapsibility
If an odds ratio changes after adjustment, ask whether change reflects confounding or non-collapsibility. Compare standardised risks or risk ratios, inspect the DAG, and avoid using change-in-estimate rules as the sole confounder-selection strategy.


Precision variables
A baseline variable that predicts outcome but not treatment may improve precision in outcome regression without being a confounder. Include it if prespecified and modelled appropriately, but do not label it a confounder merely because it is in the model.


Instruments and colliders in adjustment sets
A strong predictor of treatment that has no direct relation to outcome except through treatment can amplify bias from unmeasured confounding when adjusted for in some settings. A collider can create bias. Therefore “include every baseline variable” is not a safe rule.


Standardisation to policy populations
Suppose a trial was conducted in tertiary hospitals but the intervention will be scaled to district hospitals. If effect modifiers such as baseline severity and staffing differ, estimate transported effects by weighting or standardising to the district-hospital distribution, provided there is overlap.


Uncertainty from standardisation
Bootstrap the full process, including model fitting and prediction, rather than bootstrapping only the final average. For clustered studies, resample at the cluster level if clusters are the independent sampling units.


Model-free intuition
Even if final analysis uses machine learning, the logic remains stratification: compare outcomes among sufficiently similar individuals and average those comparisons across the target population. Flexible algorithms help estimate conditional expectations; they do not change the causal target.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Standardisation as the common language of adjustment
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Standardisation as the common language of adjustment
Many adjustment methods can be understood as ways of reconstructing outcomes under a common covariate distribution. Standardisation is therefore more than an old demographic technique; it is a bridge between classical stratified epidemiology and modern causal inference.

Direct standardisation
Suppose age-specific risks are available for exposed and unexposed groups. Choose a standard population distribution \(w_l\) and calculate:
\[R_a^{std}=\sum_l w_l R(Y=1\mid A=a,L=l).\]
The standardised risk difference is \(R_1^{std}-R_0^{std}\). By forcing both exposure groups to the same distribution of \(L\), compositional differences are removed with respect to measured strata. Regression standardisation (g-computation) generalises this idea when \(L\) is high-dimensional or continuous.


Indirect standardisation and the SMR
Indirect standardisation applies stratum-specific rates from a reference population to the study population’s covariate structure to calculate expected events. The standardised mortality ratio is:
\[SMR = O/E.\]
The SMR is useful when study-specific stratum rates are unstable, but two SMRs are not necessarily directly comparable because each is standardised to its own internal covariate distribution.


Mantel-Haenszel adjustment
For a small number of categorical confounders, stratification can estimate a common adjusted association. The Mantel-Haenszel estimator remains pedagogically powerful because it makes the adjustment process visible: compare within strata, then combine information. Regression is not conceptually different simply because software performs the weighting invisibly.


Confounder assessment should not be based on p-values
A variable is not a confounder because its coefficient is statistically significant, nor does it cease to be a confounder because \(p>0.05\). Confounding is about causal structure and the target effect. Data-driven stepwise deletion can therefore produce unstable or biased adjustment sets.


Precision variables, instruments and colliders
A strong predictor of outcome that is not caused by exposure can improve precision. A variable strongly predicting treatment but unrelated to outcome except through treatment can amplify bias from unmeasured confounding in some settings. A collider can create bias when conditioned upon. Therefore “adjust for everything available” is not a defensible graduate strategy.


Non-collapsibility
For odds ratios and hazard ratios, a conditional estimate can differ from a marginal estimate even without confounding. This is non-collapsibility, not necessarily bias. Consequently, comparing crude and adjusted odds ratios as a mechanical test for confounding can mislead. Risk differences and risk ratios have different collapsibility properties.


Sparse strata and high-dimensional adjustment
Classical stratification becomes unstable as covariates multiply. Regression, propensity methods and standardisation solve the computational problem but not the causal one. Sparse combinations of covariates can still create practical positivity problems. Examine support before trusting adjusted predictions.


Model-based standardisation workflow

State the estimand.
Fit a model for \(E(Y\mid A,L)\) flexible enough for important nonlinearities and interactions.
Create two counterfactual copies of the dataset: set everyone to \(A=1\) and then to \(A=0\).
Predict outcomes under each strategy.
Average predictions over the target covariate distribution.
Contrast the averages on the chosen scale.
Obtain uncertainty with appropriate analytic, bootstrap or influence-function methods.



Worked reasoning example
A crude analysis suggests a treatment lowers 1-year mortality from 18% to 12%. Treated patients, however, are younger. Standardisation to the combined study population produces 15% under treatment and 17% under no treatment: RD = -2 percentage points. The adjustment did not merely “control for age”; it changed the comparison to what would be expected if both strategies were applied to the same age distribution.


MSc standard
Calculate direct standardisation by hand for a small table, then reproduce the result using regression standardisation. Explain why the marginal adjusted risk is often easier to communicate than a regression coefficient.


PhD standard
State the target distribution explicitly, distinguish conditional and marginal estimands, discuss non-collapsibility, and evaluate how positivity and model misspecification affect standardised estimates. Be prepared to explain when standardising to the treated population or an external population changes the scientific question.

Minimum pass standard
A technically correct model cannot compensate for a mis-specified estimand. A learner who cannot distinguish prediction from causal inference, or cannot explain exchangeability/positivity/consistency for their analysis, has not yet demonstrated advanced epidemiological competence.

title: Time-varying treatment and marginal structural weighting
text: EPIDEMIOLOGY II · LAB 05

title: Time-varying treatment and marginal structural weighting
text:
LAB PROTOCOL · Graduate submission standard

Epidemiological question
What is the effect of a sustained treatment strategy when time-varying confounders are themselves affected by earlier treatment?


Before opening R
Write down the target population, exposure/treatment contrast, outcome, time horizon and effect measure. State the design and the assumptions that would make the proposed estimate meaningful. This paragraph is part of the submission: code without an estimand is incomplete.


Required analysis products
Construct person-period data, estimate treatment/censoring probabilities, calculate stabilised cumulative weights, fit a marginal structural model and report weight diagnostics over time.
Every numerical result should be accompanied by a plain-language interpretation. Avoid reporting software output as though coefficients interpret themselves. If a model is used, state the link function, covariates, rationale for adjustment and how uncertainty was calculated.


Diagnostics that must appear in the report
Check sequential positivity, extreme cumulative weights, treatment-history definition, censoring and whether standard time-updated regression controls a treatment-affected confounder.
A diagnostic is not a ceremonial plot. State what failure it is intended to reveal and what you would change if that failure were present.


Reproducibility requirements
Your submission should run from a clean R session. Use relative paths, set no user-specific working directory, keep data cleaning separate from analysis, label derived variables, and generate the final tables/figures from code. Include sessionInfo() or an equivalent dependency record. Do not manually copy numbers from the console into the final table.


Interpretation discipline
End with four statements: 1. Estimate: what was estimated, on what scale and with what uncertainty? 2. Assumptions: which design/identification assumptions matter most? 3. Diagnostics: what evidence supports or challenges those assumptions? 4. Claim: what can be concluded, and what stronger claim would not be justified?


PhD extension
Compare MSM results with conventional adjustment and explain the direction/mechanism of any difference; optionally emulate a dynamic treatment rule.


Suggested marking rubric (20 marks)

estimand/design logic — 4
reproducible data management and code — 3
correct analysis — 5
diagnostics/sensitivity analysis — 4
interpretation and limits of inference — 4

A technically correct model with an incoherent causal question should not receive a high distinction.

A technically correct model with an incoherent causal question should not receive a high distinction.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: ORIENT · Observational data do not become trial-like just because propensity scores are used
text:
ORIENT · Observational data do not become trial-like just because propensity scores are used
Design comes before adjustment. Quasi-experimental methods exploit assignment rules, timing or natural variation that can make counterfactual comparisons more credible.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 1 · Difference-in-differences
Difference-in-differences compares outcome changes in treated and comparison groups. The key assumption is that, absent treatment, trends would have evolved similarly.
Use multiple pre-treatment periods to examine trend plausibility. Modern DiD methods are needed when treatment timing varies and effects are heterogeneous; conventional two-way fixed-effects models can produce unintuitive weighted averages.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 2 · Interrupted time series
Interrupted time series estimates changes in level and trend after an intervention while using the pre-intervention series as a counterfactual trajectory. Model seasonality, autocorrelation and concurrent events. Controlled interrupted time series adds a comparison series when available.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 3 · Regression discontinuity
When treatment eligibility changes sharply at a cutoff, units just above and below the threshold may be comparable. The effect is local to the cutoff. Check for manipulation of the running variable, continuity of covariates and sensitivity to bandwidth and functional form.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 4 · Instrumental variables
A valid instrument influences treatment, is independent of unmeasured causes of the outcome, and affects the outcome only through treatment. Under additional monotonicity assumptions, IV methods can estimate a local average treatment effect among compliers.
Instrument validity is primarily a substantive argument; strong first-stage association alone is insufficient.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 6 · New-user active-comparator designs
In pharmacoepidemiology, comparing new users of treatment A with new users of an alternative treatment for the same indication can improve exchangeability and align time zero better than comparing prevalent users with non-users.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · Vaccine policy
Suppose a vaccine is introduced in some districts earlier than others. A naïve post-introduction comparison is confounded by district differences. A stronger design might combine pre/post data, matched comparison districts and explicit trend assessment. If individual eligibility and vaccination dates are available, a target-trial emulation may be possible.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
PHD EXTENSION
Advanced target-trial emulations address grace periods, sustained treatment, competing events, cloning/censoring/weighting and sequential trial emulation. The framework clarifies design but does not guarantee exchangeability.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Design quasi-experiments as carefully as trials
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Design quasi-experiments as carefully as trials

Difference-in-differences event studies
With staggered intervention timing, estimate event-time effects relative to treatment adoption rather than relying on a single post indicator. Plot pre-treatment coefficients to assess trend plausibility and post-treatment dynamics.
Modern estimators group units by treatment cohort to avoid problematic weighting that can occur in conventional two-way fixed-effects models when effects vary over time.


Controlled interrupted time series
Add a comparison series unaffected by the intervention but exposed to similar secular forces. This improves protection against coincident national trends. Still assess whether the comparison itself experienced different shocks.


Regression discontinuity diagnostics
Before estimating an RD effect: - plot outcome against the running variable; - test for density manipulation near the cutoff; - inspect covariate continuity; - choose bandwidth transparently; - compare local linear specifications; - report the effect as local to the threshold.


Instrument strength and weak instruments
A weak instrument produces unstable estimates and magnifies bias. Report first-stage strength but do not confuse strength with validity. An invalid strong instrument is worse than a weak valid one.


Target-trial specification table
For observational emulation, create a table with columns Protocol component, Ideal trial, Available data, Emulation rule, Remaining deviation. This makes compromises visible.


Time zero alignment
Many observational biases are time-zero problems: - eligibility measured before exposure classification; - covariates measured after treatment begins; - treatment assignment defined using future exposure; - follow-up beginning at different times by group.
Fix these in design before modelling.


Sequential target trials
When eligibility recurs over time, each eligible person-time can initiate a new emulated trial. Pool sequential trials and use appropriate weighting/standard errors. This increases information but requires careful treatment of repeated participation.


Active comparator
Choose a comparator with the same indication when possible. Comparing two plausible treatment choices can reduce confounding by healthcare-seeking and indication compared with treated-versus-untreated contrasts.


Falsification analyses
Before claiming a quasi-experimental effect, test outcomes that should not respond at the intervention date, placebo intervention dates or unaffected subgroups where appropriate. These do not prove validity but can reveal implausible patterns.


Doctoral extension · Synthetic controls
When one or few units receive an intervention, synthetic-control methods construct a weighted combination of untreated units that reproduces the pre-intervention trajectory. Inference and robustness require careful donor-pool selection and placebo analyses.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: SEMINAR NOTES · When quasi-experimental assumptions break
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · When quasi-experimental assumptions break

DiD and anticipation
If facilities change behaviour before official intervention start because they know rollout is coming, the pre-period is contaminated. Redefine treatment timing or model anticipation windows.


Spillovers
Comparison areas may be affected by the intervention through patient movement, media or neighbouring policy. This violates no-interference assumptions and can attenuate or distort estimates.


Concurrent shocks
A national drug shortage beginning at the same time as an intervention can mimic an intervention effect. Controlled series and negative-control outcomes can help diagnose this.


RD manipulation
If clinicians can manipulate the running variable to cross an eligibility threshold, units around the cutoff are no longer quasi-random. Inspect density and institutional rules.


IV exclusion restriction
Distance to facility may affect outcome through access to other services, violating exclusion. Physician prescribing preference may correlate with quality of care. Instruments require deep institutional knowledge.


Target-trial data sufficiency
A database may lack exact eligibility dates, treatment start, reasons for treatment or time-varying confounders. Do not force target-trial language onto data that cannot emulate key protocol components.


Protocol deviations table
For each target-trial component, classify emulation quality as close, approximate, or unavailable and describe likely bias. This is more informative than a generic limitations paragraph.


Estimating policy effects
Quasi-experiments often estimate local effects tied to a threshold, treated region or rollout period. Avoid transporting them automatically to populations far from the assignment mechanism.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Strong observational inference starts by designing the comparison
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Strong observational inference starts by designing the comparison
Quasi-experimental methods are valuable because they seek sources of variation that make treatment groups more comparable by design, rather than relying entirely on statistical adjustment after exposure has occurred.

Difference-in-differences estimand
For two groups and two periods, the basic DiD contrast is:
\[[E(Y_{post}\mid G=1)-E(Y_{pre}\mid G=1)]-[E(Y_{post}\mid G=0)-E(Y_{pre}\mid G=0)].\]
The critical identifying assumption is parallel untreated trends, not equality of baseline outcome levels. Multiple pre-periods help assess plausibility but cannot prove what post-treatment counterfactual trends would have been.


Staggered adoption
When units adopt intervention at different times and treatment effects vary, conventional two-way fixed-effects estimators can combine comparisons with negative or unintuitive weights, including already-treated groups acting as controls. Use cohort/time-specific estimators designed for staggered treatment.


Interrupted time series
Segmented regression may model level and slope changes:
\[Y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1t+\beta_2I_t+\beta_3(t\times I_t)+\epsilon_t.\]
Account for seasonality, autocorrelation, nonlinearity and changes in measurement. The intervention date should be substantively justified, and a controlled series can help distinguish the intervention from coincident shocks.


Regression discontinuity
Sharp RD identifies a local effect when treatment changes deterministically at a cutoff; fuzzy RD uses the cutoff as an instrument when treatment probability jumps but compliance is imperfect. Use local polynomial methods, report bandwidth choices and inspect manipulation around the threshold.


Instrumental variables
A valid IV requires relevance, independence from unmeasured outcome causes, and exclusion of pathways to outcome other than through treatment. Under monotonicity, a binary IV often identifies a local average treatment effect among compliers. The estimand may not generalise to always-takers, never-takers or other populations.


Target-trial emulation protocol
Specify eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment procedure, time zero, follow-up, outcome, causal contrast and analysis. Then map each ideal component to observable data. This reveals where observational emulation deviates from the trial question.


New-user active-comparator design
Restricting to people initiating alternative treatments for the same indication can reduce confounding by disease severity, healthcare access and treatment indication. Align covariate assessment before initiation and follow from a common time zero.


Grace periods and adherence
A protocol allowing treatment initiation within 30 days cannot classify exposure using future information without care. Clone-censor-weight or sequential-trial approaches can emulate strategies with grace periods and sustained adherence.


Emulating intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects
Observational data can target an assignment-like effect based on initiation strategy or a sustained-treatment effect. The latter requires adjustment for post-baseline adherence and censoring processes. Clearly distinguish them.


Falsification and robustness
Use negative-control outcomes, placebo intervention dates, alternative comparison groups, bandwidths, donor pools or pre-trend windows as design-specific stress tests. Robustness across arbitrary specifications is less meaningful than robustness across scientifically plausible alternatives.


MSc standard
Construct and analyse a simple DiD or interrupted-time-series study, articulate its identifying assumptions and perform at least two design-specific diagnostics.


PhD standard
Handle staggered adoption, local estimands, weak instruments or complex target-trial strategies; explicitly map protocol deviations; and justify why the quasi-experimental variation plausibly identifies the stated causal effect.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
DEMONSTRATE · Graduate standard
Submit one short methods memo or reproducible analysis in which you name the estimand first, justify the design/estimator, report diagnostics, and state one sensitivity analysis. Marks should be lost for an unjustified causal claim even when the code is technically correct.
