title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text: Foundation Person · Place · Time Epi curves Hypothesis generation

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
This week in one sentence
Describe health events systematically by person, place and time, use appropriate denominators and displays, and turn observed patterns into testable hypotheses.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
ORIENT · “Cases doubled” — is that enough?
A district reports 80 malaria cases this week compared with 40 during the same week last year. That sounds like a doubling, but an epidemiologist should immediately ask what else changed.

Did the district population change?
Did testing volume change?
Did the case definition change?
Did a new reporting facility open?
Are the cases concentrated in one place, age group or time period?
Is the comparison week an appropriate expected baseline?

Descriptive epidemiology is not “just making tables.” It is the disciplined first attempt to understand what happened, to whom, where and when, and to decide what deserves explanation.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 1 · Start by defining what you are counting
text:
LEARN 1 · Start by defining what you are counting
A descriptive analysis is only as coherent as its event definition. Before counting, specify the disease, condition, injury, behaviour or other health event.
For outbreak work, a practical case definition commonly combines clinical criteria with restrictions on time, place and person. The suspected exposure should generally not be built into the case definition when that exposure will later be evaluated, because doing so can manufacture an association.
A useful first question is therefore:

If two analysts used this definition independently, would they classify the same people in the same way?

Definitions may legitimately evolve as knowledge improves, but changes must be documented because a broader or narrower definition can change the apparent pattern.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 2 · Build the line list before the story
text:
LEARN 2 · Build the line list before the story
A line list is a compact dataset in which each row represents one case or observation and each column represents a variable needed for description or investigation.
A practical outbreak line list might include:







Domain
Example variables




Identifier
unique case ID


Person
age, sex, occupation, population group


Place
village, parish, facility, residence or exposure location


Time
date of onset, date reported, date admitted


Clinical
symptoms, laboratory status, outcome


Investigation
selected exposures, contact status, vaccination status



Before analysis, check duplicates, impossible dates, missing age or location, inconsistent categories and the relationship between onset date and report date.

A graph can make bad data look authoritative.
Inspect the line list before you admire the curve.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 3 · Time: choose the clock that matches the process
text:
LEARN 3 · Time: choose the clock that matches the process
Time can be described at very different scales.
Secular trend examines long-term change over years or decades.
Seasonality examines recurring patterns within the year.
Day-of-week or time-of-day patterns can reveal scheduled occupational, behavioural or environmental exposures.
Epidemic time focuses on the short interval relevant to an outbreak.
The x-axis should therefore match the biology and operational question. Annual bins can hide a short outbreak; hourly bins can add noise to a chronic-disease trend.
Events such as a new intervention, a reporting change or a suspected exposure can be annotated on a time plot, but temporal coincidence by itself does not prove effect.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 4 · Epidemic curves are compressed epidemiological arguments
text:
LEARN 4 · Epidemic curves are compressed epidemiological arguments
An epidemic curve plots the number of cases by time of onset, diagnosis or another clearly stated event. Its shape can suggest—but does not by itself prove—the pattern of spread.
Common patterns include:

a concentrated peak compatible with a point-source exposure;
a prolonged or irregular pattern compatible with continuous or intermittent common-source exposure;
successive waves compatible with propagated person-to-person transmission.

The curve can also reveal the magnitude and stage of an outbreak, possible outliers and a plausible exposure window when the incubation period is known.
Do not classify an outbreak from shape alone. Reporting delays, mixed exposures, secondary transmission and missing onset dates can distort the curve.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 5 · Outliers can be clues rather than rubbish

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 6 · Place is whatever geography matters to transmission or risk
text:
LEARN 6 · Place is whatever geography matters to transmission or risk
“Place” is broader than residence. Depending on the question, the relevant location may be a workplace, school, hospital ward, water point, market, travel destination or place of exposure.
Two main mapping approaches have different purposes:
Spot maps show where individual events occurred and are useful for small clusters or outbreaks.
Area maps compare numbers or rates across geographic units. When populations differ substantially, rates are usually more meaningful than raw counts.
A map shows spatial pattern; it does not automatically identify the mechanism producing that pattern. Population density, access to care, diagnostic capacity and reporting completeness can all create geographic differences.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 7 · Person: categories can reveal or conceal risk
text:
LEARN 7 · Person: categories can reveal or conceal risk
Person variables can include age, sex, occupation, socioeconomic measures, behaviours, immune status and other characteristics relevant to the problem.
Age deserves particular care. A broad 0–4 year category may hide that nearly all excess disease is concentrated among infants. Category boundaries should therefore be chosen for epidemiological meaning, not merely because they are convenient.
Similarly, an apparent difference between social groups should not be interpreted as an inherent biological difference without examining exposure, access, measurement and structural context.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 8 · Counts answer burden; rates answer comparative frequency
text:
LEARN 8 · Counts answer burden; rates answer comparative frequency
A district with 500 cases may have a lower disease frequency than a district with 100 cases if their populations differ greatly.
Counts are useful for operational planning: beds, medicines, staff and laboratory workload.
Rates or proportions put events in relation to a population at risk and are more useful for comparing groups of different sizes.
Example:



District
Cases
Population
Cases per 1,000




A
500
500,000
1.0


B
100
20,000
5.0



The smaller district has fewer cases but five times the rate.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: LEARN 9 · Description generates hypotheses; it rarely settles them
text:
LEARN 9 · Description generates hypotheses; it rarely settles them
Suppose cases cluster among children under five, peak after heavy rainfall and are concentrated around two water sources. Those observations can generate hypotheses about exposure and transmission.
A hypothesis should connect the pattern to a mechanism that can be evaluated. For example:

Households relying on selected surface-water sources experienced higher risk of acute watery diarrhoea than households using protected sources.

That hypothesis now suggests what comparison data must be collected.
Descriptive epidemiology therefore bridges observation → hypothesis, while analytic epidemiology adds a comparison capable of testing that hypothesis more rigorously.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district receives 46 reports of acute watery diarrhoea over 10 days. Thirty-four reports come from two neighbouring villages. Onset dates show a sharp rise over three days, followed by a slower decline. Most patients are children, but one case occurred a week earlier in an adult trader who regularly visits both villages. A new private clinic also began reporting during the same month.
Work through the problem before looking for an exposure:

Draft a usable working case definition.
Identify the minimum variables for the line list.
Decide whether onset date or report date should drive the epidemic curve and explain why.
Calculate village-specific rates if population denominators are available.
Identify which observations might be useful outliers.
List at least three hypotheses suggested by the person-place-time pattern.
Identify at least three non-disease explanations for the apparent increase that must be checked.
State what comparison you would need next to test your leading hypothesis.

The point is not to guess the cause. The point is to produce a description strong enough to justify the next question.

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Describing populations without being fooled by composition

title: Descriptive Epidemiology: Person, Place and Time
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

Why can an epidemic curve based on report date tell a different story from one based on symptom-onset date?
A village has twice as many cases as another village but ten times the population. Which comparison is more informative: counts or rates, and why?
What is wrong with including “drank from Water Point X” in the case definition when Water Point X is the exposure you plan to test?
Give two plausible explanations for a late outlier on an epidemic curve other than data-entry error.
Why might five-year age bands hide an important disease pattern among infants?
Does a spatial cluster around a health facility prove that the facility is the source of infection? Explain.

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

Assessment principle
The quiz is designed so that a prepared learner can read, reason and answer efficiently. Timing is a learning-and-assessment parameter to be calibrated from real response-time data, not a substitute for good question design.

Source foundation and LIPPS extensions
Primary source foundation: CDC Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition, especially its treatment of descriptive epidemiology, time, place, person, epidemic curves, spot maps, case definitions and observed-versus-expected reasoning.
LIPPS additions: the fictional district cases, the explicit data-quality workflow, modern wording around reporting-system changes, and the integrated “disease versus observation system” reasoning are instructional extensions rather than material reproduced from the source.
Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. October 2006; updated May 2012.

title: Epidemiology — Core Readings
text:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. Originally published in 2006 and subsequently updated. The LIPPS course uses this source for foundational epidemiological reasoning, frequency measures, association, descriptive epidemiology, basic study designs, surveillance and outbreak investigation.
CDC archive: https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/index.html
CDC Stacks record: https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/13178



The CDC text remains valuable for introductory applied epidemiology, but LIPPS does not treat it as the final word on modern methodology. Course pages explicitly identify later additions such as prevalence ratios, modern causal diagrams, collider bias, cluster-randomised trials, intention-to-treat, quasi-experimental designs, likelihood ratios, ROC analysis and modern critical-appraisal language as LIPPS extensions.
In institutional use, lecturers should pair the course with current discipline-specific reporting standards, ministry/WHO surveillance guidance and contemporary methodological readings appropriate to the programme level.




Weeks 1–4: CDC Lessons 1–3 plus the LIPPS lessons.
Weeks 5–8: CDC study-design sections plus current programme readings on observational and experimental design.
Week 9: current causal-inference and epidemiological-bias reading selected by the lecturer.
Week 10: current diagnostic-accuracy reading and reporting guidance selected by the lecturer.
Week 11: CDC surveillance and outbreak-investigation lessons plus current national/WHO outbreak guidance.
Week 12: a published epidemiological paper chosen for structured critical appraisal.


Important
The course teaches principles. Real surveillance definitions, outbreak protocols and clinical/diagnostic recommendations must be checked against current national and international guidance before operational use.




The CDC text remains the foundation for core measures, field epidemiology and classical study-design logic. Graduate learners should add modern sources because advanced epidemiology now requires explicit estimands, regression-based analysis, causal diagrams, missing-data reasoning and longitudinal causal methods.



Lash TL, VanderWeele TJ, Haneuse S, Rothman KJ, eds. Modern Epidemiology. 4th ed. A comprehensive reference for design, bias, confounding, effect-measure modification and causal interpretation.
Hernán MA, Robins JM. Causal Inference: What If. Freely available from Harvard. Use Part I during Epidemiology I and Parts II–III during Epidemiology II.
CDC. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice. Use especially for classical measures, surveillance, outbreak investigation and field reasoning.





STROBE for cohort, case-control and cross-sectional reporting. STROBE is a reporting guideline, not a study-quality scoring tool.
CONSORT 2025 for randomised trials; the 2025 statement supersedes CONSORT 2010.
STARD 2015 for diagnostic-accuracy studies.
Appropriate extensions such as RECORD for routinely collected health data should be introduced when the data source requires them.




The advanced pathway mirrors the kind of competencies expected in graduate epidemiology programmes: multivariable analysis of cohort and case-control data, survival analysis, correlated data, causal diagrams, missing data and explicit analysis strategies. The purpose is not to imitate another university’s syllabus but to ensure LIPPS learners can perform and defend the analyses expected of an MSc epidemiologist.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text: Advanced foundation Surveillance Outbreaks Field epidemiology

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
This week in one sentence
Use surveillance data to detect and describe public-health signals, evaluate system performance and move systematically from an unusual signal to outbreak investigation, hypothesis testing and control.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: ORIENT · A surveillance signal is not yet an outbreak

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 1 · What surveillance is
The attached CDC course describes public-health surveillance as ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination of health data for public-health decision-making and action.
Surveillance is therefore not just data collection.
A useful surveillance cycle is:
Define → Collect → Consolidate → Analyse → Interpret → Disseminate → Act → Evaluate
The surveillance system supplies information for action; the control intervention itself is conceptually distinct from surveillance.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 2 · Start with the objective, not the database
text:
LEARN 2 · Start with the objective, not the database
Surveillance design should follow the intended use.
If the objective is to identify individual cases quickly for treatment or contact follow-up, timeliness and case-level identification may be critical.
If the objective is to monitor a long-term population trend, weekly individual reports may be unnecessary.
Before building or evaluating a system ask:

What health event is under surveillance?
What is the case definition?
Who is the population under surveillance?
What action will the information support?
How quickly is information needed?
Which sources can supply the required data?
Who needs the findings and in what form?

A system that collects abundant data with no defined decision use is not automatically a strong surveillance system.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 3 · Passive, active, sentinel and syndromic approaches
text:
LEARN 3 · Passive, active, sentinel and syndromic approaches
Passive surveillance relies on routine reporting from clinicians, laboratories or facilities without the health authority actively soliciting every report.
Active surveillance involves deliberate case finding, for example calling facilities or reviewing records during an outbreak.
Sentinel surveillance uses selected reporting sites or providers to monitor a condition or trend rather than attempting full population capture.
Syndromic surveillance monitors symptom complexes or proxy signals before definitive diagnosis and can provide earlier warning, but often at the cost of lower specificity and more false alarms.
The attached text explicitly presents syndromic surveillance as a supplement rather than a universal replacement for traditional surveillance.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 4 · Analyse surveillance data by time, place and person
text:
LEARN 4 · Analyse surveillance data by time, place and person
Routine surveillance analysis should repeatedly ask:
Time: Is occurrence rising, falling, seasonal or unusual compared with prior periods?
Place: Where are counts and rates concentrated?
Person: Which age, sex, occupation, exposure or population groups are most affected?
Counts can guide resources; rates can help compare populations.
A single sudden increase deserves data-quality checks before it is interpreted as biological change. The attached source lists possibilities such as population influx, batch reporting, duplicates, laboratory/computer error and changes in reporting practice.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 6 · Cluster, outbreak and expected background
text:
LEARN 6 · Cluster, outbreak and expected background
A cluster is an aggregation of cases in time or place that appears unusual, sometimes before the expected number is known.
An outbreak or epidemic requires occurrence above what is expected for the population, place and period, although terminology and operational use can vary.
The expected level may come from previous years, previous weeks, a comparable season, registry data or another credible baseline.
Do not interpret “more reports” as “more disease” until you have examined how the observation system changed.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 7 · Outbreak investigation is systematic but not rigid

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 8 · Case definitions must serve case finding
text:
LEARN 8 · Case definitions must serve case finding
A field case definition commonly combines clinical criteria with appropriate person, place and time restrictions.
Early in an investigation, a relatively sensitive definition may help identify the full extent of illness. Later analytic work may use a more specific subset, depending on the objective.
The hypothesised exposure should generally remain outside the case definition when that same exposure will be tested analytically.
If the outbreak expands geographically or the clinical picture changes, the case definition may need revision. Document version changes because they can alter apparent counts and rates.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 9 · Case finding and the line list

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 10 · Description comes before analytic testing
text:
LEARN 10 · Description comes before analytic testing
The attached outbreak lesson emphasises descriptive epidemiology as a critical step because it identifies the population at risk, suggests source and transmission hypotheses, exposes data problems and may support immediate prevention.
Epidemic curves, maps and person-specific rates are not decorative outputs. They help determine what analytic question is worth asking.
A case-control study built on a weak or biologically implausible hypothesis can waste scarce outbreak time.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 11 · Choose the analytic design from the population structure
text:
LEARN 11 · Choose the analytic design from the population structure
For a small, well-defined outbreak population—for example, all attendees at a wedding—a retrospective cohort can often enumerate the population, calculate food-specific attack rates and compare risk directly.
When the source population is large or cannot be completely enumerated, a case-control study may be more efficient. Controls must represent the population that produced the cases, and the odds ratio becomes the natural measure.
The design follows the data-generating setting, not investigator preference.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: LEARN 12 · When the first hypothesis fails

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
LEARN 13 · Action under uncertainty
Field epidemiology is not always afforded the luxury of waiting for perfect evidence.
If a severe and plausible hazard can be controlled with a proportionate, low-harm measure, action may begin while additional evidence is collected.
The standard is not “certainty before action.” It is:

Is the evidence sufficient, given the consequences of delay and the harms of acting, to justify the intervention?

That judgement should be explicit and revisable.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional district normally reports 0–2 suspected viral haemorrhagic fever alerts per month. Over four days, six alerts are received from three health facilities. Two alerts appear to refer to the same patient; one facility recently introduced a new triage checklist; two patients attended the same funeral; laboratory confirmation is pending.
Develop an initial investigation plan:

Decide what must be verified before calling this an outbreak.
Draft a working case definition without embedding funeral attendance as a requirement.
List the first variables for a line list.
State how you would expand case finding.
Describe the data by time, place and person.
Identify the most important data-quality checks.
Propose at least two early hypotheses.
Explain when a retrospective cohort could be used around the funeral and when a case-control design might be preferable.
Name at least five surveillance-system attributes you would later evaluate.
State what control measures could be justified before final laboratory certainty and what harms those measures could create.
Specify who should receive preliminary findings and in what form.
Describe what evidence would make you revise your leading hypothesis.

title: Surveillance, Outbreak Investigation and Field Epidemiology
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Surveillance evaluation, aberration detection and modern outbreak inference
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · Surveillance evaluation, aberration detection and modern outbreak inference
Surveillance is a measurement system embedded in organisations. Its output depends on who seeks care, who is tested, who reports, how definitions change, and how quickly data move through the system.

Evaluate the system, not just the disease curve
Key surveillance attributes include usefulness, simplicity, flexibility, data quality, acceptability, sensitivity, predictive value positive, representativeness, timeliness and stability. Improvements in one attribute can worsen another. A highly sensitive alert definition may generate many false signals and overwhelm response teams.


Baselines and aberration detection
A threshold should reflect the expected distribution of reports, seasonality and reporting delay. Simple approaches include historical limits and moving averages. More formal approaches include CUSUM, EWMA and regression models for count data.
The method is less important than recognising that a signal is not automatically an outbreak. Signals require verification, denominator checks and assessment of reporting artefacts.


Capture-recapture preview
When no single surveillance source is complete, overlapping lists can sometimes be used to estimate the number of unobserved cases. Two-source capture-recapture makes strong independence and equal-catchability assumptions that are often violated in health data. The method is therefore a sensitivity tool, not a magic correction for underreporting.


Delayed reporting and nowcasting
Recent counts are often incomplete because cases diagnosed today may be reported days later. Naïve epidemic curves can therefore create a false appearance of decline at the right edge. Nowcasting methods model reporting delay to estimate recent incidence before all reports arrive.


Reproduction numbers
The basic reproduction number \(R_0\) is a theoretical quantity for a fully susceptible population under specified conditions. The effective reproduction number \(R_t\) changes over time with immunity, behaviour and control measures. Neither should be interpreted without uncertainty and the generation-interval assumptions used to estimate it.


Genomic epidemiology
Pathogen sequencing can help link cases, identify introductions and characterise transmission clusters, but genetic similarity does not automatically prove direct transmission. Sampling density, within-host evolution and unsampled intermediates matter.


Field analysis standard
During an outbreak, speed matters, but speed should not erase design principles. Descriptive epidemiology identifies who, where and when; analytic epidemiology uses a valid comparison group when a causal hypothesis needs testing. The CDC text explicitly treats comparison groups, rates, two-by-two tables and more advanced modelling as part of analytic field epidemiology.

LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 10





Intermediate Screening Sensitivity · Specificity Predictive values

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text: Intermediate Screening Sensitivity · Specificity Predictive values

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
This week in one sentence
Evaluate screening and diagnostic classification using sensitivity, specificity and predictive values, then extend interpretation to likelihood ratios, thresholds and multi-test strategies.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: ORIENT · A positive test is not the same as disease
text:
ORIENT · A positive test is not the same as disease
A screening programme uses a test with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity in a population where disease prevalence is 1%.
Many students hear “95% specificity” and expect nearly every positive test to be a true case.
That intuition is wrong because the number of false positives also depends on how many people without disease are tested.
Diagnostic interpretation is a problem of conditional probability.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 1 · Build the diagnostic two-by-two table
text:
LEARN 1 · Build the diagnostic two-by-two table
Start with true disease status determined by the best available reference classification.




Disease +
Disease −




Test +
True positive (TP)
False positive (FP)


Test −
False negative (FN)
True negative (TN)



The attached CDC material uses the same logic for surveillance-system sensitivity, specificity and predictive value positive.
The denominator determines the question being answered.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 2 · Sensitivity
Sensitivity asks:

Among people who truly have the condition, what proportion does the test identify as positive?

\[
Sensitivity = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}
\]
High sensitivity means relatively few false negatives.
Sensitivity is useful when missing true cases carries important consequences, but maximising sensitivity alone can create many false positives if specificity falls.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 3 · Specificity
Specificity asks:

Among people who truly do not have the condition, what proportion does the test correctly classify as negative?

\[
Specificity = \frac{TN}{FP+TN}
\]
High specificity means relatively few false positives.
Sensitivity and specificity condition on true disease status, not on the observed test result.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 4 · Predictive values reverse the conditioning direction
text:
LEARN 4 · Predictive values reverse the conditioning direction
Positive predictive value (PPV) asks:

Among those who test positive, what proportion truly have the condition?

\[
PPV = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}
\]
Negative predictive value (NPV) asks:

Among those who test negative, what proportion truly do not have the condition?

\[
NPV = \frac{TN}{FN+TN}
\]

Source boundary The attached CDC source explicitly develops predictive value positive in the surveillance context. NPV is included here as a LIPPS diagnostic-testing extension.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 5 · Why prevalence changes PPV
Consider 10,000 people with 1% prevalence.
There are 100 true cases and 9,900 non-cases.
With 90% sensitivity:

TP = 90
FN = 10

With 95% specificity:

TN = 9,405
FP = 495

So:
\[
PPV = \frac{90}{90+495} \approx 15.4\%
\]
Despite good sensitivity and specificity, only about 15% of positive results are true positives in this low-prevalence setting.
As prevalence rises, PPV usually rises and NPV usually falls, holding test properties constant.

This is why “the test is 95% accurate” is usually an unhelpful sentence.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 6 · Sensitivity and PPV answer different questions
text:
LEARN 6 · Sensitivity and PPV answer different questions
This distinction should become automatic.
Sensitivity: start with people who truly have disease → ask how many test positive.
PPV: start with people whose test is positive → ask how many truly have disease.
The same true-positive cell appears in both formulas, but the denominators differ.
Confusing these quantities leads directly to poor patient counselling and poor screening-policy interpretation.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 7 · Likelihood ratios

LIPPS extension Likelihood ratios are not developed in the attached CDC source.

Likelihood ratios describe how much a test result changes the odds of disease.
\[
LR+ = \frac{Sensitivity}{1-Specificity}
\]
\[
LR- = \frac{1-Sensitivity}{Specificity}
\]
A large LR+ provides stronger evidence toward disease; a small LR− provides stronger evidence against disease.
Likelihood ratios combine sensitivity and specificity and can be used with pre-test odds to obtain post-test odds.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 8 · Thresholds create trade-offs
Many tests begin with a continuous value: blood pressure, biomarker concentration, risk score or optical density. A threshold converts that value into positive/negative classification.
Lowering a threshold usually:

identifies more true cases → sensitivity rises;
also labels more non-cases positive → specificity falls.

Raising the threshold usually does the reverse.
There is no universally “best” threshold. The appropriate choice depends on the consequences of false negatives and false positives, disease prevalence, downstream testing capacity and purpose of screening.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 10 · Serial and parallel testing

LIPPS extension Multi-test algorithms are not developed in the attached source.

Serial testing: a second test is performed or required after the first positive. This tends to increase overall specificity but can reduce sensitivity.
Parallel testing: a person may be classified positive if either of two tests is positive. This tends to increase sensitivity but can reduce specificity.
The exact combined performance depends on test dependence and algorithm rules. Do not mechanically multiply test characteristics without checking assumptions.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
LEARN 11 · Agreement is not accuracy
Two tests can agree with each other and both be wrong if neither is compared with an adequate reference standard.
Accuracy questions ask how a test corresponds to true disease status.
Agreement questions ask how two raters or tests correspond to each other.
Measures such as percent agreement and kappa address agreement, not necessarily diagnostic truth.

LIPPS extension Agreement and kappa are not developed in the attached CDC lesson.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: LEARN 12 · What could fool us in a diagnostic study?
text:
LEARN 12 · What could fool us in a diagnostic study?
Important threats include:
Spectrum effects — performance differs across disease severity or patient mix.
Verification bias — only some participants, often those with positive index tests, receive the reference standard.
Imperfect reference standard — the “gold standard” itself misclassifies disease.
Incorporation bias — the index test contributes to the reference diagnosis.
Reader or review bias — interpreters know other test results.
These problems change what apparent sensitivity and specificity mean.
A diagnostic-accuracy estimate belongs to the population, threshold, specimen process and reference standard under which it was obtained.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional typhoid screening study tests 2,000 febrile patients. A reference classification identifies 200 true disease cases. The index test is positive in 170 of those 200 cases and positive in 270 of the 1,800 non-cases.

Construct the 2×2 table.
Calculate sensitivity.
Calculate specificity.
Calculate PPV.
Calculate NPV.
Calculate LR+ and LR−.
Explain why PPV would differ if the same sensitivity and specificity were applied in a much lower-prevalence general population.
If the screening threshold is lowered, predict the usual direction of change in sensitivity and specificity.
Explain why a high percent agreement with another rapid test would not establish accuracy.
Identify how the study could be biased if only index-test-positive patients received the reference test.
Write a counselling statement that avoids telling every positive patient that they “have typhoid” with certainty.

title: Screening and Diagnostic-Test Evaluation
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · From test accuracy to clinical and public-health consequences
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · From test accuracy to clinical and public-health consequences
Sensitivity and specificity are only the beginning. A test is useful when its results change decisions in a population where those decisions improve outcomes relative to their costs and harms.

Bayesian updating with likelihood ratios
Pre-test odds are converted to post-test odds by:
\[
Posttest\ odds = Pretest\ odds \times LR
\]
where:
\[
LR^+=\frac{Sensitivity}{1-Specificity},\qquad LR^-=\frac{1-Sensitivity}{Specificity}
\]
This makes prevalence or prior probability explicit. A positive result from the same assay can imply very different post-test probabilities in a high-risk referral clinic versus a low-prevalence screening programme.


ROC curves are not decision curves
The ROC curve summarises sensitivity and specificity across thresholds. The area under the curve describes ranking/discrimination, not calibration, clinical benefit or the best threshold for a programme.
A model can discriminate well while producing poorly calibrated probabilities. Conversely, a modest change in AUC can still be clinically useful if it moves patients across a meaningful treatment threshold.


Spectrum effects
Accuracy depends on who is tested. A case-control accuracy study comparing obvious severe cases with exceptionally healthy controls can overestimate performance relative to routine practice, where disease severity and alternative diagnoses form a broader spectrum.


Verification and incorporation bias
If only participants with positive index tests receive the reference standard, estimates can be biased. If the index test forms part of the reference standard, agreement is partly built into the definition of truth. Blinding and prespecified handling of indeterminate results also matter.


Comparing two tests
When two tests are applied to the same participants, their results are paired. Analyses should preserve that pairing rather than compare sensitivity estimates as though they came from independent samples.


Imperfect reference standards
Some conditions have no error-free gold standard. Options include composite reference standards, expert adjudication, follow-up information or latent-class approaches, but each adds assumptions. Report the intended use and clinical role of the index test rather than describing accuracy in the abstract.


STARD and transparent reporting
STARD 2015 asks diagnostic-accuracy studies to report participant selection, index and reference test methods, prespecified thresholds, blinding, handling of indeterminate and missing results, variability analyses, sample-size rationale and precision of accuracy estimates.


R laboratory
Use the diagnostic component in Graduate Lab 7 — Diagnostic accuracy, predictive values and decision thresholds →.

text:

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

Case-control analysis
Survival analysis
Trials and quasi-experiments
Diagnostic accuracy
Surveillance and outbreak signals

All datasets are fictional and generated for teaching. They are deliberately small enough to run on ordinary laptops. The displayed R code is non-executable in Quarto so the public site does not require an R runtime during deployment.

title: R laboratories
text:
Submission standard
A laboratory submission should include the question, estimand, reproducible code, one diagnostic/assumption check, a concise results paragraph and a What could fool us? note. A technically correct model without a defensible epidemiological interpretation is incomplete.

title: Unmatched and matched case-control analysis
text: EPIDEMIOLOGY I · R LAB 04

title: Unmatched and matched case-control analysis
text:
LAB PROTOCOL · Graduate submission standard

Epidemiological question
How does control sampling and matching determine the estimand and analysis of a case-control study?


Before opening R
Write down the target population, exposure/treatment contrast, outcome, time horizon and effect measure. State the design and the assumptions that would make the proposed estimate meaningful. This paragraph is part of the submission: code without an estimand is incomplete.


Required analysis products
Construct the 2x2 table, estimate crude OR, fit unconditional and—where matched identifiers are provided—conditional logistic models, and state what quantity each OR estimates under the sampling scheme.
Every numerical result should be accompanied by a plain-language interpretation. Avoid reporting software output as though coefficients interpret themselves. If a model is used, state the link function, covariates, rationale for adjustment and how uncertainty was calculated.


Diagnostics that must appear in the report
Check source-population eligibility, matching variables, sparse matched sets, influential exposure patterns and whether any post-exposure variable has been adjusted for.
A diagnostic is not a ceremonial plot. State what failure it is intended to reveal and what you would change if that failure were present.


Reproducibility requirements
Your submission should run from a clean R session. Use relative paths, set no user-specific working directory, keep data cleaning separate from analysis, label derived variables, and generate the final tables/figures from code. Include sessionInfo() or an equivalent dependency record. Do not manually copy numbers from the console into the final table.


Interpretation discipline
End with four statements: 1. Estimate: what was estimated, on what scale and with what uncertainty? 2. Assumptions: which design/identification assumptions matter most? 3. Diagnostics: what evidence supports or challenges those assumptions? 4. Claim: what can be concluded, and what stronger claim would not be justified?


PhD extension
Recast the dataset as risk-set sampled controls and explain why the matched OR estimates an incidence-rate ratio without invoking the rare-disease approximation.


Suggested marking rubric (20 marks)

estimand/design logic — 4
reproducible data management and code — 3
correct analysis — 5
diagnostics/sensitivity analysis — 4
interpretation and limits of inference — 4

A technically correct model with an incoherent causal question should not receive a high distinction.

title: Survey prevalence, weighting and adjusted prevalence ratios
text:
What could fool us?
Weights repair only selection mechanisms represented in their construction. A weighted estimate can still be biased by non-response, measurement error, undercoverage and poor auxiliary variables.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 07





Intermediate Cohort Incidence Follow-up

title: Cohort Studies
text: Intermediate Cohort Incidence Follow-up

title: Cohort Studies
text:
This week in one sentence
Use cohort designs to estimate incidence and compare outcome occurrence between exposure groups while accounting for follow-up, person-time and loss to observation.

The LIPPS lens
Evidence becomes useful when you can explain not only what the analysis shows, but also what the design, measurement and comparison allow you to claim.

title: Cohort Studies
Cohort Studies
text:
ORIENT · Exposure comes first
A cohort study starts with a group defined by exposure or another baseline characteristic and asks what happens afterwards.
Imagine 2,000 health workers without active tuberculosis at baseline. Half work in high-exposure clinical areas and half in lower-exposure settings. They are followed for two years and new tuberculosis diagnoses are recorded.
Because outcome-free people are observed over time, the design can estimate incidence, not merely prevalence.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 1 · The core structure
The attached CDC text describes cohort studies as observational designs in which participants are grouped by exposure and then followed to document disease occurrence.
Conceptually:
Exposed → outcome / no outcome
Unexposed → outcome / no outcome
The comparison group estimates what disease occurrence might have looked like without the exposure pattern of primary interest.
Unlike an experiment, the investigator does not assign exposure; the exposure occurs under natural or existing conditions.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 2 · Prospective and retrospective cohorts
In a prospective cohort, participants are enrolled before the outcome occurs and are followed forward.
In a retrospective cohort, both exposure and outcome may already have occurred when the study begins, but the logical sequence remains exposure → outcome. Existing records reconstruct the cohort and follow-up.
The attached CDC material emphasises this important point: retrospective does not mean case-control. A retrospective cohort still groups people by exposure and compares subsequent disease occurrence.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 3 · Cohorts estimate incidence directly
If all participants are outcome-free at baseline and follow-up is defined, you can calculate risk:
\[
Risk_E = \frac{\text{new cases among exposed}}{\text{exposed population at risk at baseline}}
\]
and similarly for the unexposed group.
You can then calculate:
\[
RR = Risk_E / Risk_U
\]
and:
\[
RD = Risk_E - Risk_U
\]
These have direct interpretations because the denominators arise from actual populations at risk rather than investigator-selected numbers of cases and controls.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 4 · A worked risk comparison
Suppose 80 of 800 exposed workers develop a condition, compared with 20 of 1,000 unexposed workers.
\[
Risk_E = 80/800 = 10\%
\]
\[
Risk_U = 20/1000 = 2\%
\]
\[
RR = 10\%/2\% = 5.0
\]
\[
RD = 10\%-2\% = 8\text{ percentage points}
\]
A careful interpretation is:

During the specified follow-up, exposed workers had five times the risk and eight additional cases per 100 workers compared with the unexposed group.

Whether that difference is causal depends on confounding, bias, measurement and the wider design.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 5 · Person-time when follow-up differs
Participants do not always contribute equal follow-up. Some enter late, migrate, die, withdraw or develop the outcome early.
Person-time accumulates the time each person remains under observation and at risk.
\[
Incidence\ rate = \frac{new\ cases}{total\ person-time\ at\ risk}
\]
The attached CDC text explains that person-time is useful precisely because it can accommodate different observation periods.
A rate ratio then compares person-time incidence rates between groups.

title: Cohort Studies
section: LEARN 6 · Censoring is not the same as failure
text:
LEARN 6 · Censoring is not the same as failure
A participant who leaves follow-up without developing the outcome does not necessarily become a case or a non-case for the whole intended period. Their observed disease-free time can still contribute information.
This is the idea behind censoring.

LIPPS extension
Formal survival-analysis methods are beyond this introductory week, but learners should understand that incomplete follow-up is handled through time-to-event methods rather than by pretending everyone was observed equally.

title: Cohort Studies
section: LEARN 7 · Loss to follow-up can create bias
text:
LEARN 7 · Loss to follow-up can create bias
Loss to follow-up first reduces information, but it becomes a threat to validity when loss is related to both exposure and outcome risk.
Example: if highly exposed workers who develop early symptoms are more likely to leave employment and disappear from records, the observed exposed cohort may look healthier than the true cohort.
Ask:

How much follow-up is missing?
Why did participants leave?
Does loss differ by exposure group?
Is outcome risk plausibly related to the reason for loss?

The percentage lost is important, but the mechanism of loss matters more.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 8 · Comparison cohort quality
An unexposed cohort should represent a credible baseline for the exposed group.
If exposed workers differ from unexposed workers in age, socioeconomic status, access to care or baseline disease risk, crude outcome differences may reflect those factors rather than exposure.
Restriction, matching, stratification and regression can sometimes address measured differences, but design-stage comparability remains fundamental.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
LEARN 9 · Time-varying exposure

LIPPS extension Many real exposures change during follow-up. A participant may start medication, change occupation, stop smoking or move between exposure categories.

Treating a changing exposure as if it remained fixed can misclassify person-time and obscure temporal relationships.
At introductory level, the key question is simple:

Does the exposure value at baseline still represent the participant’s exposure throughout the period being analysed?

If not, a more advanced longitudinal analysis may be needed.

title: Cohort Studies
Cohort Studies
text:
APPLY · Integrated public-health problem
A fictional cohort enrols 3,000 adults free of diabetes. At baseline, 1,000 have a high-risk occupational exposure and 2,000 do not. Over five years, 100 exposed and 80 unexposed participants develop diabetes. Follow-up time totals 4,200 person-years in the exposed group and 8,800 person-years in the unexposed group.

Calculate cumulative risk in each group.
Calculate the risk ratio and risk difference.
Calculate incidence rates per 1,000 person-years.
Calculate the rate ratio.
Explain why risk ratio and rate ratio answer related but not identical questions.
Suppose 20% of exposed participants with early symptoms leave employment and cannot be traced. Explain the potential direction of bias.
Identify at least three baseline variables that could confound the association.
Explain whether this observational cohort can establish causation merely because exposure was measured before disease.
If exposure status changed for many participants, state what additional information should have been collected.
Write a defensible conclusion.

title: Cohort Studies
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Time-to-event analysis, censoring and immortal time
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · Time-to-event analysis, censoring and immortal time
Once follow-up varies across people, a single risk at the end of study can hide important information. Survival analysis treats when an event occurs as part of the outcome.

Survival and hazard are different quantities
The survival function is:
\[
S(t)=P(T>t)
\]
It gives the probability of remaining event-free beyond time \(t\).
The hazard describes the instantaneous event rate among those still event-free. A hazard ratio therefore compares hazards, not cumulative risks. Even when hazards are proportional, a hazard ratio of 0.70 does not literally mean a 30% lower risk at every time point.


Kaplan-Meier estimation
The Kaplan-Meier estimator updates survival whenever an event occurs and can accommodate right censoring. It assumes that, conditional on the information used, censored participants are sufficiently comparable to those remaining under observation. If people leave because they are deteriorating and that process is not addressed, the estimate can be biased.


Cox proportional-hazards model
The Cox model relates covariates to the hazard without specifying the baseline hazard:
\[
h(t|X)=h_0(t)\exp(\beta X)
\]
The proportional-hazards assumption implies a stable hazard ratio over time. Check it rather than merely report a Cox model because software made it convenient. If the effect changes over time, consider time interactions, flexible models or reporting time-specific absolute risks.


Competing risks
If death prevents the outcome of interest, standard Kaplan-Meier methods that censor deaths can overstate the real-world probability of that outcome. Decide whether your scientific question concerns a cause-specific hazard or the cumulative incidence of the outcome in the presence of competing events.


Immortal-time bias
Immortal time is a period during which, by design, a participant must remain outcome-free to be classified as exposed. Suppose “treated” means receiving a drug within 90 days after diagnosis, but follow-up begins at diagnosis. Anyone who dies on day 20 can never become treated, while those eventually treated must survive long enough to receive treatment. Misclassifying the pre-treatment period as exposed creates an artificial survival advantage.
Time-varying exposure coding or explicit target-trial alignment can prevent this bias.


Loss to follow-up as informative censoring
Instead of reporting only the percentage lost, model the causal structure of loss. Ask whether determinants of dropout also predict the outcome and whether they differ across exposure groups. In advanced work, inverse-probability-of-censoring weights can be used under explicit assumptions.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

What feature distinguishes a retrospective cohort from a case-control study?
Why can a cohort estimate incidence directly?
When would person-time be preferable to a single baseline denominator?
How can loss to follow-up introduce bias rather than simply imprecision?
If risk is 10% versus 2%, calculate RR and RD.
Why does prospective follow-up improve temporality without eliminating confounding?

Use Practice mode to work slowly and review explanations. Mastery mode should be attempted only after you can answer these kinds of questions without searching for definitions.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
DEMONSTRATE · Week 7 mastery quiz
Pilot Mastery Quiz: 15 objective questions drawn from a Week 7 bank of 55 items.
Initial time limit: 12 minutes because several items use risk and person-time calculations.
Question style: cohort recognition, prospective/retrospective distinctions, incidence, RR/RD/rate ratios, follow-up and loss-to-follow-up scenarios.

Assessment principle
The quiz is designed so that a prepared learner can read, reason and answer efficiently. Timing is a learning-and-assessment parameter to be calibrated from real response-time data, not a substitute for good question design.

title: Cohort Studies
text:
Source foundation and LIPPS extensions
Primary source foundation: the attached CDC text’s cohort definitions, prospective and retrospective cohort examples, incidence comparison and person-time concepts.
LIPPS extensions: censoring, time-varying exposure and a more explicit loss-to-follow-up causal framework are included as introductory bridges to survival and longitudinal analysis.
Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, Third Edition: An Introduction to Applied Epidemiology and Biostatistics. October 2006; updated May 2012.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 02





Epidemiology becomes useful when counts are placed in the population and time from which they arose. This week develops the language used to describe disease occurrence: ratios, proportions, rates, incidence, prevalence, mortality and selected population-health measures.
Foundation Disease frequency Denominators Applied calculations

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
Epidemiology becomes useful when counts are placed in the population and time from which they arose. This week develops the language used to describe disease occurrence: ratios, proportions, rates, incidence, prevalence, mortality and selected population-health measures.
Foundation Disease frequency Denominators Applied calculations

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
This week in one sentence
Choose the numerator, choose the correct population and time denominator, calculate the measure, and interpret exactly what that measure describes.

The LIPPS lens
Most errors in introductory epidemiology are not arithmetic errors. They are denominator errors, population errors, time errors or interpretation errors. A perfectly calculated fraction can still answer the wrong question.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: ORIENT · Which district has more malaria?
text:
ORIENT · Which district has more malaria?
Consider this fictional teaching scenario.



District
New malaria cases in June
Population




A
900
450,000


B
600
120,000



District A has the larger count.
But if the question is, “Where was new malaria occurrence higher relative to population size?”, the count alone cannot answer it.
For a simplified population comparison:

District A: 900 / 450,000 = 2.0 per 1,000
District B: 600 / 120,000 = 5.0 per 1,000

So District A has more reported new cases, while District B has the higher occurrence relative to its population.

Two answers can both be correct
Where is the larger workload? Possibly District A.
Where is disease occurrence higher relative to population size? District B.
The measure must match the decision.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 1 · Count, ratio, proportion and rate are not interchangeable
text:
LEARN 1 · Count, ratio, proportion and rate are not interchangeable

Count
A count is simply the number of events observed: 120 measles cases, 18 maternal deaths, 450 positive tests.
Counts matter for planning beds, medicines, vaccines, staff and laboratory supplies. But counts alone usually do not permit fair comparisons between populations of different sizes.


Ratio
A ratio compares one quantity with another. The numerator does not have to be part of the denominator.
For example, if a facility has 30 nurses and 10 clinical officers, the nurse-to-clinical-officer ratio is 3:1.


Proportion
A proportion is a ratio in which the numerator is included within the denominator.
If 240 of 800 surveyed adults have hypertension:
240 / 800 = 0.30 = 30%.
All 240 people in the numerator are part of the 800 people in the denominator.


Rate
The attached CDC text defines a rate as a measure of how frequently an event occurs in a defined population over a specified period. The term rate is also used loosely in epidemiology for some measures that are mathematically proportions, such as attack rate and case-fatality rate.

Do not argue from the label alone. Inspect the fraction.
Ask whether the numerator is contained within the denominator, whether time is incorporated, and what population the denominator represents.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 2 · The denominator is part of the scientific question
text:
LEARN 2 · The denominator is part of the scientific question
A denominator should represent the population capable of contributing to the numerator.
If the numerator is new ovarian cancer cases, a denominator including people who cannot develop ovarian cancer would not represent the true population at risk. The CDC lesson uses this kind of example to show that denominators are conceptual decisions, not merely numbers taken from a census.
Before calculating any epidemiological measure, ask:

Who could have become a case?
Who was actually under observation?
At what time were they at risk?
Does the denominator correspond to the numerator?
Is this denominator complete and comparable across groups?


Denominator mismatch
Suppose a hospital reports 300 positive malaria tests among 1,000 people tested. That gives test positivity of 30% among those tested.
It does not automatically give malaria prevalence in the district, because the denominator is people tested, not the district population or a representative sample of it.
The arithmetic may be flawless while the epidemiological interpretation is wrong.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 3 · Incidence proportion: the probability of becoming a case
text:
LEARN 3 · Incidence proportion: the probability of becoming a case
Incidence concerns new events.
The attached CDC lesson distinguishes two common incidence measures: incidence proportion and incidence rate.

Incidence proportion
Incidence proportion is the proportion of an initially disease-free population that develops the health event during a specified period.
[ = ]
It may also be called risk, cumulative incidence, or—particularly during an outbreak—attack rate.


Fictional example
A cohort begins with 2,000 adults without hypertension. During one year, 140 develop hypertension.
[ 140 / 2,000 = 0.07 = 7% ]
Interpretation:

Seven percent of the initially hypertension-free cohort developed hypertension during the one-year period.

Notice what the measure requires:

new cases;
an initially disease-free population;
a defined period;
a denominator representing people who could become new cases.



What incidence proportion is NOT
It is not the proportion who have hypertension at the end of the year. Some participants may already have had hypertension before follow-up, and those belong in a prevalence calculation rather than the new-case numerator.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 4 · Attack rates and secondary attack rates
text:
LEARN 4 · Attack rates and secondary attack rates
During outbreaks, attack rate is commonly used as another name for incidence proportion.

Overall attack rate
[ ]


Exposure-specific attack rate
Suppose 80 wedding guests ate chicken and 32 became ill.
[ 32/80 = 40% ]
The food-specific attack rate among chicken eaters is 40%.
But this still does not tell us whether chicken was associated with illness. We also need the attack rate among people who did not eat chicken. The comparison itself belongs in Week 3.


Secondary attack rate
The CDC lesson describes secondary attack rate as useful for examining transmission among contacts of primary cases in households or other closed populations.
A common form is:
[ = ]
Primary cases are generally excluded from the contact denominator because they are not at risk of becoming secondary cases from themselves.


Fictional example
Twelve primary cases occur in 12 households containing 58 people in total. During the relevant secondary transmission period, 9 additional household members develop the disease.
Contacts at risk = 58 − 12 = 46.
[ 9/46 = 19.6% ]
The secondary attack rate is approximately 19.6%.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 5 · Incidence rate: when follow-up time differs
text:
LEARN 5 · Incidence rate: when follow-up time differs
Incidence proportion treats the starting population as the denominator. That works best when the cohort is reasonably closed and the observation period is clearly defined.
But people often contribute different amounts of follow-up. They enrol late, migrate, die, are lost to follow-up, or develop the outcome at different times.

Person-time solves a different denominator problem
The attached CDC text defines incidence rate (person-time rate) using:
[ = ]
One person followed disease-free for two years contributes 2 person-years. Ten people each followed for six months contribute 5 person-years in total.


Fictional example
A cohort contributes 1,850 person-years of disease-free observation and 37 participants develop tuberculosis.
[ 37 / 1,850 = 0.020 ]
or 20 new TB cases per 1,000 person-years.
This means disease occurred at a rate of 20 new cases for every 1,000 person-years of observed time at risk.


Risk and rate are not the same quantity
Incidence proportion answers approximately: What proportion of this initially at-risk population became cases during this period?
Incidence rate answers approximately: How quickly are new cases occurring in the accumulated time at risk?
Do not attach a percent sign to a person-time rate.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 6 · Prevalence: who has the condition?
text:
LEARN 6 · Prevalence: who has the condition?
Prevalence includes existing cases, not only new ones.

Point prevalence
[ = ]
If 360 of 1,200 adults surveyed today meet the definition of hypertension:
[ 360/1,200 = 30% ]
The point prevalence is 30%.


Period prevalence
Period prevalence includes people who had the condition at any time during a specified interval, whether it was already present when the interval began or developed during it.


Incidence versus prevalence
The source makes the distinction through the numerator:
Incidence numerator → new cases only
Prevalence numerator → all cases present in the relevant period
This is one of the most important distinctions in introductory epidemiology.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 7 · Why high prevalence does not necessarily mean high incidence
text:
LEARN 7 · Why high prevalence does not necessarily mean high incidence
Prevalence is influenced by both new occurrence and duration.
A condition may have high prevalence because:

many new cases are developing;
people remain affected for a long time;
survival has improved without cure; or
several of these processes occur together.

A condition may have low prevalence because:

few new cases occur;
recovery is rapid; or
mortality is rapid.


Two diseases, same incidence, different prevalence
Imagine two conditions generate the same number of new cases each year.
Condition A usually resolves in 5 days.
Condition B commonly persists for 20 years.
A cross-sectional survey is much more likely to find a larger pool of existing Condition B cases.

LIPPS warning
Do not infer the speed of disease occurrence from prevalence alone. Prevalence is a snapshot of the pool of existing disease; that pool is filled by incidence and emptied by recovery, death or other exits.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 8 · Mortality measures: death needs a denominator too
text:
LEARN 8 · Mortality measures: death needs a denominator too
A population mortality rate relates deaths occurring during a period to the population in which those deaths occurred.

Crude mortality rate
All deaths in the population, from all causes, divided by the relevant population.


Cause-specific mortality rate
Deaths from one specified cause divided by the population in which those deaths occurred.


Age-, sex- or other stratum-specific mortality rate
Both numerator and denominator are restricted to the same subgroup.
For example:
[ ]
is an age- and cause-specific mortality measure.


Why specificity matters
If the numerator contains deaths among women aged 15–49, but the denominator is the entire district population, the numerator and denominator do not describe the same population.
Always ask:

Who is represented in the numerator, and is the denominator the population from which those deaths could arise?

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 9 · Crude rates can be distorted by population structure
text:
LEARN 9 · Crude rates can be distorted by population structure
The CDC text uses the contrast between Alaska and Florida to demonstrate an important idea: one population can have a higher crude mortality rate simply because it contains more older people.
When mortality strongly varies with age, comparing crude mortality between populations with different age structures can be misleading.

Two approaches
Stratification: compare age-specific rates within comparable age groups.
Standardisation/adjustment: calculate a summary rate that removes the effect of different age distributions.
Detailed age standardisation is beyond the core calculations for this week, but the reasoning matters now:

A crude difference may partly represent population composition rather than a difference in underlying age-specific mortality.

This same principle will return later when we discuss confounding.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 10 · Case fatality is not population mortality
text:
LEARN 10 · Case fatality is not population mortality

Case-fatality measure
The CDC lesson defines case fatality as the proportion of people with a particular condition who die from that condition.
[ = ]
It is mainly a measure of severity among identified cases, not the frequency of death in the entire population.
If 8 of 200 confirmed cases die:
[ 8/200 = 4% ]
Case fatality = 4%.


Proportionate mortality
Proportionate mortality asks what share of all deaths is due to a particular cause.
[ ]
If 50 of 500 recorded deaths were from road traffic injuries, proportionate mortality due to road traffic injuries is 10%.
This does not mean 10% of the population died from road traffic injuries. The denominator contains deaths, not people in the population.


Three different questions
Population mortality: How often are people in the population dying?
Case fatality: Among people with the disease, what proportion die from it?
Proportionate mortality: Among all deaths, what share is due to this cause?

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: LEARN 11 · Maternal, neonatal and infant mortality measures
text:
LEARN 11 · Maternal, neonatal and infant mortality measures
The attached CDC lesson presents several mortality measures that use live births rather than a mid-period population as the denominator.

Neonatal mortality
Deaths among infants younger than 28 days during a period divided by live births during that period, commonly expressed per 1,000 live births.


Postneonatal mortality
Deaths from 28 days to under one year divided by live births, commonly expressed per 1,000 live births.


Infant mortality
Deaths before one year of age divided by live births in the same period, commonly expressed per 1,000 live births.
The source explicitly notes an important terminology point: the traditional infant mortality rate is not a pure population rate in the strict mathematical sense because its denominator is live births rather than the mid-year population of infants.


Maternal mortality terminology in the source
The CDC text labels the measure maternal mortality rate, but also explicitly says it is really a ratio, because pregnancy-related maternal deaths are divided by live births rather than by the population of women at risk.
That observation is a useful reminder:

The conventional name of an indicator does not remove the need to understand its numerator and denominator.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
text:
LEARN 12 · Natality measures
The CDC lesson also introduces population-based measures of birth.

Crude birth rate
[ ,000 ]


Crude fertility rate
[ ,000 ]


Low-birth-weight ratio
[ ]
The important lesson is not to memorise a table of indicators. It is to inspect how the denominator changes the question.
A crude birth rate describes births relative to the whole population. A fertility rate narrows the denominator to a population more directly related to childbearing. The low-birth-weight measure asks what proportion of births meet a defined birth-weight criterion.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: GO DEEPER · Years of potential life lost
text:
GO DEEPER · Years of potential life lost
The CDC lesson includes years of potential life lost (YPLL) as a way to describe premature mortality. Rather than treating every death as contributing equally, YPLL gives more weight to deaths occurring earlier than a selected endpoint.
Conceptually:
[ = - ]
for deaths occurring before the endpoint.
This can highlight causes that produce death at younger ages even when they are not the leading causes by total death count.
YPLL is presented here as an extension concept rather than a core Week 2 mastery calculation. The source itself notes that the choice of endpoint embeds a value judgement because earlier deaths contribute more potential years lost.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: APPLY · Choose the measure before calculating
text:
APPLY · Choose the measure before calculating
For each scenario, identify the most appropriate measure and explain the denominator.

Scenario A · New hypertension diagnoses
A closed cohort of 1,500 adults without hypertension is followed for 12 months. Ninety develop hypertension.
Best measure: Incidence proportion.
Denominator: The 1,500 adults at risk at the start.


Scenario B · Different follow-up time
A TB cohort experiences 22 new recurrences during 940 person-years of post-treatment observation.
Best measure: Incidence rate.
Denominator: 940 person-years at risk.


Scenario C · Burden today
A representative district survey finds 420 people with diabetes among 3,000 adults examined during the survey.
Best measure: Point prevalence, if status refers to the survey point/period as defined.
Denominator: The examined target population represented by the survey, subject to the survey design and weighting.


Scenario D · Severity among cases
An outbreak produces 160 confirmed cases and 12 of those people die from the disease.
Best measure: Case fatality.
Denominator: The 160 cases.


Scenario E · Cause among deaths
A district records 1,100 deaths, of which 220 are attributed to malaria.
Best measure: Proportionate mortality due to malaria.
Denominator: All 1,100 deaths.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: WORKED EXAMPLE · One dataset, four different measures
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · One dataset, four different measures
Consider a fictional boarding-school outbreak.
At the beginning of the week there are 500 students, none currently ill. During the week 75 students become ill. The 75 cases occur across several dormitories. In the dormitories of the first 20 cases, there are 80 additional susceptible roommates, and 24 of those roommates develop illness during the relevant secondary period. At the end of Friday, 30 students are still ill.

1. Weekly incidence proportion / attack rate
[ 75/500 = 15% ]
Interpretation: 15% of students at risk at the beginning became cases during the week.


2. Secondary attack rate among susceptible roommates
[ 24/80 = 30% ]
Interpretation: 30% of the defined susceptible contacts developed illness during the secondary-risk period.


3. Point prevalence on Friday
[ 30/500 = 6% ]
Interpretation: 6% of the school population was ill at the specified Friday assessment point, assuming the denominator remains appropriate.


4. Why attack rate and Friday prevalence differ
The attack rate counts new cases accumulated during the week. Friday point prevalence counts people still ill at one point in time. Students who became ill and recovered before Friday contribute to incidence but not Friday point prevalence.

Same population. Same outbreak. Different questions. Different numerators. Different measures.

title: Measuring Disease Frequency and Population Health
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Standardisation, attributable burden and dynamic populations
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · Standardisation, attributable burden and dynamic populations
Crude rates are often unsuitable for comparing populations with different structures. If District A has an older population than District B, a higher crude mortality rate may reflect age composition rather than a higher age-specific mortality experience.

Direct standardisation
Direct standardisation applies each population’s stratum-specific rates to a common standard population:
\[
R_{std}=\frac{\sum_i w_i r_i}{\sum_i w_i}
\]
where \(r_i\) is the stratum-specific rate and \(w_i\) is the standard population weight. The resulting rate is a weighted summary for comparison, not the literal rate observed in either population.
Good practice is to report the crude and standardised estimates together. The crude rate describes the observed burden; the standardised rate helps compare underlying rate patterns after controlling for the standardising variable.


Indirect standardisation and the SMR
When stratum-specific rates in the study population are unstable, you can apply external standard rates to the study population to obtain an expected number of events. The standardised mortality ratio (SMR) is:
\[
SMR=\frac{Observed\ deaths}{Expected\ deaths}
\]
An SMR above 1 indicates more deaths than expected under the standard rates. An SMR is relative to its chosen standard and is not interchangeable with a directly standardised rate.


Population attributable impact
Relative effects can be large while population impact remains small if exposure is rare. Conversely, a modest effect from a very common exposure can generate substantial population burden.
For a simple dichotomous exposure under strong causal assumptions:
\[
PAF=\frac{P(D)-P(D\mid E=0)}{P(D)}
\]
or, when an adjusted causal risk ratio and exposure prevalence can appropriately be combined, an equivalent formulation may be used. The interpretation is counterfactual: the proportion of disease that would be prevented if the exposure were eliminated under the assumptions of the causal model. A PAF is therefore not merely a descriptive percentage of cases who are exposed.


Risk, rate and odds answer different questions
Risk concerns the probability of an event over a specified interval. A rate concerns the speed at which events occur per unit person-time. Odds compare event probability with non-event probability. These quantities are related but not interchangeable.
A graduate-level interpretation should always retain the time component:

“The 2-year risk was 8%” is interpretable. “The risk was 8%” is incomplete.

Similarly, a rate of 12 per 1,000 person-years does not imply that exactly 12 of every 1,000 persons will experience the event in a year unless additional assumptions hold.


Competing events and recurrent events
A simple cumulative-incidence calculation becomes more complicated when another event prevents the outcome from occurring. Death can compete with development of end-stage renal disease; hysterectomy can prevent future cervical cancer incidence. Treating competing events as ordinary censoring can answer a different question from the one decision-makers care about.
Some outcomes can also recur. Malaria episodes, hospital admissions and asthma exacerbations are not naturally reduced to “ever/never” without losing information. Event rates, recurrent-event methods or multi-state models may be more appropriate.

MSc standard
For every frequency measure, state the numerator, denominator, population, time period and whether repeated events or competing events are possible.
