text:
LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY · WEEK 03





Week 2 asked how often disease or another health event occurs. Week 3 asks the next question: how does occurrence differ between groups? We move from counting and measuring frequency to quantifying association, absolute difference, and selected measures of public-health impact.
Foundation Comparison 2 × 2 tables Effect measures

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
Week 2 asked how often disease or another health event occurs. Week 3 asks the next question: how does occurrence differ between groups? We move from counting and measuring frequency to quantifying association, absolute difference, and selected measures of public-health impact.
Foundation Comparison 2 × 2 tables Effect measures

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
This week in one sentence
Measure the outcome in each comparison group first; only then choose a measure that expresses the comparison in a form that answers the public-health question.

The LIPPS lens
A large relative association can correspond to a small absolute difference, and a small relative association can matter greatly when the outcome is common. Never interpret the ratio without looking at the underlying risks or rates.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
Measures of Association and Effect
section: ORIENT · “Three times higher” — but three times what?
text:
ORIENT · “Three times higher” — but three times what?
Consider two fictional communities followed for one year.



Community
Population initially at risk
New cases
One-year risk




A
1,000
60
6%


B
1,000
20
2%



A report could state:

“Community A had three times the risk of disease compared with Community B.”

That is true because:
\[
RR = 0.06 / 0.02 = 3.0
\]
But the same data can also be expressed as an absolute difference:
\[
RD = 0.06 - 0.02 = 0.04 = 4\text{ percentage points}
\]
So both of these statements describe the same comparison:

relative: risk was three times as high;
absolute: there were 4 additional cases per 100 people at risk.

Neither description is automatically “better.” The useful measure depends on the question.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 1 · Comparison is the hallmark of analytic epidemiology
text:
LEARN 1 · Comparison is the hallmark of analytic epidemiology
The attached CDC text emphasises that the key to epidemiological analysis is comparison. A high disease frequency in one group becomes more interpretable when compared with an appropriate group representing what might otherwise be expected.
The broad structure is:
Observed group
versus
Comparison group
Examples include:

exposed versus unexposed;
vaccinated versus unvaccinated;
intervention versus control;
one district versus another;
one time period versus another; or
people with one characteristic versus people without it.

The source lists risk ratio, rate ratio, odds ratio and proportionate mortality ratio as examples of comparative measures.

Before calculating anything
Ask:

What exactly are the two groups?
What outcome is being compared?
Is the outcome measured as a risk, rate, prevalence, odds or mortality proportion?
Is the comparison group a defensible representation of the expected level?
Does the design allow this quantity to be estimated directly?


A measure of association cannot rescue a bad comparison group.
If the groups are not meaningfully comparable, a beautifully calculated ratio can still be misleading.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
LEARN 2 · The two-by-two table
For a binary exposure and a binary outcome, epidemiologists often begin with a two-by-two table.




Outcome +
Outcome −
Total




Exposed
a
b
a + b


Unexposed
c
d
c + d


Total
a + c
b + d
N



From this table:
\[
Risk_E = \frac{a}{a+b}
\]
\[
Risk_U = \frac{c}{c+d}
\]
\[
RR = \frac{Risk_E}{Risk_U}
\]
\[
RD = Risk_E - Risk_U
\]
\[
OR = \frac{ad}{bc}
\]

The table is not the analysis by itself
A two-by-two table is an organising device. What you calculate from it depends on the study design and the question.
For example, in a typical case-control study the investigator selects the number of cases and controls. The row or column totals therefore do not reconstruct population risks. In that setting, the odds ratio remains estimable, while risk and risk ratio generally are not.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 3 · Risk ratio: a relative comparison of risks
text:
LEARN 3 · Risk ratio: a relative comparison of risks
The attached CDC source defines the risk ratio (RR), also called relative risk, as the risk in the group of primary interest divided by the risk in the comparison group.
\[
RR = \frac{Risk_E}{Risk_U}
\]

Interpreting the null value
RR = 1.0
The risks are equal in the two groups.
RR > 1.0
Risk is higher in the numerator group.
RR < 1.0
Risk is lower in the numerator group.


Fictional example
During an outbreak, 45 of 150 people who attended Event A became ill. Among 200 people who attended Event B, 20 became ill.
\[
Risk_A = 45/150 = 0.30
\]
\[
Risk_B = 20/200 = 0.10
\]
\[
RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0
\]
Interpretation:

People in Event A had three times the risk of illness during the observation period compared with people in Event B.

Do not automatically write:

Event A caused three times more illness.

That causal wording requires more than the ratio alone.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 4 · The same ratio can hide very different public-health consequences
text:
LEARN 4 · The same ratio can hide very different public-health consequences
Consider two comparisons.

Comparison 1
Risk in exposed = 20%
Risk in unexposed = 10%
\[
RR = 2.0
\]
\[
RD = 20\%-10\%=10\text{ percentage points}
\]


Comparison 2
Risk in exposed = 2%
Risk in unexposed = 1%
\[
RR = 2.0
\]
\[
RD = 2\%-1\%=1\text{ percentage point}
\]
The relative association is identical in both examples: RR = 2.0.
But the absolute difference is very different.
This is why a report should not rely on the relative measure alone when an absolute measure can also be communicated meaningfully.

Relative measures answer: “How many times as high?”
Absolute measures answer: “How much higher?”

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
LEARN 5 · Risk difference / excess risk
The attached CDC chapter explicitly uses the term risk difference or excess risk in its vaccine-effectiveness section for the difference between risks in two groups. LIPPS expands that idea here because it is fundamental to interpreting absolute effects.
\[
RD = Risk_E - Risk_U
\]

Fictional example
Risk among exposed = 18%
Risk among unexposed = 6%
\[
RD = 0.18 - 0.06 = 0.12
\]
The risk difference is 0.12, or 12 percentage points.
Interpretation:

There were 12 additional cases per 100 people at risk in the exposed group compared with the unexposed group during the specified period.



Null value
For a difference measure, the null value is 0, not 1.

ratio measure → null = 1;
difference measure → null = 0.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 6 · Rate ratio: compare speeds, not just proportions
text:
LEARN 6 · Rate ratio: compare speeds, not just proportions
When the outcome is measured using person-time, the corresponding relative comparison is a rate ratio.
\[
Rate\ Ratio = \frac{Incidence\ rate_E}{Incidence\ rate_U}
\]
The CDC source uses the same interpretive framework as for a risk ratio:

1.0 → equal rates;
above 1.0 → higher rate in the numerator group;
below 1.0 → lower rate in the numerator group.


Fictional example
A cohort records:

exposed group: 48 cases during 2,400 person-years;
unexposed group: 30 cases during 3,000 person-years.

\[
Rate_E = 48/2400 = 0.020 = 20/1,000\ person\text{-}years
\]
\[
Rate_U = 30/3000 = 0.010 = 10/1,000\ person\text{-}years
\]
\[
Rate\ Ratio = 20/10 = 2.0
\]
Interpretation:

The incidence rate in the exposed group was twice the incidence rate in the unexposed group.

Do not call this a “twofold risk” if what you actually estimated was a rate ratio.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
LEARN 7 · Odds are not risks
Students often treat odds and risk as interchangeable. They are not.
If 20 people develop disease and 80 do not:

Risk
\[
Risk = 20/(20+80) = 0.20
\]
The risk is 20%.


Odds
\[
Odds = 20/80 = 0.25
\]
The odds are 0.25, or 1 to 4.
Risk compares cases with all people at risk.
Odds compare cases with non-cases.
When disease is rare, risk and odds are numerically close. As disease becomes more common, they diverge.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 8 · Odds ratio: the cross-product comparison
text:
LEARN 8 · Odds ratio: the cross-product comparison
From the two-by-two table:




Outcome +
Outcome −




Exposed
a
b


Unexposed
c
d



The odds ratio is:
\[
OR = \frac{a/b}{c/d} = \frac{ad}{bc}
\]
The attached CDC text notes that this is sometimes called the cross-product ratio because the diagonal products are compared.

Fictional example




Disease
No disease




Exposed
40
60


Unexposed
20
80



\[
OR = \frac{40\times80}{60\times20} = \frac{3200}{1200} = 2.67
\]
Interpretation:

The odds of disease among exposed participants were approximately 2.7 times the odds among unexposed participants.

That is the cleanest wording.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 9 · Why the odds ratio is central to case-control studies
text:
LEARN 9 · Why the odds ratio is central to case-control studies
In a typical case-control study, investigators deliberately enrol people with the outcome and people without it. The number of controls is usually chosen by the investigators rather than arising naturally from the population at risk.
Therefore, the sampled proportion of cases is not the population risk.
The attached CDC text makes the practical consequence explicit:

risk generally cannot be calculated directly from a typical case-control sample;
risk ratio generally cannot therefore be calculated directly;
rate ratio generally cannot be calculated directly; but
the odds ratio can be calculated.

That is why the odds ratio is the standard measure of association for the usual case-control design.

Design determines what can be estimated.
Do not choose a measure because it is familiar. Choose it because the sampling and follow-up structure permit it.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 10 · When OR approximates RR — and when it does not
text:
LEARN 10 · When OR approximates RR — and when it does not
The CDC chapter shows that when an outcome is uncommon, an odds ratio can be close to the corresponding risk ratio. It also warns that the more common the outcome, the further the odds ratio may be from the risk ratio.

Uncommon outcome
Risk exposed = 5%
Risk unexposed = 1%
\[
RR = 5.0
\]
The corresponding odds ratio is approximately 5.2 — very close.


Common outcome
Risk exposed = 60%
Risk unexposed = 20%
\[
RR = 3.0
\]
But:
\[
Odds_E = 0.60/0.40 = 1.5
\]
\[
Odds_U = 0.20/0.80 = 0.25
\]
\[
OR = 1.5/0.25 = 6.0
\]
The OR is 6.0, while the RR is 3.0.


The interpretation error
It would be incorrect to say:

“The exposed group was six times as likely to develop the outcome.”

The OR of 6 refers to odds, not risk.
When outcomes are common, this distinction becomes especially important.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LIPPS EXTENSION · Prevalence ratio in cross-sectional studies
text:
LIPPS EXTENSION · Prevalence ratio in cross-sectional studies
Source note: the attached CDC lesson used for Week 3 does not explicitly teach the prevalence ratio. LIPPS includes it as an extension because it is directly relevant to modern cross-sectional public-health analysis.
In a cross-sectional study, the investigator often measures the prevalence of an outcome in two groups.
\[
PR = \frac{Prevalence_E}{Prevalence_U}
\]

Fictional example
A survey finds hypertension in:

120 of 300 adults with high salt intake → 40%;
60 of 300 adults with lower salt intake → 20%.

\[
PR = 0.40/0.20 = 2.0
\]
Interpretation:

The prevalence of hypertension was twice as high among adults in the high-salt group as among adults in the lower-salt group at the time represented by the survey.

Notice the wording:
prevalence was twice as high — not “risk was twice as high” and not “high salt doubled the risk.”
A cross-sectional study usually cannot establish whether the exposure preceded the outcome.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 11 · Relative and absolute measures should be read together
text:
LEARN 11 · Relative and absolute measures should be read together
Suppose a preventive intervention reduces one-year disease risk from 4% to 2%.

Relative comparison
\[
RR = 0.02/0.04 = 0.50
\]
The intervention group had half the risk.


Absolute comparison
\[
RD = 0.02 - 0.04 = -0.02
\]
The absolute risk was 2 percentage points lower.
A communicator could truthfully say:

“Risk was reduced by 50%.”

But without the underlying risks, a reader may imagine a much larger absolute change than 4% to 2%.


LIPPS reporting rule
Where possible, report:
risk or rate in each group + relative measure + absolute measure + uncertainty.
That combination gives the reader much more information than a single dramatic ratio.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 12 · Attributable proportion among the exposed
text:
LEARN 12 · Attributable proportion among the exposed
The attached CDC source presents attributable proportion, also called attributable risk percent, as a measure of public-health impact.
A common formula is:
\[
AP_E = \frac{Risk_E - Risk_U}{Risk_E}\times100\%
\]
It can be expressed similarly using rates.

Fictional example
Risk among exposed = 30%
Risk among unexposed = 10%
\[
AP_E = \frac{0.30-0.10}{0.30}\times100 = 66.7\%
\]
Under a causal interpretation and assuming the groups are otherwise sufficiently comparable:

Approximately two-thirds of the disease occurrence among the exposed group could be attributed to the exposure.



Important restraint
The word attributable is stronger than “associated.” If the association is confounded, biased or non-causal, the attributable interpretation is not justified.
The attached source itself cautions that the measure relies on causal assumptions.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 13 · Vaccine efficacy and vaccine effectiveness
text:
LEARN 13 · Vaccine efficacy and vaccine effectiveness
The attached CDC text distinguishes:
Vaccine efficacy — performance under ideal conditions, such as a clinical trial.
Vaccine effectiveness — performance under usual field conditions.
Both are expressed as a proportionate reduction in disease among vaccinated people compared with unvaccinated people.
\[
VE = \frac{Risk_U - Risk_V}{Risk_U}\times100\%
\]
or equivalently:
\[
VE = (1-RR)\times100\%
\]
when the RR is defined as vaccinated risk divided by unvaccinated risk.

Fictional example
Risk vaccinated = 8%
Risk unvaccinated = 20%
\[
RR = 0.08/0.20 = 0.40
\]
\[
VE = (1-0.40)\times100 = 60\%
\]
Interpretation:

Disease occurrence was 60% lower among the vaccinated group relative to the unvaccinated group under the conditions represented by the study.

Again, the validity of a causal effectiveness claim depends on the design and control of alternative explanations.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 14 · Protective associations require careful wording
text:
LEARN 14 · Protective associations require careful wording
When a ratio is below 1, students sometimes become confused.
Suppose:
\[
RR = 0.70
\]
The exposed group has 70% of the risk observed in the comparison group.
The relative reduction is:
\[
1 - 0.70 = 0.30 = 30\%
\]
So one may say:

Risk was 30% lower in the exposed group.

Do not say the exposure “reduced risk by 0.70%.”
Likewise, if:
\[
OR = 0.70
\]
the clean interpretation is:

The odds were 30% lower in the exposed group.

Do not silently turn odds into risk.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 15 · Precision and the null value
text:
LEARN 15 · Precision and the null value
A point estimate is not the whole result.
A ratio of 2.0 can be estimated very precisely or very imprecisely. A risk difference of 5 percentage points can be tightly or loosely estimated.
For introductory interpretation, remember:

RR, rate ratio, OR, PR: null value = 1;
risk difference / prevalence difference: null value = 0.

Confidence intervals around these measures provide information about precision and the range of values compatible with the data and analysis assumptions.
Detailed interval estimation and critical appraisal are revisited later in the course. For now, avoid treating a point estimate as exact truth.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: LEARN 16 · Association is not automatically causation
text:
LEARN 16 · Association is not automatically causation
The attached CDC chapter states that measures such as risk ratios, rate ratios and odds ratios provide evidence about relationships between exposure and disease. That is not the same as proving that the exposure caused the disease.
A measured association can be influenced by:

selection processes;
measurement error;
confounding;
reverse temporality;
chance;
model choices; or
genuine causal effects.

Those issues are developed later in the course.

Language discipline
For an observational comparison, prefer:

“Exposure was associated with higher risk…”

rather than:

“Exposure increased risk…”

unless the design, analysis and assumptions support a causal interpretation.

LIPPS rule
The mathematical sign of an association does not tell you whether the relationship is causal.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: APPLY · Choose the measure before doing the arithmetic
text:
APPLY · Choose the measure before doing the arithmetic

Scenario A · Closed cohort
Two groups are followed for one year from a disease-free baseline. You know the number developing disease and the number initially at risk in each group.
Most direct relative measure: Risk ratio.
Useful absolute measure: Risk difference.


Scenario B · Unequal follow-up time
Two treatment groups contribute different amounts of person-time and new outcomes are counted.
Most direct relative measure: Rate ratio.


Scenario C · Case-control study
Investigators select 200 cases and 400 controls and compare prior exposure.
Natural measure: Odds ratio.


Scenario D · Cross-sectional survey
A survey measures current exposure and current hypertension status in a representative sample.
Natural descriptive relative measure: Prevalence ratio.
Causal caution: Temporality may be unclear.


Scenario E · Vaccine comparison
Risks are measured among vaccinated and unvaccinated groups.
Useful measures: Risk ratio, risk difference and vaccine efficacy/effectiveness where causal interpretation is appropriate.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: WORKED EXAMPLE · One outbreak table, several answers
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · One outbreak table, several answers
Consider a fictional foodborne-outbreak investigation among 180 event attendees.




Became ill
Did not become ill
Total




Ate goat stew
54
36
90


Did not eat goat stew
18
72
90




1. Risk among exposed
\[
54/90 = 0.60 = 60\%
\]


2. Risk among unexposed
\[
18/90 = 0.20 = 20\%
\]


3. Risk ratio
\[
RR = 0.60/0.20 = 3.0
\]
People who ate the goat stew had three times the risk of illness compared with those who did not.


4. Risk difference
\[
RD = 0.60-0.20 = 0.40
\]
There were 40 additional cases per 100 attendees among goat-stew eaters compared with non-eaters.


5. Odds ratio
\[
OR = \frac{54\times72}{36\times18}=6.0
\]
The odds of illness among goat-stew eaters were six times the odds among non-eaters.
Notice that the OR of 6 is much larger than the RR of 3 because the outcome is common.


6. Attributable proportion among the exposed
\[
AP_E = \frac{0.60-0.20}{0.60}\times100 = 66.7\%
\]
If the relationship is truly causal and alternative explanations are adequately addressed, approximately two-thirds of illness among exposed attendees could be attributed to the exposure.


What could fool us?
Even a dramatic table does not settle every question. Ask:

Was exposure recalled accurately?
Were all attendees identified?
Were cases defined consistently?
Did goat-stew eaters also share another exposure?
Could selection into the analysis differ by illness status?
Is the timing compatible with the suspected food vehicle?

This is exactly why evidence is never the whole story.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
section: GRADUATE DEEPEN · Crude, adjusted, marginal and conditional effects
text:
GRADUATE DEEPEN · Crude, adjusted, marginal and conditional effects
At graduate level, “adjusted odds ratio” is not a sufficient interpretation. You need to know what was adjusted for, why those variables were chosen, what model produced the estimate, and whether the model parameter corresponds to the scientific effect of interest.

Crude versus adjusted
A crude estimate compares the observed groups as they are. An adjusted estimate attempts to compare them after accounting for selected covariates. Adjustment can reduce confounding, but adjustment is not automatically improvement. Adjusting for a mediator can remove part of the effect you intended to estimate; adjusting for a collider can create an association that did not exist.


Marginal versus conditional effects
A marginal effect describes a population-average contrast, such as the risk under intervention A if the whole target population received A versus the risk if the whole population received B. A conditional effect describes a contrast among people with specified covariate values, often arising naturally from a regression coefficient.
The distinction matters because policy decisions often concern marginal population effects while conventional regression software returns conditional model parameters.


Odds-ratio non-collapsibility
The odds ratio has a special complication: conditional and marginal odds ratios can differ even without confounding. This is called non-collapsibility. Therefore, seeing an odds ratio change after adding a prognostic variable to a logistic model does not prove that the variable was a confounder.
This is one reason to avoid translating every logistic-regression odds ratio into causal language. Where possible, estimate and communicate risks, risk differences or risk ratios that map more directly to the decision problem.


Absolute effects belong beside relative effects
Suppose a treatment reduces 5-year disease risk from 20% to 10% in one population and from 2% to 1% in another. The risk ratio is 0.50 in both populations, but the risk differences are 10 and 1 percentage points. The intervention has very different absolute implications.
When the risk difference is causal and the horizon is meaningful, the number needed to treat is:
\[
NNT=\frac{1}{|RD|}
\]
with risk difference expressed as a proportion. NNT should not be reported without a time horizon, comparator and uncertainty interval.


Interaction depends on scale
Two exposures may interact on an additive scale but not a multiplicative scale, or vice versa. Public-health decisions often care about additive interaction because it addresses excess cases that might be prevented in a subgroup. Biological or mechanistic claims cannot be read directly from a regression-product term.

LIPPS interpretation sequence
Name the measure → give the numerical contrast → give the time horizon → distinguish relative from absolute effect → state whether the estimate is crude or adjusted → state whether a causal interpretation is justified.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
text:
PRACTISE · Check your reasoning

1. Which value is the null for a risk ratio?
A. 0
B. 1
C. 50
D. 100
Answer: B. A ratio of 1 means the two risks are equal.


2. Which value is the null for a risk difference?
A. 0
B. 1
C. −1
D. 100
Answer: A. A difference of zero means no absolute difference between the groups.


3. Risk is 30% in the exposed group and 10% in the unexposed group. What is the RR?
A. 0.20
B. 2.0
C. 3.0
D. 20
Answer: C. 0.30 / 0.10 = 3.0.


4. Using the same data, what is the risk difference?
A. 3 percentage points
B. 10 percentage points
C. 20 percentage points
D. 30 percentage points
Answer: C. 30% − 10% = 20 percentage points.


5. Which measure is most natural in a typical case-control study?
A. Incidence proportion
B. Risk ratio
C. Odds ratio
D. Point prevalence
Answer: C. The investigator determines the number of cases and controls, so population risks usually cannot be reconstructed directly.


6. Why should an OR of 4.0 not automatically be described as “four times the risk”?
A. Odds and risk are different quantities.
B. OR can never exceed 1.
C. Risk has no denominator.
D. OR is a difference measure.
Answer: A. The odds ratio compares odds, not risks.


7. In a cross-sectional survey, hypertension prevalence is 36% in Group A and 18% in Group B. What is the prevalence ratio?
A. 0.5
B. 1.0
C. 2.0
D. 18
Answer: C. 0.36 / 0.18 = 2.0.


8. A vaccine study gives RR = 0.25 for vaccinated versus unvaccinated participants. What is the corresponding relative vaccine efficacy/effectiveness?
A. 25%
B. 50%
C. 75%
D. 125%
Answer: C. (1 − 0.25) × 100 = 75%.

title: Measures of Association and Effect
Measures of Association and Effect
text:
WEEK 3 SUMMARY
The central sequence is:
Measure each group → compare the groups → choose relative and/or absolute expression → interpret in the language of the measure → check whether the design supports the claim.
Remember:
RR compares risks.
Rate ratio compares incidence rates.
OR compares odds.
PR compares prevalences.
Risk difference expresses absolute difference in risk.
Attributable proportion expresses the proportion of disease among exposed people attributable to the exposure under causal assumptions.
VE/effectiveness expresses relative reduction in disease among vaccinated people.
The measure is not the conclusion. It is one part of the evidence.

title: Epidemiology II
text:
Entry standard
This course assumes competence in disease-frequency measures, cohort/case-control/cross-sectional designs, bias and confounding, basic regression and R. It is designed to follow Epidemiology I, not replace it.
The goal is not to turn causal inference into a collection of recipes. The learner should be able to state the target estimand, identify the assumptions required to estimate it, choose an analysis that corresponds to that estimand, and explain how violations would affect interpretation.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
section: ORIENT · “The effect was significant in women but not men” is not an interaction test
text:
ORIENT · “The effect was significant in women but not men” is not an interaction test
Effect heterogeneity requires comparing effects, not comparing p-values. It also requires specifying the scale on which heterogeneity matters.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
LEARN 1 · Additive and multiplicative interaction
For binary exposures \(A\) and \(B\), additive interaction asks whether their joint excess risk differs from the sum of individual excess risks. One measure is the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI):
\[RERI=RR_{11}-RR_{10}-RR_{01}+1.\]
Multiplicative interaction asks whether the joint relative effect differs from the product of separate relative effects.
Public-health planning often benefits from additive interaction because it corresponds more directly to excess cases.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
LEARN 2 · Effect-measure modification
Effect modification is a property of the chosen measure and population. A treatment may have a constant relative effect but larger absolute benefit in higher-risk groups.
Report stratum-specific absolute and relative effects with confidence intervals. Avoid dichotomising continuous modifiers without strong justification.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
LEARN 4 · Mediator-outcome confounding
Natural direct and indirect effects require strong assumptions about confounding of the exposure-outcome, exposure-mediator and mediator-outcome relationships. Exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounders create additional complexity.
Therefore, “adjusting for the mediator and comparing coefficients” is not a general mediation analysis.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
section: LEARN 5 · Heterogeneous treatment effects and multiplicity
text:
LEARN 5 · Heterogeneous treatment effects and multiplicity
Exploring many subgroups creates false-positive findings and unstable estimates. Prespecify important modifiers, use shrinkage or hierarchical approaches where appropriate, and distinguish exploratory heterogeneity from confirmatory evidence.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
PHD EXTENSION
Modern heterogeneous-treatment-effect methods include causal forests and Bayesian hierarchical models. These methods can discover complex effect variation but still rely on identification assumptions and require careful external validation.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
APPLY
Using one intervention, specify a total-effect question, a mediation question and an effect-modification question. For each, define the estimand and explain why the same regression model cannot answer all three automatically.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Separate heterogeneity from mediation
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Separate heterogeneity from mediation
Suppose a community intervention reduces 1-year hypertension risk. You observe larger absolute benefit in older adults and hypothesise that medication adherence mediates part of the effect.
These are two different questions.

Effect modification analysis
Estimate standardised risks under intervention/control within prespecified age strata. Report both risk differences and risk ratios. If baseline risk is higher in older adults, absolute benefit can be larger even when the relative effect is constant.
A formal interaction contrast on the additive scale can be estimated by standardised risks rather than relying solely on product terms.


RERI
For binary exposure \(A\) and modifier \(B\) with a causal interpretation:
\[RERI=RR_{11}-RR_{10}-RR_{01}+1.\]
RERI > 0 suggests positive interaction on the additive scale relative to the reference group, under assumptions. Confidence intervals require appropriate delta-method, bootstrap or model-based calculations.


Mediation DAG
Draw \(A\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y\), with baseline confounders of each relation. Decide whether any mediator-outcome confounder is itself affected by exposure. If yes, conventional natural-effect mediation formulas can fail.


Controlled direct effect
Compare \(Y^{a,m}\) under two exposure levels while fixing mediator \(M\) to a specified value \(m\). This may be policy-relevant if the mediator could actually be controlled.


Natural effects
Natural direct effects compare exposure while setting the mediator to the value it would naturally take under a specified exposure state. These estimands rely on stronger cross-world assumptions and can be difficult to interpret for non-manipulable mediators.


Interventional effects
Stochastic/interventional mediation effects replace individual-level natural mediator values with draws from mediator distributions, sometimes avoiding the most problematic cross-world interpretation.


Avoiding subgroup fallacies
A significant effect in subgroup A and non-significant effect in subgroup B does not prove heterogeneity. Test the contrast directly and report confidence intervals for subgroup effects.


Multiplicity and prior plausibility
If 20 modifiers are tested, some “interactions” will appear by chance. Prespecify a small set grounded in biology, social theory or implementation logic. Treat post-hoc subgroup findings as exploratory unless replicated.


Doctoral extension · Principal stratification
When post-treatment events such as survival determine whether an outcome is defined, principal-stratification estimands compare latent groups defined by potential values of the post-treatment variable. These methods are conceptually powerful but often weakly identified without strong assumptions.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Choosing the scale that matters
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Choosing the scale that matters

Additive scale for impact
If treatment reduces risk from 30% to 20% in group A and from 3% to 2% in group B, both have RR≈0.67 but risk differences of −10 and −1 percentage points. Resource allocation may prioritise group A because more events are preventable.


Multiplicative scale for etiologic comparison
Relative effects can be useful when comparing across populations with different baseline risks. But homogeneity on a multiplicative scale does not imply homogeneity on the additive scale.


Standardised interaction
Fit a flexible outcome model with treatment, modifier and interaction, then predict counterfactual risks in each modifier stratum. Compute additive and multiplicative contrasts from predictions rather than relying solely on raw regression product terms.


Continuous modifiers
Avoid median splits. Estimate treatment effects across meaningful values of a continuous modifier using interaction splines or stratified standardisation, with simultaneous confidence bands if many points are shown.


Mediation and timing
Mediator measurement must occur after exposure and before outcome, and mediator-outcome confounders must be measured at the correct time. Cross-sectional mediator data cannot establish temporal mediation merely because software decomposes coefficients.


Proportion mediated
The “proportion mediated” can be unstable or nonsensical when direct and indirect effects have opposite signs or total effects are near zero. Report component effects and scales rather than relying on one percentage.


Policy mediation
Sometimes the useful question is not “how much is mediated?” but “what would happen if we intervened on the mediator distribution?” Interventional mediation estimands can align better with realistic policy interventions.

title: Interaction, Mediation and Heterogeneous Effects
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Effect heterogeneity, interaction and mediation answer different scientific questions
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Effect heterogeneity, interaction and mediation answer different scientific questions
Epidemiologists often use “interaction” loosely. At graduate level distinguish at least three ideas: statistical interaction in a chosen model, effect-measure modification across strata, and causal mechanisms involving joint interventions.

Additive interaction
For two binary exposures \(A\) and \(B\), additive interaction can be examined through risk differences. The relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) is:
\[RERI = RR_{11}-RR_{10}-RR_{01}+1.\]
A positive RERI indicates more joint effect on the risk-difference scale than expected from adding the individual excess risks. The attributable proportion due to interaction and synergy index provide related summaries.


Multiplicative interaction
A product term in a log-link model tests departure from multiplicativity of risks/rates; in logistic regression it tests multiplicativity of odds. Presence or absence of interaction can differ by scale. Therefore “there is no interaction” is incomplete without naming the scale.


Effect-measure modification
Report stratum-specific estimates with uncertainty rather than only a product-term p-value. A clinically important contrast may exist despite weak statistical evidence for heterogeneity, particularly in small subgroups.


Heterogeneity and transportability
Effect modifiers help explain why an intervention may perform differently across populations. Pre-specifying plausible modifiers can improve interpretation and transportability. Post hoc subgroup searches create multiplicity and selective-reporting problems.


Mediation questions
If \(A\) affects mediator \(M\), which affects \(Y\), one may ask about total effects, controlled direct effects, natural direct/indirect effects or interventional analogues. These estimands require different assumptions and have different policy interpretations.


Controlled direct effect
A controlled direct effect compares outcomes under different exposure values while fixing the mediator to a particular value for everyone:
\[E(Y^{1,m})-E(Y^{0,m}).\]
This may correspond to an intervention if setting \(M=m\) is meaningful.


Natural effects
Natural direct and indirect effects compare mediator values that would naturally arise under different exposure states. They require strong cross-world assumptions and are problematic when exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounders exist.


Interventional indirect effects
Interventional approaches replace person-specific cross-world mediator values with draws from mediator distributions under interventions. They can be more policy-relevant and avoid some cross-world constructs, though identification assumptions remain substantial.


Mediation versus adjustment
Do not “control for the mediator” in a standard regression and label the change in exposure coefficient the mediated effect. Nonlinearity, exposure-mediator interaction and mediator-outcome confounding make this decomposition generally invalid.


Heterogeneous treatment effects with machine learning
Causal forests and related methods can explore treatment-effect heterogeneity, but apparent subgroup variation can be noisy and non-replicable. Separate discovery from confirmation, use honest sample splitting/cross-fitting, and evaluate whether heterogeneity produces actionable treatment rules.


Equity
Effect heterogeneity across sex, socioeconomic position, geography or vulnerability should not be interpreted without considering differential baseline risk. A constant relative effect can generate much larger absolute benefit in high-risk groups. Equity decisions often require absolute effects and access constraints, not only subgroup interaction p-values.


MSc standard
Estimate and interpret interaction on additive and multiplicative scales, produce stratum-specific absolute effects, and distinguish effect modification from confounding.


PhD standard
Define mediation estimands formally, defend identification assumptions, address exposure-induced mediator-outcome confounding, and separate confirmatory heterogeneity analyses from exploratory subgroup discovery.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
Advanced Case-Control Methods
section: ORIENT · The case-control odds ratio has several possible targets
text:
ORIENT · The case-control odds ratio has several possible targets
Case-control efficiency comes from sampling outcomes unevenly. That efficiency is paid for with a more complicated link between sample quantities and population quantities.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text:
LEARN 1 · Incidence-density sampling
For each incident case, sample controls from individuals still at risk when the case occurs. Controls represent person-time at risk and may later become cases. Under this design, the exposure odds ratio estimates the incidence-rate ratio without requiring a rare disease.
This is often the cleanest conceptual foundation for nested case-control studies.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text:
LEARN 2 · Cumulative-incidence sampling
Controls are selected from people who remain non-cases over the risk period. The sample odds ratio approximates a risk ratio when disease is uncommon, but the approximation worsens as the outcome becomes common.
Do not teach the “rare disease assumption” as a universal property of case-control studies; it is tied to the sampling scheme and target measure.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
section: LEARN 3 · Matching and conditional logistic regression
text:
LEARN 3 · Matching and conditional logistic regression
Individual matching creates sets of cases and controls sharing matching variables. Conditional logistic regression conditions on the matched set, comparing exposure within sets. The matching variables may disappear from the regression coefficient table because their effect is conditioned out.
Matching can improve efficiency, but overmatching can erase useful exposure variation or make controls too similar to cases on variables related to exposure but not confounding.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text:
LEARN 4 · Case-cohort designs
A case-cohort study samples a subcohort from the baseline cohort and adds cases occurring outside the subcohort. Because the same subcohort can support analyses of several outcomes, case-cohort designs are attractive when biomarkers are expensive.
Weighted Cox-type methods account for the sampling. The analysis should preserve the cohort’s risk-set logic rather than treating the data as an ordinary cross-sectional case-control sample.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
section: LEARN 5 · Selection bias through control choice
text:
LEARN 5 · Selection bias through control choice
Hospital controls can be convenient but dangerous if the exposure influences the diseases that bring controls to hospital. Friend controls may be too similar to cases in socioeconomic or behavioural exposures. Population controls can have lower participation.
The correct control group is determined by the source population and case-ascertainment mechanism, not convenience.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text:
LEARN 6 · Exposure measurement after diagnosis
Recall bias is one form of differential measurement. More generally, disease status can influence record completeness, interviewer probing, biomarker availability or willingness to report sensitive exposures.
Prefer exposure data recorded before disease when feasible. If measurement differs by case status, conduct quantitative sensitivity analysis rather than only mention “recall bias.”

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text:
R LAB
Advanced Lab 2 — Risk-set sampling and matched analysis →

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
text:
PHD EXTENSION
Outcome-dependent sampling appears beyond classic case-control studies, including two-phase designs, case-cohort sampling and nested biomarker studies. Efficient analysis requires understanding the sampling probabilities and the full cohort quantity being targeted.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Design the control sampling before calculating an OR
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Design the control sampling before calculating an OR
Imagine a dynamic cohort of 100,000 adults followed for myocardial infarction. Stored blood samples make biomarker assays expensive. Rather than assay everyone, investigators identify all incident MIs and sample controls.

Incidence-density design
For each MI at time \(t\), sample controls from people still at risk at \(t\). Matching might be on age, sex and calendar time. A participant can be sampled as a control more than once and later become a case.
This surprises learners but is correct because controls sample person-time, not “people who will never become cases.” Excluding future cases from control eligibility would distort the risk set.


Conditional logistic model
With matched risk sets:
library(survival)
fit <- clogit(case ~ biomarker + smoking + strata(risk_set), data=ncc)
The model compares exposures within risk sets. The estimated odds ratio corresponds to an incidence-rate ratio under the incidence-density sampling design.


Matching ratio and efficiency
Adding controls per case increases precision, but returns diminish after roughly four controls per case in many simple settings. The optimal ratio depends on assay costs, case numbers, matching constraints and covariate distributions.


Countermatching
Sometimes controls are deliberately sampled to increase exposure variation within matched sets. This can improve efficiency for rare exposures but requires analysis weights based on the sampling scheme.


Case-cohort analysis
A random subcohort sampled at baseline can serve as the comparison group for multiple outcomes. Cases outside the subcohort are added. Because risk sets are reconstructed with sampling weights, standard Cox analysis without weights is not appropriate.


Two-phase designs
Expensive covariates can be measured in a phase-2 subsample selected using cheap phase-1 variables. Inverse-probability weighting or likelihood methods use known sampling probabilities to recover target estimates. This design is powerful when biospecimens or genotyping are expensive.


Control selection and transportability
If controls come from a hospital, the source population may be “people who would attend that hospital if they developed the disease,” not the geographic community. Make the catchment logic explicit.


Bias analysis for exposure misclassification
Suppose self-reported occupational exposure has sensitivity 0.75 among cases and 0.60 among controls, with specificity 0.90 in both. This differential sensitivity can bias the OR away from or toward the null. A probabilistic bias analysis can sample sensitivity/specificity values from plausible distributions and correct the 2×2 table repeatedly.


Doctoral extension · Semiparametric efficiency
Nested case-control and case-cohort designs can be analysed using weighted partial likelihood, pseudo-likelihood and augmented estimators. Methodological work asks how to use phase-1 information efficiently while retaining validity under the sampling design.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
section: SEMINAR NOTES · Sampling fractions and what can be recovered
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · Sampling fractions and what can be recovered
Case-control data contain deliberately distorted case fractions. Therefore intercepts and absolute risks from an ordinary logistic model do not represent population risks unless the sampling fractions are known and incorporated.

Recovering absolute risk
If the source cohort and case sampling fractions are known, weighted or likelihood-based methods can recover absolute risks. In a nested design, cohort incidence information may be available separately. Do not estimate PPV, prevalence or risk directly from a case-control sample whose case fraction was investigator-controlled.


Incidence-density OR
Under risk-set sampling, the odds of exposure among sampled cases versus controls correspond to the rate ratio because controls sample the person-time distribution of exposure. This is why no rare-disease approximation is required.


Matching variable paradox
A matched design forces case and control distributions to be similar on matching factors by construction. The association between a matching variable and disease cannot usually be estimated from the matched sample in the ordinary way. Matching variables were selected for design efficiency/confounding control, not substantive estimation.


Frequency matching
If cases and controls are frequency matched on age groups rather than individual sets, analyse with unconditional logistic regression while adjusting for the matching factor. Do not automatically use conditional logistic regression.


Selection diagrams for hospital controls
Draw hospitalisation \(H\) as a selection node. If exposure affects another condition that causes hospitalisation and outcome status also affects hospitalisation, conditioning on \(H=1\) can create collider bias. This is the graphical explanation for classic Berkson-type bias.


Rare exposure designs
Case-control studies can be efficient for rare outcomes, while cohort studies are efficient for rare exposures. If the exposure is rare, control sampling may yield too few exposed controls unless special sampling or large source populations are used.


Etiologic heterogeneity
When disease subtypes have different causes, combining them into one case definition can dilute associations. Polytomous logistic regression or subtype-specific case-control analyses may reveal etiologic heterogeneity, but multiple testing and subtype misclassification must be considered.

title: Advanced Case-Control Methods
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · The case-control odds ratio is created by the sampling design
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · The case-control odds ratio is created by the sampling design
Advanced case-control methods become much easier when controls are understood as a sample of the exposure experience of the source population, not simply “people without disease.” The validity of the odds ratio depends on how that sampling was performed.

Source population principle
Every case should arise from a population in which the selected controls could have become cases. A hospital control with a condition caused by the exposure of interest may distort exposure prevalence; neighbourhood controls may overmatch environmental or socioeconomic exposures; friend controls may overmatch behaviour. Convenience is not a design justification.


Three major control-sampling schemes
Cumulative-incidence sampling selects controls from people who remain non-cases at the end of follow-up. The resulting exposure odds ratio approximates the risk ratio under the rare-disease condition.
Incidence-density (risk-set) sampling selects controls from those at risk at the time each case occurs. A person can serve as a control before later becoming a case. The odds ratio estimates the incidence-rate ratio without requiring the disease to be rare.
Case-base (case-cohort) sampling selects controls from the source cohort at baseline, regardless of future case status. With appropriate analysis, this design can estimate risk or rate contrasts and enables one subcohort to support multiple outcomes.


Matching
Matching can improve efficiency and control design-stage confounding, but it creates an analysis obligation. Individually matched studies generally require conditional logistic regression or equivalent matched analysis. Matching does not remove confounding automatically; the matching factor has been conditioned on by design.
Overmatching can occur when controls are matched on a variable closely related to exposure but not a true confounder, reducing exposure contrast. Matching on a mediator or collider can introduce bias.


Conditional logistic regression
For matched sets, the conditional likelihood compares exposure configurations within risk sets or matched strata and removes nuisance intercepts. The resulting coefficient estimates a matched conditional odds ratio. Understand what was conditioned on before interpreting it.


Nested case-control studies
Within a defined cohort, risk-set sampling can drastically reduce biomarker assay costs while preserving valid rate-ratio estimation. Sampling fractions may vary, and specialised weighting may be needed for some estimands or secondary analyses.


Case-cohort studies
A random subcohort is selected at baseline, and all incident cases are included. Because cases outside the subcohort enter when they fail, standard Cox partial likelihood variance formulas are not automatically valid. Prentice-type weights and robust variance methods are commonly used.


Case-crossover design
Each case serves as their own control by comparing exposure during a hazard window with exposure during control windows. Time-invariant confounders are controlled by design, but time trends, carryover and selection of control periods are critical. This is suited to transient exposures with acute effects, not stable chronic exposures.


Recall and information bias
Case-control studies are especially vulnerable when exposure ascertainment occurs after disease. Differential recall, interviewer probing and proxy reporting can create spurious associations. Objective exposure records, blinded interviewers and identical instruments reduce—but do not eliminate—these concerns.


Selection diagrams
At doctoral level, draw the mechanism by which inclusion into the case-control sample depends on disease, exposure and covariates. Conditioning on sample inclusion can induce associations. The sampling design must be incorporated into the causal argument.


Worked example
Suppose 500 incident TB cases arise from a cohort of healthcare workers. For each case, four controls are sampled from workers still at risk on the diagnosis date. The exposure is recent work in a high-risk ward. Because controls are selected by incidence-density sampling, the matched OR estimates the rate ratio even if TB is not rare. Calling it a “rare disease approximation” would misunderstand the design.


MSc standard
Given a case-control paper, identify the source population, control-sampling scheme, matching structure, estimand and appropriate regression analysis.


PhD standard
Derive why risk-set sampling yields a rate-ratio estimate, critique selection mechanisms using causal diagrams, and specify weighted/robust analyses for nested case-control or case-cohort designs.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: ORIENT · Observational data do not become trial-like just because propensity scores are used
text:
ORIENT · Observational data do not become trial-like just because propensity scores are used
Design comes before adjustment. Quasi-experimental methods exploit assignment rules, timing or natural variation that can make counterfactual comparisons more credible.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 1 · Difference-in-differences
Difference-in-differences compares outcome changes in treated and comparison groups. The key assumption is that, absent treatment, trends would have evolved similarly.
Use multiple pre-treatment periods to examine trend plausibility. Modern DiD methods are needed when treatment timing varies and effects are heterogeneous; conventional two-way fixed-effects models can produce unintuitive weighted averages.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 2 · Interrupted time series
Interrupted time series estimates changes in level and trend after an intervention while using the pre-intervention series as a counterfactual trajectory. Model seasonality, autocorrelation and concurrent events. Controlled interrupted time series adds a comparison series when available.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 3 · Regression discontinuity
When treatment eligibility changes sharply at a cutoff, units just above and below the threshold may be comparable. The effect is local to the cutoff. Check for manipulation of the running variable, continuity of covariates and sensitivity to bandwidth and functional form.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 4 · Instrumental variables
A valid instrument influences treatment, is independent of unmeasured causes of the outcome, and affects the outcome only through treatment. Under additional monotonicity assumptions, IV methods can estimate a local average treatment effect among compliers.
Instrument validity is primarily a substantive argument; strong first-stage association alone is insufficient.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
LEARN 6 · New-user active-comparator designs
In pharmacoepidemiology, comparing new users of treatment A with new users of an alternative treatment for the same indication can improve exchangeability and align time zero better than comparing prevalent users with non-users.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · Vaccine policy
Suppose a vaccine is introduced in some districts earlier than others. A naïve post-introduction comparison is confounded by district differences. A stronger design might combine pre/post data, matched comparison districts and explicit trend assessment. If individual eligibility and vaccination dates are available, a target-trial emulation may be possible.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
text:
PHD EXTENSION
Advanced target-trial emulations address grace periods, sustained treatment, competing events, cloning/censoring/weighting and sequential trial emulation. The framework clarifies design but does not guarantee exchangeability.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: METHODS WORKSHOP · Design quasi-experiments as carefully as trials
text:
METHODS WORKSHOP · Design quasi-experiments as carefully as trials

Difference-in-differences event studies
With staggered intervention timing, estimate event-time effects relative to treatment adoption rather than relying on a single post indicator. Plot pre-treatment coefficients to assess trend plausibility and post-treatment dynamics.
Modern estimators group units by treatment cohort to avoid problematic weighting that can occur in conventional two-way fixed-effects models when effects vary over time.


Controlled interrupted time series
Add a comparison series unaffected by the intervention but exposed to similar secular forces. This improves protection against coincident national trends. Still assess whether the comparison itself experienced different shocks.


Regression discontinuity diagnostics
Before estimating an RD effect: - plot outcome against the running variable; - test for density manipulation near the cutoff; - inspect covariate continuity; - choose bandwidth transparently; - compare local linear specifications; - report the effect as local to the threshold.


Instrument strength and weak instruments
A weak instrument produces unstable estimates and magnifies bias. Report first-stage strength but do not confuse strength with validity. An invalid strong instrument is worse than a weak valid one.


Target-trial specification table
For observational emulation, create a table with columns Protocol component, Ideal trial, Available data, Emulation rule, Remaining deviation. This makes compromises visible.


Time zero alignment
Many observational biases are time-zero problems: - eligibility measured before exposure classification; - covariates measured after treatment begins; - treatment assignment defined using future exposure; - follow-up beginning at different times by group.
Fix these in design before modelling.


Sequential target trials
When eligibility recurs over time, each eligible person-time can initiate a new emulated trial. Pool sequential trials and use appropriate weighting/standard errors. This increases information but requires careful treatment of repeated participation.


Active comparator
Choose a comparator with the same indication when possible. Comparing two plausible treatment choices can reduce confounding by healthcare-seeking and indication compared with treated-versus-untreated contrasts.


Falsification analyses
Before claiming a quasi-experimental effect, test outcomes that should not respond at the intervention date, placebo intervention dates or unaffected subgroups where appropriate. These do not prove validity but can reveal implausible patterns.


Doctoral extension · Synthetic controls
When one or few units receive an intervention, synthetic-control methods construct a weighted combination of untreated units that reproduces the pre-intervention trajectory. Inference and robustness require careful donor-pool selection and placebo analyses.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: SEMINAR NOTES · When quasi-experimental assumptions break
text:
SEMINAR NOTES · When quasi-experimental assumptions break

DiD and anticipation
If facilities change behaviour before official intervention start because they know rollout is coming, the pre-period is contaminated. Redefine treatment timing or model anticipation windows.


Spillovers
Comparison areas may be affected by the intervention through patient movement, media or neighbouring policy. This violates no-interference assumptions and can attenuate or distort estimates.


Concurrent shocks
A national drug shortage beginning at the same time as an intervention can mimic an intervention effect. Controlled series and negative-control outcomes can help diagnose this.


RD manipulation
If clinicians can manipulate the running variable to cross an eligibility threshold, units around the cutoff are no longer quasi-random. Inspect density and institutional rules.


IV exclusion restriction
Distance to facility may affect outcome through access to other services, violating exclusion. Physician prescribing preference may correlate with quality of care. Instruments require deep institutional knowledge.


Target-trial data sufficiency
A database may lack exact eligibility dates, treatment start, reasons for treatment or time-varying confounders. Do not force target-trial language onto data that cannot emulate key protocol components.


Protocol deviations table
For each target-trial component, classify emulation quality as close, approximate, or unavailable and describe likely bias. This is more informative than a generic limitations paragraph.


Estimating policy effects
Quasi-experiments often estimate local effects tied to a threshold, treated region or rollout period. Avoid transporting them automatically to populations far from the assignment mechanism.

title: Quasi-experiments and Target-Trial Emulation
section: ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Strong observational inference starts by designing the comparison
text:
ADVANCED SYNTHESIS · Strong observational inference starts by designing the comparison
Quasi-experimental methods are valuable because they seek sources of variation that make treatment groups more comparable by design, rather than relying entirely on statistical adjustment after exposure has occurred.

Difference-in-differences estimand
For two groups and two periods, the basic DiD contrast is:
\[[E(Y_{post}\mid G=1)-E(Y_{pre}\mid G=1)]-[E(Y_{post}\mid G=0)-E(Y_{pre}\mid G=0)].\]
The critical identifying assumption is parallel untreated trends, not equality of baseline outcome levels. Multiple pre-periods help assess plausibility but cannot prove what post-treatment counterfactual trends would have been.


Staggered adoption
When units adopt intervention at different times and treatment effects vary, conventional two-way fixed-effects estimators can combine comparisons with negative or unintuitive weights, including already-treated groups acting as controls. Use cohort/time-specific estimators designed for staggered treatment.


Interrupted time series
Segmented regression may model level and slope changes:
\[Y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1t+\beta_2I_t+\beta_3(t\times I_t)+\epsilon_t.\]
Account for seasonality, autocorrelation, nonlinearity and changes in measurement. The intervention date should be substantively justified, and a controlled series can help distinguish the intervention from coincident shocks.


Regression discontinuity
Sharp RD identifies a local effect when treatment changes deterministically at a cutoff; fuzzy RD uses the cutoff as an instrument when treatment probability jumps but compliance is imperfect. Use local polynomial methods, report bandwidth choices and inspect manipulation around the threshold.


Instrumental variables
A valid IV requires relevance, independence from unmeasured outcome causes, and exclusion of pathways to outcome other than through treatment. Under monotonicity, a binary IV often identifies a local average treatment effect among compliers. The estimand may not generalise to always-takers, never-takers or other populations.


Target-trial emulation protocol
Specify eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment procedure, time zero, follow-up, outcome, causal contrast and analysis. Then map each ideal component to observable data. This reveals where observational emulation deviates from the trial question.


New-user active-comparator design
Restricting to people initiating alternative treatments for the same indication can reduce confounding by disease severity, healthcare access and treatment indication. Align covariate assessment before initiation and follow from a common time zero.


Grace periods and adherence
A protocol allowing treatment initiation within 30 days cannot classify exposure using future information without care. Clone-censor-weight or sequential-trial approaches can emulate strategies with grace periods and sustained adherence.


Emulating intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects
Observational data can target an assignment-like effect based on initiation strategy or a sustained-treatment effect. The latter requires adjustment for post-baseline adherence and censoring processes. Clearly distinguish them.


Falsification and robustness
Use negative-control outcomes, placebo intervention dates, alternative comparison groups, bandwidths, donor pools or pre-trend windows as design-specific stress tests. Robustness across arbitrary specifications is less meaningful than robustness across scientifically plausible alternatives.


MSc standard
Construct and analyse a simple DiD or interrupted-time-series study, articulate its identifying assumptions and perform at least two design-specific diagnostics.


PhD standard
Handle staggered adoption, local estimands, weak instruments or complex target-trial strategies; explicitly map protocol deviations; and justify why the quasi-experimental variation plausibly identifies the stated causal effect.

title: Standardisation and the parametric g-formula
text: EPIDEMIOLOGY II · LAB 01

title: Standardisation and the parametric g-formula
text:
LAB PROTOCOL · Graduate submission standard

Epidemiological question
What is the marginal causal risk under each treatment strategy after standardising over measured baseline confounders?


Before opening R
Write down the target population, exposure/treatment contrast, outcome, time horizon and effect measure. State the design and the assumptions that would make the proposed estimate meaningful. This paragraph is part of the submission: code without an estimand is incomplete.


Required analysis products
Fit a prespecified outcome model, generate counterfactual predictions under A=1 and A=0, report marginal risks/RD/RR with uncertainty, and compare with the crude contrast.
Every numerical result should be accompanied by a plain-language interpretation. Avoid reporting software output as though coefficients interpret themselves. If a model is used, state the link function, covariates, rationale for adjustment and how uncertainty was calculated.


Diagnostics that must appear in the report
Inspect overlap, functional form, interactions, extreme covariate patterns and whether predictions rely on unsupported extrapolation.
A diagnostic is not a ceremonial plot. State what failure it is intended to reveal and what you would change if that failure were present.


Reproducibility requirements
Your submission should run from a clean R session. Use relative paths, set no user-specific working directory, keep data cleaning separate from analysis, label derived variables, and generate the final tables/figures from code. Include sessionInfo() or an equivalent dependency record. Do not manually copy numbers from the console into the final table.


Interpretation discipline
End with four statements: 1. Estimate: what was estimated, on what scale and with what uncertainty? 2. Assumptions: which design/identification assumptions matter most? 3. Diagnostics: what evidence supports or challenges those assumptions? 4. Claim: what can be concluded, and what stronger claim would not be justified?


PhD extension
Use flexible nuisance modelling or bootstrap/influence-function inference, then compare with a simpler parametric model to distinguish model sensitivity from sampling uncertainty.


Suggested marking rubric (20 marks)

estimand/design logic — 4
reproducible data management and code — 3
correct analysis — 5
diagnostics/sensitivity analysis — 4
interpretation and limits of inference — 4

A technically correct model with an incoherent causal question should not receive a high distinction.

title: Survival, competing risks and time-updated covariates

Epidemiological question
How should a time-to-event effect be estimated when covariates change, competing events occur or proportional hazards is doubtful?


Before opening R
Write down the target population, exposure/treatment contrast, outcome, time horizon and effect measure. State the design and the assumptions that would make the proposed estimate meaningful. This paragraph is part of the submission: code without an estimand is incomplete.


Required analysis products
Report survival/cumulative incidence, Cox or alternative model results, PH diagnostics, and at least one absolute contrast such as risk at time t or RMST.
Every numerical result should be accompanied by a plain-language interpretation. Avoid reporting software output as though coefficients interpret themselves. If a model is used, state the link function, covariates, rationale for adjustment and how uncertainty was calculated.


Diagnostics that must appear in the report

A diagnostic is not a ceremonial plot. State what failure it is intended to reveal and what you would change if that failure were present.

Use relative paths, set no user-specific working directory, keep data cleaning separate from analysis, label derived variables, and generate the final tables/figures from code. Include sessionInfo() or an equivalent dependency record. Do not manually copy numbers from the console into the final table.

Diagnostics: what evidence supports or challenges those assumptions? 4. Claim: what can be concluded, and what stronger claim would not be justified?

title: Time-varying treatment and marginal structural weighting
text: EPIDEMIOLOGY II · LAB 05

title: Time-varying treatment and marginal structural weighting
text:
LAB PROTOCOL · Graduate submission standard

Epidemiological question
What is the effect of a sustained treatment strategy when time-varying confounders are themselves affected by earlier treatment?


Before opening R
Write down the target population, exposure/treatment contrast, outcome, time horizon and effect measure. State the design and the assumptions that would make the proposed estimate meaningful. This paragraph is part of the submission: code without an estimand is incomplete.


Required analysis products
Construct person-period data, estimate treatment/censoring probabilities, calculate stabilised cumulative weights, fit a marginal structural model and report weight diagnostics over time.
Every numerical result should be accompanied by a plain-language interpretation. Avoid reporting software output as though coefficients interpret themselves. If a model is used, state the link function, covariates, rationale for adjustment and how uncertainty was calculated.


Diagnostics that must appear in the report
Check sequential positivity, extreme cumulative weights, treatment-history definition, censoring and whether standard time-updated regression controls a treatment-affected confounder.
A diagnostic is not a ceremonial plot. State what failure it is intended to reveal and what you would change if that failure were present.


Reproducibility requirements
Your submission should run from a clean R session. Use relative paths, set no user-specific working directory, keep data cleaning separate from analysis, label derived variables, and generate the final tables/figures from code. Include sessionInfo() or an equivalent dependency record. Do not manually copy numbers from the console into the final table.


Interpretation discipline
End with four statements: 1. Estimate: what was estimated, on what scale and with what uncertainty? 2. Assumptions: which design/identification assumptions matter most? 3. Diagnostics: what evidence supports or challenges those assumptions? 4. Claim: what can be concluded, and what stronger claim would not be justified?


PhD extension
Compare MSM results with conventional adjustment and explain the direction/mechanism of any difference; optionally emulate a dynamic treatment rule.


Suggested marking rubric (20 marks)

estimand/design logic — 4
reproducible data management and code — 3
correct analysis — 5
diagnostics/sensitivity analysis — 4
interpretation and limits of inference — 4

A technically correct model with an incoherent causal question should not receive a high distinction.

LIPPS LEARN · EPIDEMIOLOGY II · WEEK 02





Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text: Advanced MSc / PhD Causal methods

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: ORIENT · Adjustment is a transformation of the comparison
text:
ORIENT · Adjustment is a transformation of the comparison
Suppose treated patients are older and sicker than untreated patients. A crude risk difference mixes treatment effects with baseline prognosis. Adjustment aims to reconstruct a comparison in which prognosis is balanced according to a defined target population.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
section: LEARN 1 · Stratification as the conceptual foundation
text:
LEARN 1 · Stratification as the conceptual foundation
Within levels of confounders \(L\), compare treated and untreated outcomes, then standardise stratum-specific estimates to a target covariate distribution.
For a binary outcome, the standardised risk under treatment \(a\) can be written:
\[P(Y^a=1)=\sum_l P(Y=1\mid A=a,L=l)P(L=l).\]
This is the g-formula for a simple point treatment. Regression is often used because direct stratification becomes sparse with many covariates.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 2 · Outcome regression and g-computation
Fit a model for the outcome conditional on exposure and confounders. Then create two copies of the study population: set everyone to treatment and predict outcomes; set everyone to no treatment and predict again. Average predictions within each scenario.
This separates modelling from estimand construction. The regression coefficients are intermediate quantities; the final marginal risks can be more interpretable for public-health decisions.
fit <- glm(outcome ~ treatment + age + severity + facility,
           family = binomial(), data = d)
d1 <- transform(d, treatment = 1)
d0 <- transform(d, treatment = 0)
r1 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata=d1, type="response"))
r0 <- mean(predict(fit, newdata=d0, type="response"))
c(RD=r1-r0, RR=r1/r0)

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 3 · Model dependence
Outcome-regression standardisation is valid only if the outcome model is sufficiently correct in the parts of covariate space used for prediction. Flexible modelling can reduce rigid functional-form assumptions, but all methods still require data support.
Check continuous covariate form, interactions that matter for outcome prediction, influential observations and extrapolation into unsupported regions.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 4 · Conditional versus marginal targets
A logistic-regression coefficient estimates a conditional log odds ratio under the model. Standardised risks create a marginal, population-average contrast. These quantities need not agree numerically even without confounding because odds ratios are non-collapsible.
Decide whether the scientific question is about an individual covariate-defined stratum or a population-average intervention effect.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
LEARN 5 · Standard population choice
You can standardise to the study population, exposed population, unexposed population or an external target population. Each choice defines a different estimand.
The average treatment effect (ATE) standardises to the whole target population. The average treatment effect among the treated (ATT) standardises to the treated population. Do not use these labels without defining the population.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
WORKED EXAMPLE · Hypertension outreach
A programme compares community outreach with usual facility-based screening. Outreach communities are younger and more urban. Crude detection is higher with outreach. The analysis models 6-month diagnosis as a function of strategy, age, sex, urbanicity and baseline care access, then standardises to the entire eligible population.
Report: standardised risk under outreach, standardised risk under usual care, risk difference and risk ratio. Then state that causal interpretation requires no important unmeasured confounding and adequate overlap.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
text:
WHAT COULD FOOL US?

Treating every baseline predictor as a confounder.
Using data-driven covariate selection without a causal model.
Interpreting conditional odds ratios as population-average risk ratios.
Standardising to an undefined population.
Ignoring unsupported combinations of confounders and treatment.

title: Standardisation and Confounding Adjustment
